1: This Official Statement is provided to furnish information in connection with the offering by the Houston Independent School
1: District (the “District”) of its $342,790,000 Limited Tax Refunding Bonds, Series 2026 (the “Bonds”).
1: Payment Terms…The Bonds will mature as shown on page i hereof. Interest on the Bonds will accrue from the Delivery Date
1: (as defined below), will be payable February 15 and August 15 of each year, commencing August 15, 2026, until maturity, and
1: will be calculated on the basis of a 360-day year consisting of twelve 30-day months. The Bonds will be issued as fully registered
1: obligations in denominations of $5,000 or any integral multiple thereof for any one stated maturity. The definitive Bonds will be
1: initially registered and delivered only to Cede & Co., the nominee of The Depository Trust Company, New York, New York (“DTC”)
1: pursuant to the book-entry-only system described herein. Beneficial ownership of the Bonds may be acquired in authorized
1: denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples thereof. No physical delivery of the Bonds will be made to the beneficial
1: owners thereof. The initial Paying Agent/Registrar is The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, National Association. See
1: “THE BONDS - Paying Agent/Registrar.” Principal of, premium, if any, and interest on the Bonds will be payable by the Paying
1: Agent/Registrar to Cede & Co., which will make distribution of the amounts so paid to the participating members of DTC for
1: subsequent payment to the beneficial owners of the Bonds. See “APPENDIX C - BOOK-ENTRY-ONLY SYSTEM” herein.
1: Authority for Issuance…The Bonds are issued pursuant to the Constitution and general laws of the State of Texas (the “State”),
1: including particularly Chapters 1207 and 1371, Texas Government Code, as amended (together, the “Act”), and an order adopted
1: by the School Board of the District (the “Board”) on November 13, 2025, authorizing the issuance of the Bonds (the “Bond Order”).
1: As permitted by the Act, in the Bond Order the Board delegated pricing of the Bonds and certain other matters to an authorized
1: official of the District who approved and executed a pricing certificate that contains the final pricing information for the Bonds
1: on May 4, 2026 (the “Pricing Certificate”). The Bond Order and the Pricing Certificate are collectively referred to herein as the
1: “Order,” except as otherwise indicated herein. See “THE BONDS - Authority for Issuance.”
1: Security and Source of Payment…The Bonds are direct obligations of the District, payable from a continuing direct annual
1: ad valorem tax levied, within the limits prescribed by law, on all taxable property located within the District, as provided in
1: the Order. See “THE BONDS – Security and Source of Payment.” See also “THE SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM AS APPLIED
1: TO THE DISTRICT.” The District received conditional approval from the Texas Education Agency for the Bonds
1: to be guaranteed by the Permanent School Fund Guarantee Program of the State of Texas, which guarantee will
1: automatically become effective upon approval of the Bonds by the Attorney General of Texas. See “THE PERMANENT
1: SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM” and “APPENDIX D – THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE
1: PROGRAM.”
1: Purpose…Proceeds from the sale of the Bonds will be used to (i) refund a portion of the District’s outstanding debt, as more
1: particularly described in SCHEDULE I – SCHEDULE OF REFUNDED BONDS (the “Refunded Bonds”) in order to lower the
1: overall debt service requirements of the District, and (ii) pay the costs associated with the issuance of the Bonds. See “PLAN OF
1: FINANCING – Purpose of the Bonds.”
1:                                                See Maturity Schedule on Page i
1: No Redemption… The Bonds are not subject to redemption prior to stated maturity.
1: Legality and Delivery…The Bonds are offered for delivery when, as and if issued and received by the underwriters listed below
1: (the “Underwriters”) and subject to the approving opinion of the Attorney General of Texas and the opinion of Jackson Walker
1: LLP, Houston, Texas, Bond Counsel. Certain legal matters will be passed upon for the District by Bracewell LLP, Houston, Texas,
1: Disclosure Counsel. Certain legal matters will be passed upon for the Underwriters by Winstead PC, Houston, Texas, and Cantu
1: Harden Montoya LLP, Houston, Texas, Co-Counsel for the Underwriters. It is expected that the Bonds will be available for
1: delivery through DTC on or about May 27, 2026 (the “Delivery Date”).

5:                                                                  OFFICIAL STATEMENT SUMMARY
5: This summary is subject in all respects to the more complete information and definitions contained or incorporated in this Official Statement
5: (which includes the Schedule and Appendices hereto). The offering of the Bonds to potential investors is made only by means of this entire
5: Official Statement. No person is authorized to detach this summary from this Official Statement or to otherwise use it without the entire
5: Official Statement (which includes the Schedule and Appendices hereto).
5: THE DISTRICT .............................................      Houston Independent School District (the “District”), a political subdivision of the State of
5:                                                                 Texas (the “State”) located within Harris County, is the nation’s tenth largest public school
5:                                                                 system, and the largest school district in the State. The District comprises 333 square miles
5:                                                                 within Harris County, Texas and includes approximately 51% of the current geographic area
5:                                                                 of the City of Houston, Texas, and all or part of four other cities or villages, and certain
5:                                                                 unincorporated areas which include all or part of five utility districts. See “INTRODUCTION
5:                                                                 - THE DISTRICT.”
5: THE BONDS .................................................     The $342,790,000 Limited Tax Refunding Bonds, Series 2026 (the “Bonds”) mature as shown
5:                                                                 on page i hereof. Interest on the Bonds accrues from the Delivery Date (as defined on the
5:                                                                 cover page) and is payable August 15, 2026 and each February 15 and August 15 thereafter
5:                                                                 until maturity. See “THE BONDS - DESCRIPTION OF THE BONDS.”
5: AUTHORITY FOR ISSUANCE .........................                The Bonds are issued pursuant to the Constitution and general laws of the State, including
5:                                                                 particularly Chapters 1207 and 1371, Texas Government Code, as amended, and an order
5:                                                                 adopted by the School Board of the District (the “Board”) on November 13, 2025, authorizing
5:                                                                 the issuance of the Bonds in which the Board delegated pricing of the Bonds and certain other
5:                                                                 matters to an authorized official of the District who approved and executed a pricing
5:                                                                 certificate that contains the final pricing information for the Bonds on May 4, 2026 (together,
5:                                                                 the “Order”). See “THE BONDS - AUTHORITY FOR ISSUANCE.”
5: SECURITY FOR THE BONDS .........................                The Bonds constitute direct obligations of the District, payable from a continuing direct
5:                                                                 annual ad valorem tax levied, within the limits prescribed by law, on all taxable property
5:                                                                 within the District. See “THE BONDS – SECURITY AND SOURCE OF PAYMENT.” Also see
5:                                                                 “STATE AND LOCAL FUNDING OF SCHOOL DISTRICTS IN TEXAS” and “CURRENT
5:                                                                 PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM” for a discussion of recent developments in State
5:                                                                 law affecting the financing of school districts in the State. Additionally, the District received
5:                                                                 conditional approval for the payment of the Bonds to be guaranteed by the Permanent School
5:                                                                 Fund of the State of Texas. See “THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE
5:                                                                 PROGRAM” and “APPENDIX D – THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE
5:                                                                 PROGRAM.”
5: USE OF PROCEEDS.......................................          Proceeds from the sale of the Bonds will be used to (i) refund a portion of the District’s
5:                                                                 outstanding debt, as more particularly described in SCHEDULE I – SCHEDULE OF
5:                                                                 REFUNDED BONDS (the “Refunded Bonds”) in order to lower the overall debt service
5:                                                                 requirements of the District and (ii) pay the costs associated with the issuance of the Bonds.
5:                                                                 See “PLAN OF FINANCING.”
5: PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE...                              The District received conditional approval from the Texas Education Agency for the Bonds
5:                                                                 to be guaranteed by the corpus of the Permanent School Fund of the State of Texas. See
5:                                                                 “THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM” and “APPENDIX D –
5:                                                                 THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM.”
5: NO REDEMPTION ........................................          The Bonds are not subject to redemption prior to stated maturity.
5: TAX MATTERS ............................................        In the opinion of Bond Counsel, under existing law, interest on the Bonds (i) is excludable
5:                                                                 from gross income for federal income tax purposes under section 103 of the Internal Revenue
5:                                                                 Code of 1986, as amended, and (ii) is not an item of tax preference for purposes of the
5:                                                                 alternative minimum tax on individuals. See “TAX MATTERS” herein, including
5:                                                                 information regarding potential alternative minimum tax consequences for corporations.
5: RATINGS......................................................   The Bonds are rated “Aaa” by Moody’s Ratings Inc. (“Moody’s”) and “AAA” by S&P Global
5:                                                                 Ratings, a division of Standard & Poor’s Financial Services LLC (“S&P”) by virtue of the
5:                                                                 guarantee by the Permanent School Fund of the State of Texas. See “OTHER
5:                                                                 INFORMATION – RATINGS,” “THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE
5:                                                                 PROGRAM” and “APPENDIX D – THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE
5:                                                                 PROGRAM.” The District’s outstanding tax-supported debt, without consideration of the
5:                                                                 Permanent School Fund Guarantee or other credit enhancement, is rated “Aaa” by Moody’s
5:                                                                 and “AA+” by S&P.
5: BOOK-ENTRY-ONLY SYSTEM .....................                    The definitive Bonds will be initially registered and delivered only to Cede & Co., the
5:                                                                 nominee of The Depository Trust Company (“DTC”) pursuant to the book-entry-only system
5:                                                                 described herein. Beneficial ownership of the Bonds may be initially acquired in
5:                                                                 denominations of $5,000. No physical delivery of the Bonds will be made to the beneficial
5:                                                                 owners thereof. Principal of, premium, if any, and interest on the Bonds will be payable by
5:                                                                                        iv

6:                                                        Agent/Registrar, to Cede & Co., which will make distribution of the amounts so paid to the
6:                                                        participating members of DTC for subsequent payment to the beneficial owners of the Bonds.
6:                                                        See “APPENDIX C - BOOK-ENTRY-ONLY SYSTEM.”
6: PAYMENT RECORD .....................................   The District has never defaulted in payment of its debt, including its tax-supported debt.

9:                                                                    INTRODUCTION
9: This Official Statement (the “Official Statement”), which includes the cover page, the Schedule and Appendices hereto, provides certain information
9: regarding the issuance by the Houston Independent School District (the “District”) of its $342,790,000 Limited Tax Refunding Bonds, Series 2026 (the
9: “Bonds”). Capitalized terms used in this Official Statement have the same meanings assigned to such terms in the order adopted by the School Board
9: (the “Board”) of the Houston Independent School District (the “District”) on November 13, 2025, authorizing the issuance of the Bonds (the “Bond
9: Order”). In the Bond Order, the Board delegated pricing of the Bonds and certain other matters to an authorized official of the District who approved
9: and executed a pricing certificate that contains the final pricing information for the Bonds on May 4, 2026 (the “Pricing Certificate”). The Bond Order
9: and the Pricing Certificate are collectively referred to herein as the “Order,” except as otherwise indicated herein.
9: The District received conditional approval from the Texas Education Agency for the Bonds to be guaranteed by the corpus of the Permanent School
9: Fund of the State of Texas.
9: There follows in this Official Statement descriptions of the Bonds and certain information regarding the District and its finances. All descriptions of
9: documents contained herein are only summaries and are qualified in their entirety by reference to each such document. Copies of such documents may
9: be obtained from the District’s Municipal Advisor, Estrada Hinojosa, Houston, Texas by electronic mail or upon payment of reasonable copying,
9: handling, and delivery charges.
9: This Official Statement speaks only as of its date, and the information contained herein is subject to change. A copy of the final Official Statement for
9: the Bonds will be submitted to the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board (“MSRB”) through its Electronic Municipal Market Access (“EMMA”)
9: System. See “CONTINUING DISCLOSURE OF INFORMATION” for a description of the District’s undertaking to provide certain information on
9: a continuing basis.
9: THE DISTRICT
9: The District, an independent school district and political subdivision of the State of Texas (the “State”), comprises approximately 333 square miles
9: within Harris County, Texas. The District encompasses approximately 51% of the current geographic area of the City of Houston, Texas (the “City”),
9: and all or part of four other cities or villages, and certain unincorporated areas which include all or part of five utility districts.
9: The District is the nation’s tenth largest public school system and the largest school district in the State. Harris County, certain county-wide political
9: entities, the City, and the various cities, villages and utility districts within the District each have authority to levy ad valorem taxes. See “TABLE 7 –
9: ESTIMATED OVERLAPPING DEBT.”
9: The District operates 274 campuses, which consist of 8 early childhood centers, 159 elementary schools, 39 middle schools, 37 high schools and 31
9: combination/alternative sites. The District’s curriculum focuses on students graduating with the necessary skills to contribute to the global workforce
9: and emphasizes art, literacy, dual language, technology, including community and business partnerships for college and career readiness. The District’s
9: program to support underserved and underperforming District schools to increase student achievement is named the New Education System (“NES”)
9: and provides high-quality instruction, diverse courses to extend student experiences, and ensures individualized support to meet each child's unique
9: needs.
9: DISTRICT ENROLLMENT
9: Over the past five school years, student enrollment in the District has declined. In school year 2020-2021, the District’s enrollment was approximately
9: 196,943 and in school year 2025-2026, the District’s enrollment was approximately 168,812, a reduction of approximately 28,131 students or 14.3%
9: over this five year period. The reduction is attributable to many factors, including for example, a decline in pre-kindergarten enrollment, rising housing
9: costs, demographic changes and increasing competition with charter schools and private education. For the 2025-2026 school year, the District’s
9: enrollment decreased by 7,915 students from the 2024-2025 school year, exceeding the District’s 2025-2026 budget’s estimated reduction of
9:                                                                             1
9: 
10: approximately 6,700 students. As of March 24, 2026, the District’s enrollment was approximately 166,608. See the District’s “Annual Comprehensive
10: Financial Report for the Fiscal Year ended June 30, 2025 – Statistical Section – 2025 Operating Information.”
10: Ongoing enrollment reductions have required the consolidation of certain campuses. Specifically, the District is consolidating under-enrolled campuses
10: as part of a cost-reduction initiative. Such initiative is expected to yield long-term operational efficiencies. In February 2026, the District’s School
10: Board unanimously voted to close 12 schools at the end of the 2025-2026 school year.
10: The District continues to develop strategies to address student enrollment by, for example, hosting community-based enrollment events, updating the
10: District’s enrollment website, increasing use of social media, tracking progress of students in the enrollment process, creating a student enrollment
10: department, providing enrollment application assistance, conducting quarterly reviews of student/parent exit survey data, canvassing neighborhoods in
10: the District and developing how to guides and videos for families. As further described in “THE SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM AS APPLIED TO
10: THE DISTRICT,” the District’s expenditures to reduce its excess local revenues (i.e., recapture obligation) increases as enrollment declines. While the
10: District is committed to developing and implementing strategies to increase student enrollment, decreased enrollment has continued and no assurance
10: can be given that enrollment will increase.
10: DISTRICT GOVERNANCE
10: TEA Oversight.      As required by H.B. 1842, passed in 2015 by the Texas legislature, the Texas Education Commissioner (the “Education
10: Commissioner”) appointed the nine-member Board of Managers (“Board”) to temporarily replace the elected board of trustees on June 1, 2023. The
10: Board has the same authority as the elected trustees and is responsible for overseeing the management of the District. Based on legislative authority
10: codified in the Texas Education Code, the Board (1) has exclusive power and duty to govern and oversee the District; (2) can acquire and hold real and
10: personal property, sue and be sued, and hold all rights and titles to school property; (3) has power to levy and collect taxes and to issue bonds; (4) can
10: contract for appointed officers, teachers, and other personnel as well as for goods and services; and (5) has the right of eminent domain to acquire real
10: property. On June 2, 2025, the TEA announced the extension of its intervention in the District to June 1, 2027 and the appointment of four new Board
10: members. In addition to appointing the Board in June 2023, the Education Commissioner also named Mike Miles the new superintendent of the District.
10: In June 2025, the Board extended Mr. Miles’ contract for a term of five years. In February 2025, the TEA named Anastasia Anderson as the District’s
10: new conservator.
10: State Accreditation. The District’s accreditation status for the 2025-2026 school year was “Accredited” based on a financial rating of “A - Superior
10: Achievement” and an academic accountability rating of “B.” The District’s accreditation status for the 2024-2025 and 2023-2024 school years was
10: “Accredited” based on a financial rating of “A - Superior Achievement” and an academic accountability rating of “C.” The District’s accreditation
10: status for the 2022-2023 school year was “Accredited” based on a financial rating of “C - Meets Standard Achievement” and an academic accountability
10: rating of “B.” Recognizing the impact of COVID-19 and the unique challenges schools faced, the TEA did not issue accountability ratings for the
10: 2021-2022 and 2020-2021 school years.

10: York Mellon Trust Company, National Association (the “Escrow Agent”) pursuant to an escrow agreement (the “Escrow Agreement”) between the
10: District and the Escrow Agent.
10: The Order provides that on the Delivery Date the District will deposit a portion of the proceeds of the sale of the Bonds with the Escrow Agent in an
10: amount which, when added to the investment earnings thereon, will be sufficient to accomplish the discharge and final payment of the Refunded Bonds.

10: the order authorizing the issuance of the Refunded Bonds (the “Escrow Securities”). Under the Escrow Agreement, the Escrow Fund is irrevocably
10: pledged to the payment of principal of and interest on the Refunded Bonds.

10: will mature and pay interest in such amounts which, together with uninvested funds, if any, in the Escrow Fund, will be sufficient to pay, when due,
10: the principal of and interest on the Refunded Bonds on their scheduled redemption dates. Such maturing principal of and interest on the Escrow
10: Securities will not be available to pay the debt service on the Bonds. See “OTHER INFORMATION – VERIFICATION AGENT.”

13: BONDHOLDERS’ REMEDIES
13: The Order does not provide for the appointment of a trustee to represent the interests of the registered owners upon any failure of the District to perform
13: in accordance with the terms of the Order or upon any other condition and, in the event of any such failure to perform, the registered owners would be
13: responsible for the initiation and cost of any legal action to enforce performance of the Order. Furthermore, the Order does not establish specific events
13: of default with respect to the Bonds and, under State law, there is no right to the acceleration of maturity of the Bonds upon the failure of the District
13: to observe any covenant under the Order. A registered owner of Bonds could seek a judgment against the District if a default occurred in the payment
13: of principal of or interest on any such Bonds; however, such judgment could not be satisfied by execution against any property of the District and a
13: suit for monetary damages could be vulnerable to the defense of sovereign immunity.
13: A registered owner’s only practical remedy, if a default occurs, is a mandamus or mandatory injunction proceeding to compel the District to levy,
13: assess and collect an annual ad valorem tax sufficient, within the limits prescribed by law, to pay principal of and interest on the Bonds as it becomes
13: due or perform other material terms and covenants contained in the Order; however, this may be limited by the District’s M&O tax rate required to
13: satisfy its Tier One Tax Rate and Enrichment Tax Rate. See “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS” herein. In general, Texas courts have held that a writ of
13: mandamus may be issued to require a public official to perform legally imposed ministerial duties necessary for the performance of a valid contract,
13: and Texas law provides that, following their approval by the Texas Attorney General and issuance, the Bonds are valid and binding obligations for all
13: purposes according to their terms. However, the enforcement of any such remedy may be difficult and time consuming and a registered owner could
13: be required to enforce such remedy on a periodic basis.
13: Chapter 1371, Texas Government Code, as amended (“Chapter 1371”), which pertains to the issuance of public securities by issuers such as the District,
13: permits the District to waive sovereign immunity in the proceedings authorizing its bonds. The District has not waived the defense of sovereign
13: immunity with respect thereto. Because it is unclear whether the Texas legislature has effectively waived the District’s sovereign immunity from a suit
13: for money damages outside of Chapter 1371, Bondholders may not be able to bring such a suit against the District for breach of the Bonds or Order
13: covenants. Even if a judgment against the District could be obtained, it could not be enforced by direct levy and execution against the District’s
13: property.
13: The District is also eligible to seek relief from its creditors under Chapter 9 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code (“Chapter 9”). Although Chapter 9 provides
13: for the recognition of a security interest represented by a specifically pledged source of revenues, the pledge of taxes in support of a general obligation
13: of a bankrupt entity is not specifically recognized as a security interest under Chapter 9. Chapter 9 also includes an automatic stay provision that would
13: prohibit, without Bankruptcy Court approval, the prosecution of any other legal action by creditors or registered owners of an entity which has sought
13: protection under Chapter 9. Therefore, should the District avail itself of Chapter 9 protection from creditors, the ability to enforce would be subject to
13: the approval of the Bankruptcy Court (which could require that the action be heard in Bankruptcy Court instead of other federal or state court); and the
13:                                                                             5
13: 
14: Bankruptcy Code provides for broad discretionary powers of a Bankruptcy Court in administering any proceeding brought before it. The opinion of
14: Bond Counsel will note that all opinions relative to the enforceability of the Order and the Bonds are qualified with respect to the customary rights of
14: debtors relative to their creditors, including rights afforded to creditors under the Bankruptcy Code and general principles of equity that permit the
14: exercise of judicial discretion.
14: See “APPENDIX D - THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM” herein for a description of the procedures to be followed
14: for payment of the Bonds by the Permanent School Fund in the event that the District fails to make a payment on the Bonds when due.
14:                                          THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM
14: Subject to satisfying certain conditions, the payment of the Bonds will be guaranteed by the corpus of the Permanent School Fund of the State of Texas.
14: In the event of default, registered owners will receive all payments due on the Bonds from the Permanent School Fund, and the Charter District Bond
14: Guarantee Reserve would be the first source to pay debt service if a charter school was unable to make such payment. See “Appendix D – THE
14: PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM” for pertinent information regarding the Permanent School Fund Guarantee Program.
14: The disclosure regarding the Permanent School Fund Guarantee Program in Appendix D is incorporated herein and made a part hereof for all purposes.
14:                                       STATE AND LOCAL FUNDING OF SCHOOL DISTRICTS IN TEXAS
14: LITIGATION RELATING TO THE TEXAS PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM
14: On seven occasions in the last thirty years, the Texas Supreme Court (the “Court”) has issued decisions assessing the constitutionality of the Texas
14: public school finance system (the “Finance System”). The litigation has primarily focused on whether the Finance System, as amended by the Texas
14: Legislature (the “Legislature”) from time to time (i) met the requirements of article VII, section 1 of the Texas Constitution, which requires the
14: Legislature to “establish and make suitable provision for the support and maintenance of an efficient system of public free schools,” or (ii) imposed a
14: statewide ad valorem tax in violation of article VIII, section 1-e of the Texas Constitution because the statutory limit on property taxes levied by school
14: districts for maintenance and operation purposes had allegedly denied school districts meaningful discretion in setting their tax rates. In response to the
14: Court’s previous decisions, the Legislature enacted multiple laws that made substantive changes in the way the Finance System is funded in efforts to
14: address the prior decisions declaring the Finance System unconstitutional.
14: On May 13, 2016, the Court issued its opinion in the most recent school finance litigation, Morath, et.al v. The Texas Taxpayer and Student Fairness
14: Coalition, et al., 490 S.W. 3d 826 (Tex.2016) (“Morath”). The plaintiffs and intervenors in the case had alleged that the Finance System, as modified
14: by the Legislature in part in response to prior decisions of the Court, violated article VII, section 1 and article VIII, section 1-e of the Texas Constitution.
14: In its opinion, the Court held that “[d]espite the imperfections of the current school funding regime, it meets minimum constitutional requirements.”
14: The Court also noted that:
14:           Lawmakers decide if laws pass, and judges decide if those laws pass muster. But our lenient standard of review in this policy-laden
14:           area counsels modesty. The judicial role is not to second-guess whether our system is optimal, but whether it is constitutional. Our
14:           Byzantine school funding “system” is undeniably imperfect, with immense room for improvement. But it satisfies minimum
14:           constitutional requirements.
14: POSSIBLE EFFECTS OF CHANGES IN LAW ON DISTRICT BONDS
14: The Court’s decision in Morath upheld the constitutionality of the Finance System but noted that the Finance System was “undeniably imperfect.”
14: While not compelled by the Morath decision to reform the Finance System, the Legislature could enact future changes to the Finance System. Any
14: such changes could benefit or be a detriment to the District. If the Legislature enacts future changes to, or fails adequately to fund the Finance System,
14: or if changes in circumstances otherwise provide grounds for a challenge, the Finance System could be challenged again in the future. In its 1995
14: opinion in Edgewood Independent School District v. Meno, 917 S.W.2d 717 (Tex. 1995), the Court stated that any future determination of
14: unconstitutionality “would not, however, affect the district’s authority to levy the taxes necessary to retire previously issued bonds, but would instead
14: require the Legislature to cure the system’s unconstitutionality in a way that is consistent with the Contract Clauses of the U.S. and Texas Constitutions”
14: (collectively, the “Contract Clauses”), which prohibit the enactment of laws that impair prior obligations of contracts.
14: Although, as a matter of law, the Bonds, upon issuance and delivery, will be entitled to the protections afforded previously existing contractual
14: obligations under the Contract Clauses, the District can make no representations or predictions concerning the effect of future legislation, or any
14: litigation that may be associated with such legislation, on the District’s financial condition, revenues or operations. While the enactment of future
14: legislation to address school funding in Texas could adversely affect the financial condition, revenues or operations of the District, the District does
14: not anticipate that the security for payment of the Bonds, specifically, the District’s obligation to levy a limited debt service tax and any Permanent
14: School Fund guarantee of the Bonds would be adversely affected by any such legislation. See “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM.”

15:                                                  CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM
15: OVERVIEW
15: The following language constitutes only a summary of the public school finance system (the “Finance System”) as it is currently structured. The
15: information contained under the captions “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM” and “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS” is subject to
15: change and only reflects the District’s understanding based on information available to the District as of the date of this Official Statement. For a more
15: complete description of school finance and fiscal management in the State, reference is made to Chapters 43 through 49 of the Texas Education Code,
15: as amended. Additionally, prospective investors are encouraged to review the Property Tax Code (as defined herein) for definitive requirements for the
15: levy and collection of ad valorem taxes and the calculation of the defined tax rates.
15: Local funding for school districts is derived from collections of ad valorem taxes levied on property located within each school district’s boundaries.
15: School districts are authorized to levy two types of property taxes: (i) a maintenance and operations (“M&O”) tax to pay current expenses and (ii) an
15: interest and sinking fund (“I&S”) tax to pay debt service on bonds. School districts are prohibited from levying an M&O tax rate for the purpose of
15: creating a surplus in M&O tax revenues to pay the district’s debt service. School districts are required to demonstrate their ability to pay debt service
15: on outstanding bonded indebtedness through the levy of an I&S tax at a rate not to exceed $0.50 per $100 of taxable value at the time bonds are issued.
15: Once bonds are issued, however, school districts generally may levy an I&S tax sufficient to pay debt service on such bonds unlimited as to rate or
15: amount (however, the District may only levy an I&S tax rate within the limits prescribed by law and pursuant to the Tax Election (as defined herein)).
15: See “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS – I&S Tax Rate Limitations” herein. Because property values vary widely among school districts, the amount of
15: local funding generated by school districts with the same I&S tax rate and M&O tax rate is subject to wide variation; however, the public school finance
15: funding formulas are designed to generally equalize local funding generated by a school district’s M&O tax rate.
15: 2025 LEGISLATIVE SESSIONS
15: The regular session of the 89th Texas Legislature convened on January 14, 2025 and concluded on June 2, 2025 (the “89th Regular Session”). The
15: Texas Legislature (the “Legislature”) meets in regular session in odd numbered years for 140 days. When the Legislature is not in session, the Governor
15: may call one or more special sessions, at the Governor's discretion, each lasting no more than 30 days, and for which the Governor sets the agenda.
15: The Governor has called and the Legislature has concluded two special sessions since the conclusion of the 89th Regular Session.
15: During the 89th Regular Session, the Legislature adopted a general appropriations act and legislation affecting the Finance System and ad valorem
15: taxation procedures and exemptions, and investments, among other legislation affecting school districts and the administrative agencies that oversee
15: school districts. Legislation passed by both houses of the Legislature increases: (1) the State mandated general homestead exemption from $100,000
15: to $140,000, (2) the additional exemption on the residence homesteads of those at least sixty-five (65) years of age or disabled from $10,000 to $60,000,
15: and (3) the exemption for tangible personal property used in the production of income from the current $2,500 to $125,000. Voters approved
15: constitutional amendments authorizing the new exemptions at a statewide election held on November 4, 2025. Additionally, the Legislature passed
15: legislation authorizing roughly $8.5 billion in funding for public schools and provided districts with a $55 per-student increase to their base funding
15: beginning September 1, 2025, as well as additional funding for teacher and staff salaries, educator preparation, special education, safety requirements
15: and early childhood learning.
15: Finally, legislation passed by the Legislature created an Education Savings Account (“ESA”) Program (commonly referred to as vouchers) for students
15: that attend private schools or are homeschooled. The legislation became effective September 1, 2025, when the State fiscal biennium began, though
15: families will not receive ESA funds until the 2026-2027 school year. The amount spent for purposes of the program for the 2025-2027 biennium may
15: not exceed $1 billion. Beginning on September 1, 2027, the legislation requires the Legislature to reappropriate funds for the program for each
15: subsequent State fiscal biennium. Such program could impact attendance in the District by incentivizing students to homeschool or attend private
15: schools, which could negatively affect the District's attendance-based funding.
15: The District is still in the process of reviewing legislation passed during the 89th Regular Session. At this time, the District cannot make any
15: representations as to the full impact of such legislation. Further, the District can make no representations or predictions regarding the scope of legislation
15: that may be considered in any special session or future session of the Legislature or the potential impact of such legislation at this time. The District
15: does intend to monitor applicable legislation related thereto.
15: LOCAL FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS
15: A school district’s M&O tax rate is composed of two distinct parts: the “Tier One Tax Rate”, which is the local M&O tax rate required for a school
15: district to receive any part of the basic level of State funding (referred to herein as “Tier One”) under the Foundation School Program, as further
15: described below, and the “Enrichment Tax Rate”, which is any local M&O tax effort in excess of its Tier One Tax Rate. Formulas for the State
15: Compression Percentage and Maximum Compressed Tax Rate (each as described below) are designed to compress M&O tax rates in response to year-
15: over-year increases in property values across the State and within a school district, respectively. The discussion in this subcaption “LOCAL FUNDING
15: FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS” is generally intended to describe funding provisions applicable to all school districts; however, there are distinctions in the
15: funding formulas for school districts that generate local M&O tax revenues in excess of the school districts’ funding entitlements. Such distinctions are
15: discussed under the subcaption “– Local Revenue Level In Excess of Entitlement” herein.
15:                                                                               7
15: 
16: State Compression Percentage. The “State Compression Percentage” or “SCP” is the lesser of three alternative calculations: (i) 93% or a lower
16: percentage set by appropriation for a school year; (ii) a percentage determined by formula if the estimated total taxable property value of the State (as
16: submitted annually to the Legislature by the State Comptroller) has increased by at least 2.5% over the prior year; and (iii) the prior year SCP. For any
16: year, the maximum SCP is 93%. For the State fiscal year ending in 2026, the SCP is set at 63.22%.
16: Maximum Compressed Tax Rate. The “Maximum Compressed Tax Rate” or the “MCR” is the tax rate per $100 of valuation of taxable property at
16: which a school district must levy its Tier One Tax Rate (described below) to receive the full amount of the Tier One funding to which the school district
16: is entitled. The MCR is equal to the lesser of two alternative calculations: (1) the “State Compression Percentage” (as discussed above) multiplied by
16: 100; or (2) a percentage determined by formula if the school district experienced a year-over-year increase in property value of at least 2.5% (if the
16: increase in property value is less than 2.5%, then MCR is equal to the prior year’s MCR). However, each year the TEA shall evaluate the MCR for
16: each school district in the State, and for any given year, if a school district’s MCR is calculated to be less than 90% of any other school district’s MCR
16: for the current year, then the school district’s MCR is instead equal to the school district’s prior year MCR, until TEA determines that the difference
16: between the school district’s MCR and any other school district’s MCR is not more than 10%. These compression formulas are intended to more closely
16: equalize local generation of Tier One funding among districts with disparate tax bases and generally reduce the Tier One Tax Rates of school districts
16: as property values increase. During the 2025 Legislative Session, the Legislature took action to reduce the maximum MCR for the 2025-2026 school
16: year. The MCR for the 2025-2026 school year is $0.6322 and the floor is $0.5689.
16: In calculating and making available school districts’ MCRs for the 2025-2026 school year, the TEA calculated and made available the rates as if the
16: increase in the residence homestead exemption under Section 1-b(c), Article VIII, Texas Constitution, as proposed by the 89th Legislature, Regular
16: Session, 2025, took effect. Such calculation for the 2025-2026 school year expires September 1, 2026. At a Statewide election held on November 4,
16: 2025, voters approved constitutional amendments which increase (1) the State mandated general homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000,
16: and (2) the additional exemption on the residence homesteads of those at least sixty-five (65) years of age or disabled from $10,000 to $60,000. Such
16: constitutional amendments take effect for the tax year beginning January 1, 2025.
16: Tier One Tax Rate. A school district’s Tier One Tax Rate is defined as a school district’s M&O tax rate levied that does not exceed the school district’s
16: MCR.
16: Enrichment Tax Rate. The Enrichment Tax Rate is the number of cents a school district levies for M&O in excess of the Tier One Tax Rate, up to an
16: additional $0.17. The Enrichment Tax Rate is divided into two components: (i) “Golden Pennies” which are the first $0.08 of tax effort in excess of a
16: school district’s Tier One Tax Rate; and (ii) “Copper Pennies” which are the next $0.09 in excess of a school district’s Tier One Tax Rate plus Golden
16: Pennies.
16: School districts may levy an Enrichment Tax Rate at a level of their choice, subject to the limitations described under “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS –
16: Public Hearing and Voter-Approval Tax Rate.” However to levy any of the Enrichment Tax Rate in a given year, a school district must levy a Tier One
16: Tax Rate equal to the school district’s MCR for such year. Additionally, a school district’s levy of Copper Pennies is subject to compression if the
16: guaranteed yield (i.e., the guaranteed level of local tax revenue and State aid generated for each cent of tax effort) of Copper Pennies is increased from
16: one year to the next (see “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM – State Funding for School Districts – Tier Two”).
16: STATE FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS
16: State funding for school districts is provided through the two-tiered Foundation School Program, which guarantees certain levels of funding for school
16: districts in the State. School districts are entitled to a legislatively appropriated guaranteed yield on their Tier One Tax Rate and Enrichment Tax Rate.
16: When a school district’s Tier One Tax Rate and Enrichment Tax Rate generate tax revenues at a level below the respective entitlement, the State will
16: provide “Tier One” funding or “Tier Two” funding, respectively, to fund the difference between the school district’s entitlements and the calculated
16: M&O revenues generated by the school district’s respective M&O tax rates.
16: The first level of funding, Tier One, is the basic level of funding guaranteed to all school districts based on a school district’s Tier One Tax Rate. Tier
16: One funding may then be “enriched” with Tier Two funding. Tier Two provides a guaranteed entitlement for each cent of a school district’s Enrichment
16: Tax Rate, allowing a school district to increase or decrease its Enrichment Tax Rate to supplement Tier One funding at a level of the school district’s
16: own choice. While Tier One funding may be used for the payment of debt service (except for school districts subject to the recapture provisions of
16: Chapter 49 of the Texas Education Code, as amended (see “– Local Revenue Level In Excess of Entitlement”)), and in some instances is required to
16: be used for that purpose (see “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS – I&S Tax Rate Limitations” herein), Tier Two funding may not be used for the payment
16: of debt service or capital outlay.
16: The Finance System also provides an Existing Debt Allotment (“EDA”) to subsidize debt service on eligible outstanding school district bonds, an
16: Instructional Facilities Allotment (“IFA”) to subsidize debt service on newly issued bonds, and a New Instructional Facilities Allotment (“NIFA”) to
16: subsidize operational expenses associated with the opening of a new instructional facility. IFA primarily addresses the debt service needs of property-
16: poor school districts.
16: Tier One and Tier Two allotments represent the State’s share of the cost of M&O expenses of school districts, with local M&O taxes representing the
16: school district’s local share. EDA and IFA allotments supplement a school district’s local I&S taxes levied for debt service on eligible bonds issued to
16: construct, acquire and improve facilities, provided that a school district qualifies for such funding and that the Legislature makes sufficient
16: appropriations to fund the allotments for a State fiscal biennium. Tier One and Tier Two allotments and existing EDA and IFA allotments are generally
16: required to be funded each year by the Legislature.
16:                                                                             8
16: 
17: Tier One. Tier One funding is the basic level of programmatic funding guaranteed to a school district, consisting of a State-appropriated baseline level
17: of funding (the “Basic Allotment”) for each student in “Average Daily Attendance” (being generally calculated as the sum of student attendance for
17: each State mandated day of instruction divided by the number of State mandated days of instruction, defined herein as “ADA”). The Basic Allotment
17: is revised downward if a school district’s Tier One Tax Rate is less than the State-determined threshold. The Basic Allotment is supplemented by
17: additional State funds, allotted based upon the unique school district characteristics, the demographics of students in ADA, and the educational programs
17: the students are being served in, to make up most of a school district’s Tier One entitlement under the Foundation School Program.
17: The Basic Allotment for school districts with a Tier One Tax Rate equal to the school district’s MCR, is $6,160 plus the guaranteed yield increment
17: adjustment (the “GYIA”) for each student in ADA and is revised downward for school districts with a Tier One Tax Rate lower than the school district’s
17: MCR. The GYIA is established by October 1 of each even-numbered year for the subsequent biennium. For the 2026-27 biennium, the GYIA is set at
17: $55. The Basic Allotment is then supplemented for all school districts by various weights to account for differences among school districts and their
17: student populations. Such additional allotments include, but are not limited to, increased funds for students in ADA who: (i) attend a qualified special
17: education program, (ii) are diagnosed with dyslexia or a related disorder, (iii) are economically disadvantaged, or (iv) have limited English language
17: proficiency. Additional allotments to mitigate differences among school districts include, but are not limited to: (i) a transportation allotment for mileage
17: associated with transporting students who reside two miles or more from their home campus, (ii) a fast growth allotment (for school districts in the top
17: 25% of enrollment growth relative to other school districts), (iii) a college, career and military readiness allotment to further the State’s goal of
17: increasing the number of students who attain a post-secondary education or workforce credential, and (iv) a teacher incentive allotment to increase
17: teacher compensation retention in disadvantaged or rural school districts. A school district’s total Tier One funding, divided the district’s Basic
17: Allotment is a school district’s measure of students in “Weighted Average Daily Attendance” (“WADA”), which serves to calculate Tier Two funding.
17: The fast growth allotment weights are 0.48 for districts in the top 40% of school districts for growth, 0.33 for districts in the middle 30% of school
17: districts for growth and 0.18 for districts in the bottom 30% of school districts for growth. The fast growth allotment is limited to $320 million for each
17: year of the 2026-2027 state fiscal biennium.
17: Beginning with the 2026-2027 fiscal biennium, school districts will also receive an annual allotment of $106 per enrolled student. The funds under this
17: allotment may only be used for specific operational costs related to transportation, hiring retired teachers, providing health insurance and employee
17: benefits and paying for payroll taxes, contributions and other costs related to member contributions under the Teacher Retirement System of Texas,
17: utilities, and property and casualty insurance.
17: Tier Two. Tier Two supplements Tier One funding and provides two levels of enrichment with different guaranteed yields (i.e., Golden Pennies and
17: Copper Pennies) depending on the school district’s Enrichment Tax Rate. Golden Pennies generate a guaranteed yield equal to the Basic Allotment
17: multiplied by 0.02084. For the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium, school districts are guaranteed a yield on each Golden Penny levied of $129.52 per
17: student in WADA. Copper Pennies generate a guaranteed yield per student in WADA equal to the school district’s Basic Allotment multiplied by
17: 0.008. For the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium, school districts are guaranteed a yield on each Copper Penny levied of $49.72 per student in WADA.
17: Existing Debt Allotment, Instruction Facilities Allotment, and New Instructional Facilities Allotment. The Foundation School Program also includes
17: facilities funding components consisting of the IFA and the EDA, subject to legislative appropriation each State fiscal biennium. To the extent funded
17: for a biennium, these programs assist school districts in funding facilities by, generally, equalizing a school district’s I&S tax effort. The IFA guarantees
17: each awarded school district a specified amount per student (the “IFA Yield”) in State and local funds for each cent of I&S tax levied to pay the
17: principal of and interest on eligible bonds issued to construct, acquire, renovate or improve instructional facilities. The IFA Yield has been $35 since
17: the program first began in 1997. New awards of IFA are only available if appropriated funds are allocated for such purpose by the Legislature. To
17: receive an IFA award, in years where new IFA awards are available, a school district must apply to the Education Commissioner in accordance with
17: rules adopted by the TEA before issuing the bonds to be paid with IFA State assistance. The total amount of debt service assistance over a biennium
17: for which a school district may be awarded is limited to the lesser of (1) the actual debt service payments made by the school district in the biennium
17: in which the bonds are issued; or (2) the greater of (a) $100,000 or (b) $250 multiplied by the number of students in ADA. The IFA is also available
17: for lease-purchase agreements and refunding bonds meeting certain prescribed conditions. Once a school district receives an IFA award for bonds, it
17: is entitled to continue receiving State assistance for such bonds without reapplying to the Education Commissioner. The guaranteed level of State and
17: local funds per student per cent of local tax effort applicable to the bonds may not be reduced below the level provided for the year in which the bonds
17: were issued. For the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium, the State Legislature did not appropriate any funds for new IFA awards; however, awards
17: previously granted in years the State Legislature did appropriate funds for new IFA awards will continue to be funded.
17: State financial assistance is provided for certain existing eligible debt issued by school districts through the EDA program. The EDA guaranteed yield
17: (the “EDA Yield”) is the lesser of (i) $40 per student in ADA or a greater amount for any year provided by appropriation; or (ii) the amount that would
17: result in a total additional EDA of $60 million more than the EDA to which school districts would have been entitled to if the EDA Yield were $35.
17: The portion of a school district’s local debt service rate that qualifies for EDA assistance is limited to the first $0.29 of its I&S tax rate (or a greater
17: amount for any year provided by appropriation by the Legislature). In general, a school district’s bonds are eligible for EDA assistance if (i) the school
17: district made payments on the bonds during the final fiscal year of the preceding State fiscal biennium, or (ii) the school district levied taxes to pay the
17: principal of and interest on the bonds for that fiscal year. Each biennium, access to EDA funding is determined by the debt service taxes collected in
17: the final year of the preceding biennium. A school district may not receive EDA funding for the principal and interest on a series of otherwise eligible
17: bonds for which the school district receives IFA funding.
17: Since future-year IFA awards were not funded by the State Legislature for the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium and debt service assistance on school
17: district bonds that are not yet eligible for EDA is not available, debt service payments during the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium on new bonds issued
17: by school districts in the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium to construct, acquire and improve facilities must be funded solely from local I&S taxes,
17: except to the extent the bonds of a school district are eligible for hold harmless funding from the State for local tax revenue lost as a result of an increase
17: in the mandatory homestead exemption.

18: A school district may also qualify for a NIFA allotment, which provides assistance to school districts for operational expenses associated with opening
18: new instructional facilities or a renovated portion of an instructional facility to be used for the first time to provide high-cost and undersubscribed career
18: and technology education programs, as determined by the Education Commissioner. In the 89th Regular Session, the Legislature appropriated funds in
18: the amount of $150,000,000 for each fiscal year of the 2026-2027 State fiscal biennium for NIFA allotments.
18: Tax Rate and Funding Equity. The Education Commissioner may proportionally reduce the amount of funding a school district receives under the
18: Foundation School Program and the ADA calculation if the school district operates on a calendar that provides less than the State mandated minimum
18: instruction time in a school year. The Education Commissioner may also adjust a school district’s ADA as it relates to State funding where disaster,
18: flood, extreme weather or other calamity has a significant effect on a school district’s attendance.
18: For the 2026-2027 school year, school districts will be held harmless and entitled to additional state aid to the extent that state and local revenue used
18: to service eligible debt is less than the state and local revenue that would have been available to the district under state law providing for state aid to
18: districts to account for increases in the general residence homestead exemption and the elderly or disabled tax ceiling as such state law existed on
18: January 1, 2025, if any increase in a residence homestead exemption under the Texas Constitution, and any additional limitation on tax increases under
18: the elderly or disabled tax ceiling had not occurred.
18: LOCAL REVENUE LEVEL IN EXCESS OF ENTITLEMENT
18: A school district that has sufficient property wealth per student in ADA to generate local revenues on the school district’s Tier One Tax Rate and
18: Copper Pennies in excess of the school district’s respective funding entitlements (a “Chapter 49 school district”), is subject to the local revenue reduction
18: provisions contained in Chapter 49 of Texas Education Code, as amended (“Chapter 49”). Additionally, in years in which the amount of State funds
18: appropriated specifically excludes the amount necessary to provide the guaranteed yield for Golden Pennies, local revenues generated on a school
18: district’s Golden Pennies in excess of the school district’s respective funding entitlement are subject to the local revenue reduction provisions of Chapter
18: 49. To reduce local revenue, Chapter 49 school districts are generally subject to a process known as “recapture”, which requires a Chapter 49 school
18: district to exercise certain options to remit local M&O tax revenues collected in excess of the Chapter 49 school district’s funding entitlements to the
18: State (for redistribution to other school districts) or otherwise expending the respective M&O tax revenues for the benefit of students in school districts
18: that are not Chapter 49 school districts, as described in the subcaption “Options for Local Revenue Levels in Excess of Entitlement”. Chapter 49 school
18: districts receive their allocable share of funds distributed from the constitutionally-prescribed Available School Fund, but are generally not eligible to
18: receive State aid under the Foundation School Program, although they may continue to receive State funds for certain competitive grants and certain
18: programs that remain outside the Foundation School Program.
18: Recapture is measured by the “local revenue level” (being the M&O tax revenues generated in a school district) in excess of the entitlements
18: appropriated by the State Legislature each fiscal biennium. Therefore, school districts are now guaranteed that recapture will not reduce revenue below
18: their statutory entitlement.
18: Options for Local Revenue Levels in Excess of Entitlement. Under Chapter 49, a school district has six options to reduce local revenues to a level that
18: does not exceed the school district’s respective entitlements: (1) a school district may consolidate by agreement with one or more school districts to
18: form a consolidated school district; all property and debt of the consolidating school districts vest in the consolidated school district; (2) a school district
18: may detach property from its territory for annexation by a property-poor school district; (3) a school district may purchase attendance credits from the
18: State; (4) a school district may contract to educate nonresident students from a property-poor school district by sending money directly to one or more
18: property-poor school districts; (5) a school district may execute an agreement to provide students of one or more other school districts with career and
18: technology education through a program designated as an area program for career and technology education; or (6) a school district may consolidate
18: by agreement with one or more school districts to form a consolidated taxing school district solely to levy and distribute either M&O taxes or both
18: M&O taxes and I&S taxes. A Chapter 49 school district may also exercise any combination of these remedies. Options (3), (4) and (6) require prior
18: approval by the Chapter 49 school district’s voters. A district that enters into an agreement to exercise an option to reduce the district’s local revenue
18: level in excess of entitlement under options (3), (4), or (5) for the 2025-2026 school year and that has not previously held an election to exercise said
18: options may request and may receive approval from the Education Commissioner to delay the date of the election otherwise required to be ordered
18: before September 1. The Education Commissioner shall set a date by which each district that receives approval to delay an election must order the
18: election and requires the Education Commissioner, not later than the 2026-2027 school year, to order detachment and annexation of district property
18: or consolidation as necessary to reduce the district's excess local revenue to the level established by law for a district that receives approval to delay an
18: election and subsequently fails to hold the election or does not receive voter approval at the election. A district that receives approval of a request to
18: delay the date of an election shall pay for credit purchased in equal monthly payments as determined by the Education Commissioner beginning March
18: 15, 2026, and ending August 15, 2026. Alternatively, the district may pay for credit purchased with one lump sum payment made not later than August
18: 15, 2026, provided that the district notifies the Education Commissioner of the district's election to pay through a lump sum not later than March 15,
18: 2026.
18: Furthermore, a school district may not adopt a tax rate until its effective local revenue level is at or below the level that would produce its guaranteed
18: entitlement under the Foundation School Program. If a school district fails to exercise a permitted option, the Education Commissioner must reduce
18: the school district’s local revenue level to the level that would produce the school district’s guaranteed entitlement, by detaching certain types of
18: property from the school district and annexing the property to a property-poor school district or, if necessary, consolidate the school district with a
18: property-poor school district. Provisions governing detachment and annexation of taxable property by the Education Commissioner do not provide for
18: assumption of any of the transferring school district’s existing debt.

19:                                       THE SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM AS APPLIED TO THE DISTRICT
19: For the 2025-2026 school year, the District was designated as an “excess local revenue” district by the TEA. The amount of local revenue in excess of
19: the District’s entitlement in any year is determined by a number of variables, but is primarily driven by property values and student attendance as
19: described above under “—LOCAL REVENUE LEVEL IN EXCESS OF ENTITLEMENT.” Pursuant to an election held on May 6, 2017, the District
19: exercises the option of purchasing attendance credits from the State to reduce local revenues to a level that does not exceed the District’s entitlements,
19: as described as option (3) under “—LOCAL REVENUE LEVEL IN EXCESS OF ENTITLEMENT—Options for Local Revenue Levels in Excess of
19: Entitlement” above.
19: The District’s expenditures to reduce excess local revenues (i.e., recapture obligation) for fiscal years 2021, 2022 and 2023 were approximately $198
19: million, $187 million and $275 million, respectively. For fiscal year 2024, the District had $0 in recapture obligation due to tax compression and the
19: homestead exemption. The District’s recapture obligation was approximately $65 million for fiscal year 2025. For fiscal year 2026, the District does
19: not anticipate a recapture obligation. Amounts of local revenue in excess of the District’s entitlement for any fiscal year may be adjusted by the TEA
19: during the five subsequent fiscal years.
19: In each year that the District’s local revenues exceed its funding entitlements, the District must reduce its local revenues by exercise of one of the
19: options described above under “—LOCAL REVENUE LEVEL IN EXCESS OF ENTITLEMENT— Options for Local Revenue Levels in Excess of
19: Entitlement.” The District expects to continue to purchase attendance credits from the State, as necessary, as further described above. However, if the
19: District were to consolidate (or consolidate its tax base for all purposes) with a property-poor district, the outstanding debt of each district could become
19: payable from the consolidated district’s combined property tax base, and the District’s ratio of taxable property to debt could become diluted. If the
19: District were to detach property voluntarily, a portion of its outstanding debt could be assumed by the district to which the property is annexed, in
19: which case timely payment could become dependent in part on the financial performance of the annexing district. See “–Local Revenue Level in
19: Excess of Entitlement” above. See “TABLE 11 – GENERAL FUND REVENUE AND EXPENDITURE HISTORY,” for a discussion of the District’s
19: budget for the 2025-2026 school year.
19: A district’s local revenue levels must be tested for each future school year and, if local revenues exceed the district’s entitlements, the district must
19: reduce its wealth per student by the exercise of one of the permitted wealth equalization options. Accordingly, if the District’s local revenues should
19: exceed its entitlements in future school years, it will be required to exercise one or more of the permitted options to reduce local revenues.
19: For the State fiscal year ending in 2026 (the 2025-2026 school year), the State Compression Percentage is set at $0.6322. For a detailed discussion of
19: State funding for school districts, see “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM – STATE FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS” herein.
19:                                                          AD VALOREM TAX PROCEDURES
19: The following is a summary of certain provisions of State law as it relates to ad valorem taxation and is not intended to be complete. Prospective
19: investors are encouraged to review Title I of the Texas Tax Code, as amended (the “Property Tax Code”), for identification of property subject to ad
19: valorem taxation, property exempt or which may be exempted from ad valorem taxation if claimed, the appraisal of property for ad valorem tax
19: purposes, and the procedures and limitations applicable to the levy and collection of ad valorem taxes. See “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE
19: SYSTEM – 2025 Legislative Sessions” for information on legislation affecting ad valorem taxation exemptions.
19: VALUATION OF TAXABLE PROPERTY
19: The Property Tax Code provides for countywide appraisal and equalization of taxable property values and establishes in each county of the State an
19: appraisal district and an appraisal review board (the “Appraisal Review Board”) responsible for appraising property for all taxing units within the
19: county. The appraisal of property within the District is the responsibility of the Harris Central Appraisal District (the “Appraisal District”). Except as
19: generally described below, the Appraisal District is required to appraise all property within the Appraisal District as of January 1 of each year and on
19: the basis of 100% of its market value and is prohibited from applying any assessment ratios. In determining market value of property, the Appraisal
19: District is required to consider the cost method of appraisal, the income method of appraisal and the market data comparison method of appraisal, and
19: use the method the chief appraiser of the Appraisal District considers most appropriate. The Property Tax Code requires appraisal districts to reappraise
19: all property in its jurisdiction at least once every three (3) years. A taxing unit may require annual review at its own expense, and is entitled to challenge
19: the determination of appraised value of property within the taxing unit by petition filed with the Appraisal Review Board. See “ – DISTRICT AND
19: TAXPAYER REMEDIES.”
19: State law requires the appraised value of an owner’s principal residence (“homestead” or “homesteads”) to be based solely on the property’s value as
19: a homestead, regardless of whether residential use is considered to be the highest and best use of the property. State law further limits the appraised
19: value of a homestead to the lesser of (1) the market value of the property or (2) 110% of the appraised value of the property for the preceding tax year
19: plus the market value of all new improvements to the property. The 10% increase is cumulative, meaning the maximum increase is 10% times the
19: number of years since the property was last appraised.
