20: Unless extended by the Legislature, through December 31, 2026, an appraisal district is prohibited from increasing the appraised value of real property
20: during the 2026 tax year on certain non-homestead properties (the “Subjected Property”) whose appraised values are not more than $5.32 million
20: dollars (the “maximum property value”) to an amount not to exceed the lesser of: (1) the market value of the Subjected Property for the most recent
20: tax year that the market value was determined by the appraisal office or (2) the sum of: (a) 20 percent of the appraised value of the Subjected Property
20: for the preceding tax year; (b) the appraised value of the Subjected Property for the preceding tax year; and (c) the market value of all new improvements
20: to the Subjected Property. The maximum property value may be increased or decreased by the product of the preceding state fiscal year’s increase or
20: decrease in the consumer price index, as applicable, to the maximum property value.
20: State law provides that eligible owners of both agricultural land and open-space land, including open-space land devoted to farm or ranch purposes or
20: open-space land devoted to timber production, may elect to have such property appraised for property taxation on the basis of its productive capacity.
20: The same land may not be qualified as both agricultural and open-space land.
20: The appraisal values set by the Appraisal District are subject to review and change by the Appraisal Review Board. The appraisal rolls, as approved by
20: the Appraisal Review Board, are used by taxing units, such as the District, in establishing their tax rolls and tax rates (see “ – DISTRICT AND TAXPAYER
20: REMEDIES”).
20: STATE MANDATED HOMESTEAD EXEMPTIONS
20: State law grants, with respect to each school district in the State, (1) a $140,000 exemption of the appraised value of all homesteads, (2) a $60,000
20: exemption of the appraised value of the homesteads of persons sixty-five (65) years of age or older and the disabled, and (3) various exemptions for
20: disabled veterans and their families, surviving spouses of members of the armed services killed in action and surviving spouses of first responders
20: killed or fatally wounded in the line of duty.
20: LOCAL OPTION HOMESTEAD EXEMPTIONS
20: The governing body of a taxing unit, including a city, county, school district, or special district, at its option may grant: (1) an exemption of up to 20%
20: of the appraised value of all homesteads (but not less than $5,000) and (2) an additional exemption of at least $3,000 of the appraised value of the
20: homesteads of persons sixty-five (65) years of age or older and the disabled. Each taxing unit decides if it will offer the local option homestead
20: exemptions and at what percentage or dollar amount, as applicable. The exemption described in (2), above, may also be created, increased, decreased
20: or repealed at an election called by the governing body of a taxing unit upon presentment of a petition for such creation, increase, decrease, or repeal
20: of at least 20% of the number of qualified voters who voted in the preceding election of the taxing unit.
20: Cities, counties and school districts are prohibited from repealing or reducing an optional homestead exemption that was granted in tax year 2022
20: through December 31, 2027.
20: STATE MANDATED FREEZE ON SCHOOL DISTRICT TAXES
20: Except for increases attributable to certain improvements, a school district is prohibited from increasing the total ad valorem tax on the homestead of
20: persons sixty-five (65) years of age or older or of disabled persons above the amount of tax imposed in the year such homestead qualified for such
20: exemption. This freeze is transferable to a different homestead if a qualifying taxpayer moves and, under certain circumstances, is also transferable to
20: the surviving spouse of persons sixty-five (65) years of age or older, but not the disabled.
20: The total amount of ad valorem taxes that may be imposed for general elementary and secondary public school purposes on the residence homestead
20: of a person who is sixty-five (65) years old or older or disabled may be adjusted to reflect any statutory reduction from the preceding tax year in the
20: MCR of the M&O taxes imposed for those purposes on the homestead.
20: PERSONAL PROPERTY
20: Tangible personal property (furniture, machinery, supplies, inventories, etc.) used in the “production of income” is taxed based on the property’s market
20: value. Taxable personal property includes income-producing equipment and inventory. Intangibles such as goodwill, accounts receivable, and
20: proprietary processes are not taxable. Tangible personal property not held or used for production of income, such as household goods, automobiles or
20: light trucks, and boats, is exempt from ad valorem taxation unless the governing body of a taxing unit elects to tax such property. Legislation passed
20: by the Legislature during the 89th Regular Session and approved by voters provides a person an exemption from taxation by a taxing unit of $125,000
20: of the appraised value of tangible personal property the person owns that is held or used for the production of income and has taxable situs at the same
20: location in the taxing unit. A person who leases tangible personal property is also entitled to a tax exemption of $125,000, regardless of where the
20: property is located in the taxing unit.
20: FREEPORT AND GOODS-IN-TRANSIT EXEMPTIONS
20: Certain goods that are acquired in or imported into the State to be forwarded outside the State, and are detained in the State for 175 days or less for the
20: purpose of assembly, storage, manufacturing, processing or fabrication (“Freeport Property”) are exempt from ad valorem taxation unless a taxing unit
20:                                                                             12
20: 
21: took official action to tax Freeport Property before April 1, 1990, and has not subsequently taken official action to exempt Freeport Property. Decisions
21: to continue taxing Freeport Property may be reversed in the future; decisions to exempt Freeport Property are not subject to reversal.
21: Certain goods, that are acquired in or imported into the State to be forwarded to another location within or outside the State, stored in a location that is
21: not owned by the owner of the goods and are transported to another location within or outside the State within 175 days (“Goods-in-Transit”), are
21: generally exempt from ad valorem taxation; however, the Property Tax Code permits a taxing unit, on a local option basis, to tax Goods-in-Transit if
21: the taxing unit takes official action, after conducting a public hearing, before January 1 of the first tax year in which the taxing unit proposes to tax
21: Goods-in-Transit. Goods-in-Transit and Freeport Property do not include oil, natural gas or petroleum products, and Goods-in-Transit does not include
21: aircraft or special inventories such as manufactured housing inventory, or a dealer’s motor vehicle, boat, or heavy equipment inventory.
21: A taxpayer may receive only one of the Goods-in-Transit or Freeport Property exemptions for items of personal property.
21: TEMPORARY EXEMPTION FOR QUALIFIED PROPERTY DAMAGED BY A DISASTER
21: The Property Tax Code entitles the owner of certain qualified (i) tangible personal property used for the production of income, (ii) improvements to
21: real property, and (iii) manufactured homes located in an area declared by the Governor to be a disaster area following a disaster and is at least 15
21: percent damaged by the disaster, as determined by the chief appraiser, to an exemption from taxation of a portion of the appraised value of the property.
21: The amount of the exemption ranges from 15 percent to 100 percent based upon the damage assessment rating assigned by the chief appraiser. The
21: governing body of the taxing unit is not required to take any action in order for the taxpayer to be eligible for the exemption. If a taxpayer qualifies for
21: the exemption after the beginning of the tax year, the amount of the exemption is prorated based on the number of days left in the tax year following
21: the day on which the Governor declares the area to be a disaster area. The Texas Legislature amended Section 11.35 of the Property Tax Code to clarify
21: that “damage” for purposes of such statute is limited to physical damage. For more information on the exemption, reference is made to Section 11.35
21: of the Property Tax Code, as amended.
21: OTHER EXEMPT PROPERTY
21: Other major categories of exempt property include property owned by the State or its political subdivisions if used for public purposes, property exempt
21: by federal law, property used for pollution control, farm products owned by producers, property of nonprofit corporations used for scientific research
21: or educational activities benefitting a college or university, designated historic sites, solar and wind-powered energy devices, and certain classes of
21: intangible personal property. Beginning with the 2026 tax year, all intangible personal property is exempt from State taxation.
21: TAX INCREMENT REINVESTMENT ZONES
21: A city or county, by petition of the landowners or by action of its governing body, may create one or more tax increment reinvestment zones (“TIRZ”)
21: within its boundaries. At the time of the creation of the TIRZ, a “base value” for the real property in the TIRZ is established and the difference between
21: any increase in the assessed valuation of taxable real property in the TIRZ in excess of the base value is known as the “tax increment.” During the
21: existence of the TIRZ, all or a portion of the taxes levied against the tax increment by a city or county, and all other overlapping taxing units that elected
21: to participate, are restricted to paying only planned project and financing costs within the TIRZ and are not available for the payment of other obligations
21: of such taxing units.
21: Until September 1, 1999, school districts were able to reduce the value of taxable property reported to the State to reflect any taxable value lost due to
21: TIRZ participation by the school district. The ability of the school district to deduct the taxable value of the tax increment that it contributed prevented
21: the school district from being negatively affected in terms of state school funding. However, due to a change in law, local M&O tax rate revenue
21: contributed to a TIRZ created on or after May 31, 1999 will count toward a school district’s Tier One entitlement (reducing Tier One State funds for
21: eligible school districts) and will not be considered in calculating any school district’s Tier Two entitlement (see “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL
21: FINANCE SYSTEM – STATE FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS” and “DISTRICT APPLICATION OF THE PROPERTY TAX CODE”).
21: TAX LIMITATION AGREEMENTS
21: The Texas Economic Development Act (Chapter 313, Texas Tax Code, as amended), allowed school districts to grant limitations on appraised property
21: values to certain corporations and limited liability companies to encourage economic development within the school district. Generally, during the last
21: eight (8) years of the ten-year term of a tax limitation agreement, a school district may only levy and collect M&O taxes on the agreed-to limited
21: appraised property value. For the purposes of calculating its Tier One and Tier Two entitlements, the portion of a school district’s property that is not
21: fully taxable is excluded from the school district’s taxable property values. Therefore, a school district will not be subject to a reduction in Tier One or
21: Tier Two State funds as a result of lost M&O tax revenues due to entering into a tax limitation agreement (see “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL
21: FINANCE SYSTEM – STATE FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS”). The 87th Texas Legislature did not vote to extend this program, which expired by
21: its terms effective December 31, 2022.
21: In the 88th Legislative Session, House Bill 5 (“HB 5” or “The Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation Act”) was adopted to create an economic
21: development program, subject to state oversight, which would attract jobs and investment to Texas through school district property tax abatement
21: agreements with businesses. HB5 was codified as Chapter 403, Subchapter T, Texas Government Code (“Chapter 403”) and had an effective date of
21:                                                                              13
21: 
22: January 1, 2024. Under Chapter 403, a school district may offer a 50% abatement on taxable value for maintenance and operations property taxes for
22: certain eligible projects, except that projects in a federally designated economic opportunity zone receive a 75% abatement. Chapter 403 also provides
22: a 100% abatement of maintenance and operations taxes for eligible property during a project’s construction period. Taxable valuation for purposes of
22: the debt service tax securing a series of bonds cannot be abated under Chapter 403. Eligible projects must involve manufacturing, dispatchable power
22: generation facilities, technology research/development facilities, or critical infrastructure projects and projects must create and maintain jobs, as well
22: as meet certain minimum investment requirements.
22: For a discussion of how the various exemptions described above are applied by the District, see “DISTRICT APPLICATION OF THE PROPERTY
22: TAX CODE.”
22: DISTRICT AND TAXPAYER REMEDIES
22: Under certain circumstances, taxpayers and taxing units, including the District, may appeal the determinations of the Appraisal District by timely
22: initiating a protest with the Appraisal Review Board. Additionally, taxing units such as the District may bring suit against the Appraisal District to
22: compel compliance with the Property Tax Code.
22: Owners of certain property with a taxable value in excess of the current year “minimum eligibility amount”, as determined by the State Comptroller,
22: and situated in a county with a population of one million or more, may protest the determinations of an appraisal district directly to a three-member
22: special panel of the appraisal review board, appointed by the chairman of the appraisal review board, consisting of highly qualified professionals in the
22: field of property tax appraisal. The minimum eligibility amount was set at $62,883,169 for the 2026 tax year, and is adjusted annually by the State
22: Comptroller to reflect the inflation rate.
22: The Property Tax Code sets forth notice and hearing procedures for certain tax rate increases by the District and provides for taxpayer referenda that
22: could result in the repeal of certain tax increases (see “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS – PUBLIC HEARING AND VOTER-APPROVAL TAX RATE”). The
22: Property Tax Code also establishes a procedure for providing notice to property owners of reappraisals reflecting increased property value, appraisals
22: which are higher than renditions, and appraisals of property not previously on an appraisal roll.
22: LEVY AND COLLECTION OF TAXES
22: The District is responsible for the collection of its taxes, unless it elects to transfer such functions to another governmental entity. Taxes are due October
22: 1, or when billed, whichever comes later, and become delinquent after January 31 of the following year. A delinquent tax incurs a penalty of six percent
22: (6%) of the amount of the tax for the first calendar month it is delinquent, plus one percent (1%) for each additional month or portion of a month the
22: tax remains unpaid prior to July 1 of the year in which it becomes delinquent. If the tax is not paid by July 1 of the year in which it becomes delinquent,
22: the tax incurs a total penalty of twelve percent (12%) regardless of the number of months the tax has been delinquent and incurs an additional penalty
22: of up to twenty percent (20%) of the delinquent tax, penalty, and interest collected, if imposed by the District. The delinquent tax also accrues interest
22: at a rate of one percent (1%) for each month or portion of a month it remains unpaid. The Property Tax Code also makes provision for the split payment
22: of taxes, discounts for early payment and the postponement of the delinquency date of taxes for certain taxpayers. Furthermore, the District may
22: provide, on a local option basis, for the split payment, partial payment, and discounts for early payment of taxes under certain circumstances.
22: DISTRICT’S RIGHTS IN THE EVENT OF TAX DELINQUENCIES
22: Taxes levied by the District are a personal obligation of the owner of the property. On January 1 of each year, a tax lien attaches to property to secure
22: the payment of all state and local taxes, penalties, and interest ultimately imposed for the year on the property. The lien exists in favor of each taxing
22: unit, including the District, having power to tax the property. The District’s tax lien is on a parity with tax liens of such other taxing units. A tax lien
22: on real property takes priority over the claim of most creditors and other holders of liens on the property encumbered by the tax lien, whether or not
22: the debt or lien existed before the attachment of the tax lien; however, whether a lien of the United States is on a parity with or takes priority over a tax
22: lien of the District is determined by applicable federal law. Personal property, under certain circumstances, is subject to seizure and sale for the payment
22: of delinquent taxes, penalty, and interest.
22: At any time after taxes on property become delinquent, the District may file suit to foreclose the lien securing payment of the tax, to enforce personal
22: liability for the tax, or both. In filing a suit to foreclose a tax lien on real property, the District must join other taxing units that have claims for delinquent
22: taxes against all or part of the same property.
22: Collection of delinquent taxes may be adversely affected by the amount of taxes owed to other taxing units, adverse market conditions, taxpayer
22: redemption rights, or bankruptcy proceedings which restrain the collection of a taxpayer’s debt.
22: Federal bankruptcy law provides that an automatic stay of actions by creditors and other entities, including governmental units, goes into effect with
22: the filing of any petition in bankruptcy. The automatic stay prevents governmental units from foreclosing on property and prevents liens for post petition
22: taxes from attaching to property and obtaining secured creditor status unless, in either case, an order lifting the stay is obtained from the bankruptcy
22: court. In many cases, post-petition taxes are paid as an administrative expense of the estate in bankruptcy or by order of the bankruptcy court.

23:                                              DISTRICT APPLICATION OF PROPERTY TAX CODE
23: In addition to the State mandated property tax exemptions described above, the District grants an additional exemption of 20% of the market value of
23: residence homesteads; minimum exemption of $5,000.
23: The District grants an additional $65,000 residence homestead exemption for persons 65 years of age or older and the disabled.
23: The District does not grant an exemption for freeport property and has not taken action to tax goods-in-transit.
23: The District does not permit split payments, and discounts are not allowed.
23: The District does not offer tax abatements. See “TABLE 3 – EXEMPTIONS.”
23: The District participates in 12 tax increment reinvestment zones (each, a “TIRZ,” and collectively, the “TIRZs”) created by the City of Houston, Texas.
23: The District has entered into interlocal agreements with each TIRZ to contribute a certain amount of tax increments realized in each TIRZ. Under the
23: interlocal agreements, the District is remitted a portion of its tax increment to use for school facilities throughout the District. In fiscal year 2025, the
23: District recognized approximately $38 million in net revenue from TIRZs.
23:                                                               TAX RATE LIMITATIONS
23: GENERAL
23: The maximum tax rate for the District is $1.70 per $100 of assessed valuation, as approved by the voters of the District at an election held on April 7,
23: 1962 pursuant to Article 2784g, Texas Revised Civil Statutes (the “Tax Election”).
23: M&O TAX RATE LIMITATIONS
23: The maximum M&O tax rate per $100 of taxable value that may be adopted by the District may not exceed the lesser of (A) $1.70 less the District’s
23: I&S tax rate and (B) the sum of $0.17 (subject to compression of the nine available copper pennies in a year in which the State increases the guaranteed
23: yield on those pennies) and the school district’s MCR. A school district’s MCR is, generally, inversely proportional to the change in taxable property
23: values both within the school district and the State, and is subject to recalculation annually. For any year, the highest possible MCR for a school district
23: is $0.93. See “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL FINANCE SYSTEM – LOCAL FUNDING FOR SCHOOL DISTRICTS.”
23: Furthermore, a school district cannot annually increase its tax rate in excess of the school district’s Voter-Approval Tax Rate without submitting such
23: tax rate to an election and a majority of the voters voting at such election approving the adopted rate. See “TAX RATE LIMITATIONS – PUBLIC
23: HEARING AND VOTER-APPROVAL TAX RATE.”
23: I&S TAX RATE LIMITATIONS
23: The District may authorize the issuance of bonds and levy taxes for payment therefore subject to voter approval of one or more propositions submitted
23: to the voters under Section 45.003(b)(2), Texas Education Code, as amended. Pursuant to the Tax Election, the District’s I&S tax rate may not exceed
23: $1.00 per $100 of taxable valuation. See “THE BONDS – SECURITY AND SOURCE OF PAYMENT.”
23: Section 45.0031 of the Texas Education Code, as amended, requires a school district to demonstrate to the Texas Attorney General that it has the
23: prospective ability to pay its maximum annual debt service on a proposed issue of bonds and all previously issued bonds, other than bonds approved
23: by voters of a school district at an election held on or before April 1, 1991 and issued before September 1, 1992 (or debt issued to refund such bonds,
23: collectively, “exempt bonds”), from a tax levied at a rate of $0.50 per $100 of assessed valuation before bonds may be issued (the “50-cent Test”). In
23: demonstrating the ability to pay debt service at a rate of $0.50, a school district may take into account EDA and IFA allotments to the school district,
23: which effectively reduces the school district’s local share of debt service, and may also take into account Tier One funds allotted to the school district.
23: If a school district exercises this option, it may not adopt an I&S tax until it has credited to the school district’s I&S fund an amount equal to all State
23: allotments provided solely for payment of debt service and any Tier One funds needed to demonstrate compliance with the threshold tax rate test and
23: which is received or to be received in that year. Additionally, a school district may demonstrate its ability to comply with the 50-cent Test by applying
23: the $0.50 tax rate to an amount equal to 90% of projected future taxable value of property in the school district, as certified by a registered professional
23: appraiser, anticipated for the earlier of the tax year five (5) years after the current tax year or the tax year in which the final payment for the bonds is
23: due. However, if a school district uses projected future taxable values to meet the 50-cent Test and subsequently imposes a tax at a rate greater than
23: $0.50 per $100 of valuation to pay for bonds subject to the test, then for subsequent bond issues, the Attorney General must find that the school district
23: has the projected ability to pay principal and interest on the proposed bonds and all previously issued bonds subject to the 50-cent Test from a tax rate
23: of $0.45 per $100 of valuation. Once the prospective ability to pay such tax has been shown and the bonds are issued, the District may levy an I&S tax
23: rate not to exceed $1.00 per $100 of taxable value, subject to the limitations imposed by the Tax Election. Refunding bonds issued pursuant to Chapter
23: 1207, Texas Government Code, are not subject to the 50-cent Test; however, taxes levied to pay debt service on such bonds (other than bonds issued
23:                                                                              15
23: 
24: to refund exempt bonds) are included in maximum annual debt service for calculation of the 50-cent Test when applied to subsequent bond issues that
24: are subject to the 50-cent Test. The Bonds are being issued as refunding bonds pursuant to Chapter 1207 and are not subject to the 50-cent Test.
24: PUBLIC HEARING AND VOTER-APPROVAL TAX RATE
24: A school district’s total tax rate is the combination of the M&O tax rate and the I&S tax rate. Generally, the highest rate at which a school district may
24: levy taxes for any given year without holding an election to approve the tax rate is the “Voter- Approval Tax Rate”, as described below.
24: A school district is required to adopt its annual tax rate before the later of September 30 or the sixtieth (60th) day after the date the certified appraisal
24: roll is received by the taxing unit, except that a tax rate that exceeds the Voter-Approval Tax Rate must be adopted not later than the seventy-first (71st)
24: day before the next occurring November uniform election date. A school district’s failure to adopt a tax rate equal to or less than the Voter-Approval
24: Tax Rate by September 30 or the sixtieth (60th) day after receipt of the certified appraisal roll, will result in the tax rate for such school district for the
24: tax year to be the lower of the “no-new-revenue tax rate” calculated for that tax year or the tax rate adopted by the school district for the preceding tax
24: year. A school district’s failure to adopt a tax rate in excess of the Voter-Approval Tax Rate on or prior to the seventy-first (71st) day before the next
24: occurring November uniform election date, will result in the school district adopting a tax rate equal to or less than its Voter-Approval Tax Rate by the
24: later of September 30 or the sixtieth (60th) day after receipt of the certified appraisal roll. “No-new-revenue tax rate” means the rate that will produce
24: the prior year’s total tax levy from the current year’s total taxable values, adjusted such that lost values are not included in the calculation of the prior
24: year’s taxable values and new values are not included in the current year’s taxable values.
24: The Voter-Approval Tax Rate for a school district is the sum of (i) the school district’s MCR; (ii) the greater of (a) the school district’s Enrichment
24: Tax Rate for the preceding year, less any amount by which the school district is required to reduce its current year Enrichment Tax Rate pursuant to
24: Section 48.202(f), Education Code, as amended, or (b) the rate of $0.05 per $100 of taxable value; and (iii) the school district’s current I&S tax rate. A
24: school district’s M&O tax rate may not exceed the rate equal to the sum of (i) $0.17 (subject to compression of the nine available copper pennies in a
24: year in which the State increases the guaranteed yield on those pennies) and (ii) the school district’s MCR. See “CURRENT PUBLIC SCHOOL
24: FINANCE SYSTEM” herein, for more information regarding the State Compression Percentage, MCR, and the Enrichment Tax Rate.
24: The governing body of a school district generally cannot adopt a tax rate exceeding the school district's Voter-Approval Tax Rate without approval by
24: a majority of the voters approving the higher rate at an election to be held on the next uniform election date. Further, subject to certain exceptions for
24: areas declared disaster areas, State law requires the board of trustees of a school district to conduct an efficiency audit before seeking voter approval to
24: adopt a tax rate exceeding the Voter-Approval Tax Rate and sets certain parameters for conducting and disclosing the results of such efficiency audit.
24: An election is not required for a tax increase to address increased expenditures resulting from certain natural disasters in the year following the year in
24: which such disaster occurs; however, the amount by which the increased tax rate exceeds the school district’s Voter-Approval Tax Rate for such year
24: may not be considered by the school district in the calculation of its subsequent Voter-Approval Tax Rate.
24: The calculation of the Voter-Approval Tax Rate may limit or impact the District’s ability to set an I&S tax rate in each year sufficient to pay
24: debt service on all of the District’s tax-supported debt obligations, including the Bonds.
24: Before adopting its annual tax rate, a public meeting must be held for the purpose of adopting a budget for the succeeding year. A notice of public
24: meeting to discuss the school district’s budget and proposed tax rate must be published in the time, format and manner prescribed in Section 44.004 of
24: the Texas Education Code. Section 44.004(e) of the Texas Education Code provides that a person who owns taxable property in a school district is
24: entitled to an injunction restraining the collection of taxes by the school district if the school district has not complied with such notice requirements
24: or the language and format requirements of such notice as set forth in Section 44.004(b), (c), (c-1), (c-2), and (d), and, if applicable, subsection (i) of
24: the Texas Education Code, and if such failure to comply was not in good faith. Section 44.004(e) of the Texas Education Code further provides the
24: action to enjoin the collection of taxes must be filed before the date the school district delivers substantially all of its tax bills. A school district that
24: elects to adopt a tax rate before the adoption of a budget for the fiscal year that begins in the current tax year may adopt a tax rate for the current tax
24: year before receipt of the certified appraisal roll, so long as the chief appraiser of the appraisal district in which the school district participates has
24: certified to the assessor for the school district an estimate of the taxable value of property in the school district. If a school district adopts its tax rate
24: prior to the adoption of its budget, both the no-new-revenue tax rate and the Voter-Approval Tax Rate of the school district shall be calculated based
24: on the school district’s certified estimate of taxable value. A school district that adopts a tax rate before adopting its budget must hold a public hearing
24: on the proposed tax rate followed by another public hearing on the proposed budget rather than holding a single hearing on the two items.
24: A school district must annually calculate and prominently post on its internet website and submit to the county tax assessor-collector for each county
24: in which all or part of the school district is located, its Voter-Approval Tax Rate in accordance with forms prescribed by the State Comptroller.

31: RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH BUILD AMERICA BONDS
31: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (“ARRA”) authorized the issuance of Build America Bonds, which
31: permitted issuers to elect to receive payments equal to 35% of the interest payable on the Build America Bonds. The District issued
31: and currently receives payments from the federal government with respect to its Limited Tax Schoolhouse Bonds Taxable Series
31: 2009A-2 (Build America Bonds - Direct Payment to Issuer) and its Limited Tax Schoolhouse Bonds Taxable Series 2009A-3
31: (Build America Bonds - Direct Payment to Issuer).
31: Pursuant to the requirements of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, as amended, payments to certain
31: state and local government filers claiming payments applicable to certain qualified bonds are subject to sequestration. This means
31: that payments from the federal government for Build America Bonds processed on or after October 1, 2020 were reduced by 5.7%,
31: and will remain at this level until on or before September 30, 2030. The sequestration reduction rate will be applied unless and until
31: a law is enacted that cancels or otherwise impacts the sequester, at which time the sequestration reduction rate is subject to change.
31: The District makes no representation with respect to any future changes in funding subsidies on Build America Bonds.

31: EMPLOYEES’ RETIREMENT PLANS

31: Retirement System of Texas (“TRS”). State contributions are made to cover costs of the TRS retirement plan up to certain statutory
31: limits. The District is obligated for a portion of TRS costs relating to employee salaries that exceed the statutory limit. For the
31: District’s fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, the State contributed $81,617,665 to TRS on behalf of the District, District employees
31: paid $128,535,260 and contributions from the District were $72,193,127.

31: as required to be reported in the District’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report as of June 30, 2025. The NPL was measured
31: as of August 31, 2023, and rolled forward to August 31, 2024 and the total pension liability used to calculate the NPL was
31: determined by an actuarial valuation as of August 31, 2023.

33: TABLE 11 - GENERAL FUND REVENUE AND EXPENDITURE HISTORY
33: The District maintains four separate principal funds: a general fund used to finance a majority of its current operations; a special
33: revenue fund for certain State and federal grants made for specific operating purposes; a debt service fund; and a capital renovation
33: fund. All ad valorem taxes and a major portion of State and federal grants are allocated among such funds. All ad valorem taxes
33: levied for maintenance are allocated to the general fund. All ad valorem taxes levied for debt service are allocated to the debt
33: service fund.
33: All federal and State funds, except those for designated purposes, are placed in the general fund. Other non-revenue receipts are
33: designated for the capital renovation fund. The general and special revenue funds are generally utilized for operating expenditures.
33: The debt service fund and the capital renovation fund are restricted for debt service and capital renovation purposes, respectively.

33: by the District.

33: anticipates an approximately $14.6 million budget deficit. Due to budget reduction measures, the shortfall may be less than

35: The District may invest its investable funds (including bond proceeds and money pledged to the payment of or as security for bonds
35: or other indebtedness issued by the District or obligations under a lease, installment sale, or other agreement of the District) in
35: investments authorized by State law in accordance with investment policies approved by the governing body of the District. Both
35: State law and the District’s investment policies are subject to change.
35: LEGAL INVESTMENTS
35: Under State law, the District is authorized to invest in (1) obligations, including letters of credit, of the United States or its agencies
35: and instrumentalities, including the Federal Home Loan Banks; (2) direct obligations of the State or its agencies and
35: instrumentalities; (3) collateralized mortgage obligations directly issued by a federal agency or instrumentality of the United States,
35: the underlying security for which is guaranteed by an agency or instrumentality of the United States; (4) other obligations, the
35: principal and interest of which are unconditionally guaranteed or insured by, or backed by the full faith and credit of, the State or
35: the United States or their respective agencies and instrumentalities, including obligations that are fully guaranteed or insured by
35: the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or by the explicit full faith and credit of the United States; (5) obligations of states,
35: agencies, counties, cities, and other political subdivisions of any state rated as to investment quality by a nationally recognized
35: investment rating firm not less than “A” or its equivalent; (6) bonds issued, assumed or guaranteed by the State of Israel; (7)
35: interest-bearing banking deposits that are guaranteed or insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or its successor, or
35: the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund or its successor; (8) interest-bearing banking deposits other than those described
35: by clause (7) if (A) the funds invested in the banking deposits are invested through: (i) a broker with a main office or branch office
35: in this State that the District selects from a list the governing body of the District or designated investment committee of the District
35: adopts as required by Section 2256.025, Texas Government Code; or (ii) a depository institution with a main office or branch office
35: in the State that the District selects; (B) the broker or depository institution selected as described by (A) above arranges for the
35: deposit of the funds in the banking deposits in one or more federally insured depository institutions, regardless of where located,
35: for the District’s account; (C) the full amount of the principal and accrued interest of the banking deposits is insured by the United
35: States or an instrumentality of the United States; and (D) the District appoints as the District’s custodian of the banking deposits
35: issued for the District’s account: (i) the depository institution selected as described by (A) above; (ii) an entity described by Section
35: 2257.041(d), Texas Government Code; or (iii) a clearing broker dealer registered with the SEC and operating under SEC Rule
35: 15c3-3; (9) (i) certificates of deposit or share certificates meeting the requirements of Chapter 2256, Texas Government Code (the
35: “Public Funds Investment Act”), that are issued by an institution that has its main office or a branch office in the State and are

35: law, or (B) a depository institution that has its main office or branch office in the State that is selected by the District, (b) the broker
35: or the depository institution selected by the District arranges for the deposit of the funds in certificates of deposit in one or more

36: Section 270.2a-7), promulgated under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. Section 80a-1 et seq.); and (15) no-load
36: mutual funds registered with the SEC that have an average weighted maturity of less than two years, and have either (a) a duration
36: of one year or more and invest exclusively in obligations described in under this heading, or (b) a duration of less than one year

36: may be invested in guaranteed investment contracts that have a defined termination date and are secured by obligations, including
36: letters of credit, of the United States or its agencies and instrumentalities, other than the prohibited obligations described below, in
36: an amount at least equal to the amount of bond proceeds invested under such contract.
36: A political subdivision such as the District may enter into securities lending programs if (i) the securities loaned under the program
36: are 100% collateralized, a loan made under the program allows for termination at any time and a loan made under the program is
36: either secured by (a) obligations that are described in clauses (1) through (8) above, other than the prohibited obligations described
36: below, (b) irrevocable letters of credit issued by a state or national bank that is continuously rated by a nationally recognized
36: investment rating firm at not less than A or its equivalent or (c) cash invested in obligations described in clauses (1) through (8)
36: above, clauses (13) through (15) above, or an authorized investment pool; (ii) securities held as collateral under a loan are pledged
36: to the District, held in the District’s name and deposited at the time the investment is made with the District or a third party
36: designated by the District; (iii) a loan made under the program is placed through either a primary government securities dealer or
36: a financial institution doing business in the State; and (iv) the agreement to lend securities has a term of one year or less.
36: The District may invest in such obligations directly or through government investment pools that invest solely in such obligations
36: provided that the pools are rated no lower than “AAA” or “AAA-m” or an equivalent by at least one nationally recognized rating
36: service if the governing body of the District authorizes such investment in the particular pool by order, ordinance, or resolution and
36: the investment pool complies with the requirements of Section 2256.016, Texas Government Code.
36: The District may also contract with an investment management firm registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (15
36: U.S.C. Section 80b-1 et seq.) or with the State Securities Board to provide for the investment and management of its public funds
36: or other funds under its control for a term up to two years, but the District retains ultimate responsibility as fiduciary of its assets.
36: In order to renew or extend such a contract, the District must do so by order, ordinance, or resolution.
36: The District is specifically prohibited from investing in: (1) obligations whose payment represents the coupon payments on the
36: outstanding principal balance of the underlying mortgage-backed security collateral and pays no principal; (2) obligations whose
36: payment represents the principal stream of cash flow from the underlying mortgage-backed security and bears no interest;
36: (3) collateralized mortgage obligations that have a stated final maturity of greater than 10 years; and (4) collateralized mortgage
36: obligations the interest rate of which is determined by an index that adjusts opposite to the changes in a market index.
36: As a school district that qualifies as an issuer under Chapter 1371, the District is also authorized to purchase, sell, and invest its
36: funds in corporate bonds that, at the time of purchase, are rated by a nationally recognized investment rating firm “AA-” or the
36: equivalent and have a stated final maturity that is not later than the third anniversary of the date the corporate bonds were purchased.
36: Texas law defines “corporate bonds” as senior secured debt obligations issued by a domestic business entity and rated not lower
36: than “AA-” or the equivalent by a nationally recognized investment rating firm. The term does not include a debt obligation that is
36: convertible into stocks or shares in the entity issuing the bond (or an affiliate or subsidy thereof) or any unsecured debt. Corporate
36: bonds must finally mature not later than 3 years from their date of purchase by the school district. A school district may not (1)
36: invest more than 15% of its monthly average fund balance (excluding bond proceeds, reserves, and other funds held for the payment
36: of debt service) in corporate bonds; or (2) invest more than 25% of the funds invested in corporate bonds in any one domestic
36: business entity (including subsidiaries and affiliates thereof). Corporate bonds held by a school district must be sold if they are at
36: any time downgraded below “AA-” (or the equivalent thereof) or, with respect to a corporate bond rated “AA-” (or the equivalent
36: thereof), such corporate bond is placed on negative credit watch. Corporate bonds are not an eligible investment for a public funds
36: investment pool. To invest in corporate bonds, an eligible school district must first (i) amend its investment policy to authorize
36: corporate bonds as an eligible investment, (ii) adopt procedures for monitoring rating changes in corporate bonds and liquidating
36: an investment in corporate bonds, and (iii) identify funds eligible to be invested in corporate bonds. The District has taken these
36: steps to authorize the investment of District funds in corporate bonds.
36: ADDITIONAL PROVISIONS
36: Under State law, the District is additionally required to: (1) annually review its adopted policies and strategies; (2) adopt a written
36: instrument by rule, order, ordinance or resolution stating that it has reviewed its investment policy and investment strategies and
36: recording any changes made to either its investment policy or investment strategy; (3) require any investment officers with personal
36: business relationships or relatives with firms seeking to sell securities to the District to disclose the relationship and file a statement
36: with the Texas Ethics Commission and the Board; (4) require the qualified representative of a business organization offering to
36: engage in an investment transaction with the District to: (a) receive and review the District’s investment policy, (b) acknowledge
36: that reasonable controls and procedures have been implemented to preclude investment transactions conducted between the District
36: and the business organization that are not authorized by the District’s investment policy (except to the extent that this authorization
36: is dependent on an analysis of the makeup of the District’s entire portfolio or requires an interpretation of subjective investment
36:                                                                     28
36: 
37: standards), and (c) deliver a written statement in a form acceptable to the District and the business organization attesting to these
37: requirements (a business organization as defined by statute to be either an investment pool or an investment management firm
37: under contract to manage the District’s portfolio with discretionary authority); (5) perform an annual audit of the management
37: controls on investments and adherence to the District’s investment policy; (6) provide specific investment training for the treasurer,
37: chief financial officer and investment officers; (7) restrict reverse repurchase agreements to not more than 90 days and restrict the
37: investment of reverse repurchase agreement funds to no greater than the term of the reverse repurchase agreement; (8) restrict the
37: investment in no-load mutual funds in the aggregate to no more than 15% of the District’s monthly average fund balance, excluding
37: bond proceeds and reserves and other funds held for debt service; (9) require local government investment pools to conform to the
37: new disclosure, rating, net asset value, yield calculation, and advisory board requirements; and (10) at least annually review, revise
37: and adopt a list of qualified brokers that are authorized to engage in investment transactions with the District.
37: DISTRICT’S INVESTMENT POLICY
37: The District maintains a conservative investment policy. The District’s goal is to minimize credit and market risks while
37: maintaining a competitive yield on its portfolio. Funds of the District are invested either in Certificates of Deposit, short-term U.S.
37: Government or Agency Notes and Discount Notes, TexPool, the Lone Star Investment Pool, TexSTAR, municipal bonds, or money
37: market accounts. All cash deposits are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) or are secured by collateral
37: held at the Federal Reserve Bank or through Federal Home Loan Bank Letters of Credit. The District does not currently own, nor
37: does it anticipate the inclusion of derivative products in the District’s portfolio. Please refer to Note No. 3 of the District’s Audited
37: Financial Statement (APPENDIX A) for a more complete description of the District’s investments.

37: regulations, rulings and court decisions, and assuming, among other matters, the accuracy of certain representations and compliance
37: with certain covenants, interest on the Bonds is excluded from gross income for federal income tax purposes under Section 103 of
37: the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (the “Code”). Bond Counsel is of the further opinion that interest on the Bonds is not a specific
37: preference item for purposes of the federal individual alternative minimum tax. Bond Counsel expresses no opinion regarding any
37: other tax consequences related to the ownership or disposition of, or the amount, accrual or receipt of interest on, the Bonds. The
37: proposed form of opinion of Bond Counsel is set forth in APPENDIX B hereto.
37: To the extent the issue price of any maturity of the Bonds is less than the amount to be paid at maturity of such Bonds (excluding
37: amounts stated to be interest and payable at least annually over the term of such Bonds), the difference constitutes “original issue
37: discount,” the accrual of which, to the extent properly allocable to each Beneficial Owner thereof, is treated as interest on the Bonds
37: which is excluded from gross income for federal income tax purposes. For this purpose, the issue price of a particular maturity of
37: the Bonds is the first price at which a substantial amount of such maturity of the Bonds is sold to the public (excluding bond houses,
37:                                                                    29
37: 
38: brokers, or similar persons or organizations acting in the capacity of underwriters, placement agents or wholesalers). The original
38: issue discount with respect to any maturity of the Bonds accrues daily over the term to maturity of such Bonds on the basis of a
38: constant interest rate compounded semiannually (with straight-line interpolations between compounding dates). The accruing
38: original issue discount is added to the adjusted basis of such Bonds to determine taxable gain or loss upon disposition (including
38: sale, redemption, or payment on maturity) of such Bonds. Beneficial Owners of the Bonds should consult their own tax advisors
38: with respect to the tax consequences of ownership of Bonds with original issue discount, including the treatment of Beneficial
38: Owners who do not purchase such Bonds in the original offering to the public at the first price at which a substantial amount of
38: such Bonds is sold to the public.
38: Bonds purchased, whether at original issuance or otherwise, for an amount higher than their principal amount payable at maturity
38: (or, in some cases, at their earlier call date) (“Premium Bonds”) will be treated as having amortizable bond premium. No deduction
38: is allowable for the amortizable bond premium in the case of obligations, like the Premium Bonds, the interest on which is excluded
38: from gross income for federal income tax purposes. However, the amount of tax-exempt interest received, and a Beneficial Owner’s
38: basis in a Premium Bond, will be reduced by the amount of amortizable bond premium properly allocable to such Beneficial Owner.
38: Beneficial Owners of Premium Bonds should consult their own tax advisors with respect to the proper treatment of amortizable
38: bond premium in their particular circumstances.
38: The Code imposes various restrictions, conditions and requirements relating to the exclusion from gross income for federal income
38: tax purposes of interest on obligations such as the Bonds. The District has made certain representations and covenanted to comply
38: with certain restrictions, conditions and requirements designed to ensure that interest on the Bonds will not be included in federal
38: gross income. Inaccuracy of these representations or failure to comply with these covenants may result in interest on the Bonds
38: being included in gross income for federal income tax purposes, possibly from the date of original issuance of the Bonds. The
38: opinion of Bond Counsel assumes the accuracy of these representations and compliance with these covenants. Bond Counsel has
38: not undertaken to determine (or to inform any person) whether any actions taken (or not taken), or events occurring (or not
38: occurring), or any other matters coming to Bond Counsel’s attention after the date of issuance of the Bonds may adversely affect
38: the value of or the tax status of interest on the Bonds. Accordingly, the opinion of Bond Counsel is not intended to, and may not,
38: be relied upon in connection with any such actions, events or matters.
38: Although Bond Counsel is of the opinion that interest on the Bonds is excluded from gross income for federal income tax purposes,
38: the ownership or disposition of, or the accrual or receipt of amounts treated as interest on the Bonds may otherwise affect a
38: Beneficial Owner’s federal, state or local tax liability. The nature and extent of these other tax consequences depends upon the
38: particular tax status of the Beneficial Owner or the Beneficial Owner’s other items of income or deduction. Bond Counsel expresses
38: no opinion regarding any such other tax consequences.
38: Current and future legislative proposals, if enacted into law, clarification of the Code or court decisions may cause interest on the

40:                                                         WEATHER EVENTS
40: The District is located near the Texas Gulf Coast. The region is prone to seasonal hurricane activity; major hurricanes and related
40: storms may develop. Owing in part to its relatively flat topography and moist coastal climate, certain areas of the region are subject
40: to periodic flooding and associated severe property damage because of hurricanes and storms. For example, the District was
40: impacted by Tropical Storm Beryl in July 2024 and a Derecho in May 2024. Tropical Storm Beryl caused structural damage to
40: multiple District campuses and widespread power outages, while Derecho resulted in significant roof and infrastructure damage
40: across at least 60 campuses. Despite these challenges, the District successfully recovered much of the associated costs through
40: insurance claims and FEMA assistance.
40: If a future weather event significantly damaged all or part of the properties comprising the tax base within the District, the assessed
40: value of property within the District could be substantially reduced, which could result in a decrease in tax revenues and/or
40: necessitate an increase the District’s tax rate. Texas law allows school districts to increase property tax rates without voter approval
40: upon the occurrence of certain disasters such as floods and upon a gubernatorial or presidential declaration of disaster. See “TAX
40: RATE LIMITATIONS – Public Hearing and Voter-Approval Tax Rate.” There can be no assurance that a casualty loss to taxable
40: property within the District will be covered by insurance (or that property owners will even carry flood or other casualty insurance),
40: that any insurance company will fulfill its obligation to provide insurance proceeds, or that insurance proceeds will be used to
40: rebuild or repair any damaged improvements within the District or be sufficient for such purposes. Even if insurance proceeds are
40: available and improvements are rebuilt, there could be a lengthy period in which assessed values within the District could be
40: adversely affected.
40: The District has developed procedures for storm damage mitigation and prevention. The procedures include, for example,
40: developing storm emergency and disaster plans, coordinating with local authorities, equipping a facility service emergency
40: command center and assigning responsibilities for certain officials regarding storm preparation and disaster response. In addition,
40: many school and facility sites that were reconstructed in the 100-year flood plain have been elevated during reconstruction to
40: reduce damage due to flooding.
40:                                                                    32
40: 
41:                                                        CYBERSECURITY
41: The District, like other school districts in the State, utilizes technology in conducting its operations. As a user of technology, the
41: District potentially faces cybersecurity threats (e.g., hacking, phishing, viruses, malware and ransomware) on its technology
41: systems. Accordingly, the District may be the target of a cyber-attack on its technology systems that could result in adverse
41: consequences to the District.
41: The District has taken steps to enhance and protect information systems and information of the District. In 2013, the District began
41: implementing an Information Security Program, which authorizes the District’s Chief Information Officer to manage District-wide
41: information technology risk and develop a District-wide information security program. Since 2019, the District has been required
41: by State law to maintain a cybersecurity plan and require employees to receive annual cybersecurity training, among other
41: requirements. The District also currently conducts annual cybersecurity risk audits. The District has adopted certain practices for
41: the establishment and maintenance of information technology security controls. Specific objectives of the security plan include (i)
41: establishing a secure infrastructure and a stable processing environment; (ii) effectively managing the risk of information
41: technology security exposure or compromise within the District’s environment; (iii) protecting the District’s reputation, schools,
41: and image; (iv) supporting the establishment and maintenance of an Information Security Program within the District; (v)
41: establishing and communicating accountability for acceptable and unacceptable use of the District’s information assets, supporting
41: systems and processes; (vi) communicating the responsibilities for the protection of information to each individual, as
41: representatives of the District; (vii) protecting and preserving management’s options in the event of an information asset misuse,
41: loss or unauthorized disclosure; and (viii) providing controls over access to data by a combination of adequate physical, system,
41: remote access and application security.
41: While the District has taken steps to enhance and protect information systems and requires employees to receive cybersecurity
41: training, as required by State law, among other efforts, cybersecurity breaches could cause material disruptions to the District’s
41: finances or operations. The costs of remedying such breaches or protecting against future cyber-attacks could be substantial.
41: Further, cybersecurity breaches could expose the District to litigation and other legal risks, which could cause the District to incur
41: other costs related to such legal claims or proceedings.
41:                                          EXPOSURE TO OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY
41: In the past, the greater Houston area has been affected by adverse conditions in the oil and gas industry, and adverse conditions in
41: the oil and gas industry and spillover effects into other industries could adversely impact the businesses of ad valorem property
41: taxpayers and the property values in the District, resulting in a reduction in property tax revenue. The Bonds are secured by a
41: continuing direct annual ad valorem tax levied, within the limits prescribed by law, on all taxable property located within the
41: District, and a reduction in property values may require an increase in the ad valorem tax rate required to pay the Bonds. Reductions
41: in oil and gas revenues may also have an adverse effect on State revenues available during the next biennium, which may impact
41: how the State funds education.

42: LEGAL INVESTMENTS AND ELIGIBILITY TO SECURE PUBLIC FUNDS IN TEXAS
42: Under the Texas Public Security Procedures Act (Texas Government Code, Chapter 1201), the Bonds are (i) negotiable instruments,
42: (ii) investment securities to which Chapter 8 of the Texas Business and Commerce Code applies, and (iii) legal and authorized
42: investments for (A) an insurance company, (B) a fiduciary or trustee, or (C) a sinking fund of a municipality or other political
42: subdivision or public agency of the State of Texas. The Bonds are eligible to secure deposits of any public funds of the State, its
42: agencies and political subdivisions, and are legal security for those deposits to the extent of their market value. For political
42: subdivisions in Texas which have adopted investment policies and guidelines in accordance with the Public Funds Investment Act
42: (Texas Government Code, Chapter 2256), the Bonds may have to be assigned a rating of at least “A” or its equivalent as to
42: investment quality by a national rating agency before such obligations are eligible investments for sinking funds and other public
42: funds (see “RATINGS”).
42: In addition, various provisions of the Texas Finance Code provide that, subject to a prudent investor standard, the Bonds are legal
42: investments for state banks, savings banks, trust companies with at least $1 million of capital and savings and loan associations.
42: The District has made no investigation of other laws, rules, regulations or investment criteria which might apply to such institutions
42: or entities or which might limit the suitability of the Bonds for any of the foregoing purposes or limit the authority of such
42: institutions or entities to purchase or invest in the Bonds for such purposes. The District has made no review of laws in other states

56: financial operations to the Board of Managers (the "Board"), taxpayers, grantor agencies, employees, the Texas
56: Education Agency, and other interested parties.
56: The Texas Education Code requires that all school districts file an annual report with the Texas Education Agency
56: (TEA) within 150 days of the close of each fiscal year. However, due to delays in both the development of TEA's
56: new audit application and the release of the final 2025 Office of Management and Budget (0MB) Compliance
56: Supplement, the submission deadline has been extended to February 2026. The annual report must be prepared in
56: accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) as applicable to governmental entities and must
56: be audited by a firm of independent licensed certified public accountants. This Annual Comprehensive Financial
56: Report is submitted in fulfillment of that requirement. An audit was conducted in accordance with Government
56: Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States and the requirements ofTitle 2 U.S. Code
56: of Federal Regulations Part 200, Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements
56: for Federal Awards Uniform Guidance and Texas Grant Management Standards (TxGMS). The financial statements
56: of the District have been audited by Weaver and Tidwell, L.L.P.
56: To the best of our knowledge and belief, the enclosed information is accurate in all material respects and is
56: reported in a manner designed to fairly present the financial position as well as the financial condition of the District.
56: Disclosures necessary to enable the reader to gain understanding of such financial operations have been included .
56: Responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of the data presented, as well as the presentation of this report,
56: rests with District management.
56: GAAP requires that management provide a narrative introduction, overview, and analysis to accompany the basic
56: financial statements in the form of Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A). This letter of transmittal is
56: designed to complement the MD&A and should be read in conjunction with it. The District's MD&A can be found
56: immediately following the report of the independent auditors.
56: PROFILE OF THE HOUSTON INDEPENDENT SCHOOL DISTRICT
56: The District was created and incorporated by an act of the Thirty-Eighth Legislature of the State of Texas in 1923.
56: As required by House Bill 1842, passed in 2015 by the Texas legislature, Texas Education Commissioner Mike
56: Morath appointed the nine-member Board of Managers to temporarily replace the elected board of trustees on
56: June 1, 2023. The Board of Managers has the same authority as the elected trustees and will be responsible for
56: overseeing the management of the school district. Based on legislative authority codified in the Texas Education
56: Code, the Board (1) has exclusive power and duty to govern and oversee the District; (2) can acquire and hold real
56: and personal property, sue and be sued, and hold all rights and titles to school property; (3) shall have power to levy
56: and collect taxes and to issue bonds; (4) can contract for appointed officers, teachers, and other personnel as well
56: as for goods and services; and (5) has the right of eminent domain to acquire real property.
56: HISD, with an enrollment of 176,727 students, is the tenth-largest public school system in the nation and the largest
56: in Texas. The District encompasses 333 square miles within Harris County, Texas including 51 % of the current
56: geographic area of the City of Houston and all or part of four other cities or villages. HISD is an ethnically diverse
56: district as 61 .8 percent of all students are Hispanic, 20.9 percent are African American, 9.9 percent are White, 5.1
56: percent are Asian and 2.3 percent are of other ethnicities.
56:                                                            -2-
56: 
57:                 ~    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
57:                 1 SCHOOL DISTRICT
57: Board of Education
57: January 15, 2026
57: Houston Independent School District provides services through 274 schools, of which 8 are early childhood centers
57: (pre-kindergarten for four-year-old students), 159 elementary schools (grades K-5), 39 middle schools (grades 6-8),
57: 37 high schools (grades 9-12) and 31 combination/alternative sites. The average age of the District's schools is 46
57: years. A list of school buildings with year of construction can be found in the Statistical Data Section. (See pages
57: 131-152)
57: Four division superintendents oversee the elementary, middle, high school and alternative/charter schools.
57: Approximately four senior executive directors, twelve executive directors of instruction, and four executive directors
57: of support report to the division superintendents. These individuals provide leadership to principals, align resources
57: and support for teachers, and ensure that the district is providing equitable and quality educational opportunities to
57: students. HISD's organization is designed to emphasize teaching and learning, align school goals and programs
57: for sustained improvement, eliminate duplicated services, and provide greater oversight of data and compliance
57: with state laws and regulations.
57: The District serves its diverse student population through an intensive core curriculum and specialized instructional
57: and career programs. The District provides a full range of programs and services to its students, including elementary
57: and secondary courses for general, vocational, and college preparatory levels, as well as magnet, and gifted and
57: talented programs. Academic programs are supplemented by a variety of co-curricular and extracurricular activities.
57: In addition to the regular educational programs, the District offers programs in special education, bilingual, and
57: compensatory education . HISD contracted for the operation of 7 external performance (charter) schools which are
57: funded with state funds that flow through the District.
57: ECONOMIC OUTLOOK
57: Houston is the largest city in Texas and the fourth most populous city in the United States with a population of 2.4
57: million, and 7.8 million people in the Houston metro area. The region's largest industries are energy, aerospace and
57: aviation, life sciences and biotechnology, and transportation and logistics. Employment in the Houston Metropolitan
57: Statistical Area stood at 3.730 million people in June 2025 per the Texas Workforce Commission, up 1% percent from
57: one year earlier. Houston's economy continues to grow, but at a slower pace than in previous years. Per the Greater
57: Houston Partnership, Houston's economy is performing well but uncertainty and rising material costs are leading
57: businesses to take a cautious posture. Local sales and use tax collections are up, indicating robust spending .
57: Construction and airport traffic are down when compared to last year, but home and vehicle sales have risen.
57: LONG-TERM FINANCIAL PLANNING
57: The District is subject to the state's target revenue formula for school district funding . Under the allocation
57: methodology, the District's maintenance and operations revenue from property taxes and state aid is determined
57: by a state formula based on weighted average daily attendance. As collections from property taxes increase, state
57: aid is reduced . The District is challenged with providing salary increases and other inflationary fixed costs within
57: this allocation methodology. The District is constantly adjusting future projections as costs in the market shift and as
57: changes are proposed or adopted by the Texas Legislature.
57: Enrollment decreased from the 2023-24 school year by 7,382 students. The 2025-26 budget includes an additional
57: reduction of 6,528 students. As of October 2025, the District's certified net taxable value for the 2025 tax year
57: increased by 2.8 percent. The collection rate for fiscal year 2025 was 97 percent. The District expects to maintain
57: a 97 percent collection rate.
57: With the 2017 fiscal year, the Houston Independent School District began paying recapture, now known as
57: "contracted instructional services between public schools". Under the current state finance system, the District
57: sends funds to the state if local revenue exceeds its entitlement. As of June 30, 2025, the District's "contracted
57: instructional services between public schools" expense was $56.9 million.

58: ACCOUNTING AND BUDGETARY CONTROLS
58: The diverse nature of the District's operations and the necessity of legal compliance preclude recording the financial
58: transactions of the District in a single fund . The District's accounting system is organized and operated on a "fund
58: basis." Each fund is a distinct, self-balancing accounting entity. The various funds are fully described in Note 1 of
58: the "Notes to the Basic Financial Statements" starting on page 39.
58: In developing, evaluating, and improving the District's accounting system, consideration is given to the adequacy
58: of the internal control structure. Internal controls are designed to provide management with reasonable, but not
58: absolute, assurance that assets are safeguarded against loss from unauthorized use or disposition and those
58: transactions are executed in accordance with management's authorization and recorded properly to permit the
58: preparation of financial statements in accordance with GMP. The concept of reasonable assurance recognizes
58: that the cost of a control should not exceed the benefits likely to be derived, and the evaluation of costs and benefits
58: requires estimates and judgments by management.
58: All internal control evaluations occur within the above-mentioned framework. We believe the District's internal
58: control structure adequately safeguards assets and provides reasonable assurance of the proper recording of
58: financial transactions.
58: As a recipient of federal, state, and local grants, the District is also responsible for an adequate internal control
58: structure that ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations related to these grants. All funded grants are
58: subject to testing as part of the District's Single Audit as mandated by the Uniform Guidance. The internal control
58: structure is subject to ongoing reviews by management. As a part of the District's Single Audit, tests are conducted
58: to determine the adequacy of the internal control structure as related to state and federal award programs as well
58: as compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The Single Audit reports are included in the compliance section
58: of this report.
58: The District utilizes a line-item budget of proposed expenditures and the means of financing them. The emphasis
58: of the budget process is to identify the activities requiring resources and to rank those activities according to the
58: needs of the entire District. Budgetary control is maintained at the function level by organizational unit through the
58: encumbrance of estimated purchase amounts to coincide with the execution of contracts, approval of personnel
58: transactions, or release of purchase orders to vendors. The Board approves annual budgets for the General Fund,
58: Debt Service Fund, and Nutrition Services Fund. Budgets for Special Revenue funds (other than the Food Service
58: Fund) and Capital Projects Fund are prepared on a project basis, based on grant regulations or applicable bond
58: requirements.
58: MAJOR INITIATIVES
58: Houston ISD has continued advancing several major academic, operational, and governance initiatives aligned with
58: Superintendent Miles' Destination 2035 framework and the New Education System (NES).
58: Academic and Instructional Initiatives
58:      • Curriculum Standardization: Nearly all HISD campuses-all but five-have opted into the district-developed
58:        curriculum for implementation in the 2025-26 school year, ensuring consistent, high-quality instructional
58:        materials across schools.
58:       • Expansion of NES Campuses: The district extended the NES model to 45 additional campuses in 2024-25,
58:         reallocating central resources to support historically underperforming schools. It is important to note that of
58:         the 121 D and F school the current administration started with there are only 18 D schools left at the end of
58:         school year 2025. Also, the goal is by 2027 there will only be A and B schools.
58: Human Capital and Teacher Quality
58:    • HISD issued over 7,000 teacher contracts for the 2025-26 school year, with increased emphasis on
58:      certification compliance and performance accountability.
58:                                                           -4-
58: 
59:                 ~    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
59:                 1 SCHOOL DISTRICT
59: Board of Education
59: January 15, 2026
59:       • Teacher staffing adjustments reflect continued focus on instructional excellence and differentiated
59:         compensation models introduced under NES.
59: Operational Improvements
59:      • Transportation System Overhaul: HISD restructured the transportation department for 2025-26, redesigning
59:        roles and setting new ride-time standards to enhance efficiency and student access.
59:       • Unified Family Communication Platform: The district launched ParentSquare, consolidating multiple
59:         systems into a single communication platform for parents and guardians.
59:       • Facilities and Infrastructure Upgrades: Following the defeat of the 2024 bond proposal, HISD approved
59:         approximately $120 million in Maintenance Tax Notes to address priority facility needs, including HVAC,
59:         roofing, technology, and transportation upgrades, and to fund development of the new Career and Technical
59:         Education (GTE) Center at the Grimes Facility.
59: Governance and Oversight
59:      • The Texas Education Agency (TEA) extended its intervention in HISD through June 2027, with four new
59:        members appointed to the Board of Managers to continue oversight of district reforms and performance
59:        outcomes.
59: Collectively, these initiatives reflect HISD's continued progress toward sustainable academic improvement,
59: operational efficiency, and accountability. The district remains focused on aligning resources, systems, and
59: governance with long-term strategic goals under Destination 2035.

59: Perhaps no responsibility is as great as that of educating our youth, and all of our efforts lead back to the classroom.

59: ASBO Certificate of Excellence
59: The District received the Association of School Business Officials' ("ASBO") Certificate of Excellence in Financial
59: Reporting for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. The District has received this award for 46 consecutive years.
59: This award certifies that the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report substantially conforms to the principles and
59: standards of financial reporting as recommended and adopted by ASBO.
59: GFOA Certificate of Achievement
59: The Government Finance Officers Association of the United States and Canada ("GFOA") awarded a Certificate
59: of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting to the District for its Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
59: for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. This was the 52st consecutive year that the District has achieved this
59: prestigious award.
59: GTOT Certificate of Distinction
59: The District received the Government Treasurers' Organization of Texas ("GTOT") Certificate of Distinction in
59: October 2024. The certificate is good for a two-year period. This award recognized the District's commitment to
59: maintaining a comprehensive written investment policy that meets the criteria set forth in the GTOT Investment
59: Policy Checklist.
59: TASBO Award of Merit for Purchasing Operations
59: The District received the Texas Association of School Business Officials' ("TASBO") Award of Merit of Purchasing
59: Operations in February 2025. This award honors school districts that uphold professional standards in acquiring
59: goods and services.
