71:                                               Independent Auditor’s Report
71:    To the School Board and Management of
71:    Houston Independent School District
71:    Houston, Texas
71:    Report on the Audit of the Financial Statements
71:    Opinions
71:    We have audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, the business-type activities, each major
71:    fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of Houston Independent School District (the District), as of
71:    and for the year ended June 30, 2025, and the related notes to the financial statements, which collectively comprise
71:    the District’s basic financial statements as listed in the table of contents.
71:    In our opinion, the accompanying financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the respective financial
71:    position of the governmental activities, the business-type activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining
71:    fund information of the District, as of June 30, 2025 and the respective changes in financial position and, where
71:    applicable, cash flows thereof for the year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted
71:    in the United States of America.
71:    Basis for Opinions
71:    We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America
71:    (GAAS) and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the
71:    Comptroller General of the United States. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the
71:    Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of our report. We are required to be
71:    independent of the District and to meet our other ethical responsibilities, in accordance with the relevant ethical
71:    requirements relating to our audit. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate
71:    to provide a basis for our audit opinions.
71:    Emphasis of Matter
71:    As discussed in Note 1 to the basic financial statements, during the year ended June 30, 2025, the District
71:    implemented Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences.
71:    Beginning net position has been restated as a result of the implementation of this statement. Our opinions are not
71:    modified with respect to this matter.
71:    Responsibilities of Management for the Financial Statements
71:    The District’s management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of the financial statements in
71:    accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, and for the design,
71:    implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial
71:    statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
71:    In preparing the financial statements, management is required to evaluate whether there are conditions or events,
71:    considered in the aggregate, that raise substantial doubt about the District’s ability to continue as a going concern
71:    for twelve months beyond the financial statement date, including any currently known information that may raise
71:    substantial doubt shortly thereafter.

72: Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements
72: Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from
72: material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that includes our opinions.
72: Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not absolute assurance and therefore is not a guarantee
72: that an audit conducted in accordance with GAAS and Government Auditing Standards will always detect a material
72: misstatement when it exists. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than
72: for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or
72: the override of internal control. Misstatements are considered material if there is a substantial likelihood that,
72: individually or in the aggregate, they would influence the judgment made by a reasonable user based on the
72: financial statements.
72: In performing an audit in accordance with GAAS and Government Auditing Standards, we:
72:     •   Exercise professional judgment and maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit.
72:     •   Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or
72:         error, and design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks. Such procedures include
72:         examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements.
72:     •   Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that
72:         are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness
72:         of the District’s internal control. Accordingly, no such opinion is expressed.
72:     •   Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of significant accounting
72:         estimates made by management, as well as evaluate the overall presentation of the financial statements.
72:     •   Conclude whether, in our judgment, there are conditions or events, considered in the aggregate, that raise
72:         substantial doubt about the District’s ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period of time.
72: We are required to communicate with those charged with governance regarding, among other matters, the planned
72: scope and timing of the audit, significant audit findings, and certain internal control–related matters that we
72: identified during the audit.
72: Required Supplementary Information
72: Accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America require that the Management’s Discussion
72: and Analysis, Schedule of Revenues, Expenditures, and Changes in Fund Balance – Budget and Actual – General
72: Fund, Schedule of the District’s Proportionate Share of the Net Pension Liability – Teacher Retirement System,
72: Schedule of the District’s Contributions for Pension – Teacher Retirement System, Schedule of District’s
72: Proportionate Share of the Net OPEB Liability – Teacher Retirement System, and Schedule of the District’s
72: Contributions for Other Postemployment Benefits – Teacher Retirement System, be presented to supplement the
72: basic financial statements. Such information is the responsibility of management and, although not a part of the
72: basic financial statements, is required by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board who considers it to be an
72: essential part of financial reporting for placing the basic financial statements in an appropriate operational,
72: economic, or historical context. We have applied certain limited procedures to the required supplementary
72: information in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America, which
72: consisted of inquiries of management about the methods of preparing the information and comparing the
72: information for consistency with management’s responses to our inquiries, the basic financial statements, and other
72: knowledge we obtained during our audit of the basic financial statements. We do not express an opinion or provide
72: any assurance on the information because the limited procedures do not provide us with sufficient evidence to
72: express an opinion or provide any assurance.

75:                                 MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
75:                                             (UNAUDITED)
75: Our discussion and analysis of Houston Independent School District's (the "District") financial performance
75: provides an overview of the District's financial activities for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025. It should be read
75: in conjunction with the transmittal letter at the front of this report and the basic financial statements which follow
75: this section.
75: The Management's Discussion and Analysis provides information on both government-wide financial statements
75: and fund financial statements.
75: FINANCIAL HIGHLIGHTS
75:     • The District's total net position as presented on the Government-wide Statement of Net Position is $2.2
75:       billion. For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, the net position of the District decreased by $156 million
75:       from operations.
75:     • The District's governmental funds financial statements reported a combined ending fund balance of $1 .032
75:       billion. This balance consists of$748 million in the General Fund of which $33.71 million is assigned , $127.39
75:       million is restricted, $21 .09 million is nonspendable, $101 .13 million is committed, and $464.76 million is
75:       unassigned and available for spending at the District's discretion. The remaining restricted fund balance of
75:       $284 million consists of the Special Revenue Fund, the Debt Service Fund, and the Capital Project Fund. The
75:       Capital Project Fund's fund balance also includes $(16.37) million in unassigned.
75:     • For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, total revenue and transfers from governmental activities in the
75:       Statement of Activities was $2.748 billion. Program revenues accounted for $573 million. General revenues
75:       and transfers accounted for $2.175 billion .
75:     • The General Fund had $1 .940 billion in revenues of which $1 .523 billion is property taxes. General Fund
75:       expenditures and other financing sources were $2.25 billion and $11.47 million, respectively. This resulted in
75:       a decrease to fund balance of $299.11 million.
75:     • A portion of the debt obligations of the District are rated "Aaa" by Moody's Investors Service, Inc. ("Moody's")
75:       and "AAA" by Standard & Poor's Global Ratings, a business unit of Standard & Poor's Financial Services
75:       LLC ("S&P") by virtue of a guarantee by the Texas Permanent School Fund Bond Guarantee Program. The
75:       outstanding unenhanced tax-supported debt of the District is rated "Aaa" by Moody's and "AA+" by S&P. In
75:       addition , lease revenue bonds issued by the District's Public Facility Corporation received ratings of "Aa1" by
75:       Moody's. Rating information referenced is as of the last rating reviews in February of 2025 by Moody's and
75:       February of 2025 by S&P.
75: OVERVIEW OF THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
75: This discussion and analysis is intended to serve as an introduction to the District's basic financial statements.
75: The District's basic financial statements are comprised of three components: 1) government-wide financial
75: statements, 2) fund financial statements, and 3) notes to the basic financial statements. This report also contains
75: required supplementary information and other supplementary information in addition to the basic financial
75: statements themselves.
75: Government-Wide Financial Statements
75: The government-wide financial statements are designed to provide readers a broad overview of the District's
75: finances in a manner similar to a private-sector business and are comprised of the Statement of Net Position and
75: the Statement of Activities. These statements provide information about the activities of the District as a whole
75: and present both long-term and short-term information about the District's overall financial status. The District's
75: basic services are primarily financed by property taxes and include instruction, instructional resources and media
75:                                                          - 17 -
75: 
76:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
76:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
76: services, instructional staff development, instructional leadership, school leadership, guidance, counseling, and
76: evaluation services, social work services, health services, student transportation , food service, co-curricular/
76: extracurricular activities, general administration, plant maintenance and operations, security and monitoring
76: services, data processing services, community services, fiscal agent/member districts of shared services, juvenile
76: justice alternative education program, tax reinvestment zone payments, tax appraisal and collection, and interest
76: on long-term debt.
76: The Statement of Net Position presents information on all the District's assets, deferred outflows, liabilities, and
76: deferred inflows with the difference reported as net position . Over time, increases or decreases in net position may
76: serve as a useful indicator of whether the District's financial position is improving or deteriorating . The Statement
76: of Net Position includes the District's non-fiduciary assets and liabilities.
76: The Statement of Activities presents information for all the current fiscal year's revenues and expenses. This
76: activity is reported as soon as the underlying event giving rise to the activity occurs, regardless of the timing of
76: related cash flows. Therefore, revenues and expenses are reported in this statement for some items that will result
76: in cash flows in future fiscal periods (e.g., uncollected taxes and earned but unused vacation leave).
76: Both of the government-wide financial statements distinguish functions of the District that are principally supported
76: by taxes and intergovernmental revenues (governmental activities) from business-type activities that are intended
76: to recover all or a significant portion of their costs through user fees and charges.
76: Fund Financial Statements
76: The fund financial statements focus on individual parts of the government, reporting the District's operations in
76: more detail than the government-wide statements. Funds are accounting devices that the District uses to keep
76: track of specific sources of funding and spending for particular purposes. Some funds are required by state law
76: and by bond covenants. The Board of Trustees establishes other funds to control and manage resources and
76: expenditures for particular purposes or to delineate the use of certain taxes and grants.
76: The District has three kinds of funds:
76: Governmental funds are used to account for essentially the same functions reported as governmental activities
76: in the government-wide financial statements. Most of the District's activities are included in governmental funds
76: which focus on (1) how cash and other financial assets can readily be converted to cash flow in and out, and
76: (2) the balances left at year end that are available. However, unlike the government-wide financial statements,
76: governmental fund financial statements provide a detailed short-term view that helps determine whether there are
76: more or fewer financial resources that can be spent in the near future to finance the District's programs. Because
76: this information does not encompass the additional long-term focus of the government-wide statements, we provide
76: additional information on the subsequent page that explains the relationship (or differences) between them.
76: The District maintains four governmental funds. Information is presented separately in the governmental fund
76: balance sheet and in the governmental fund statement of revenues, expenditures, and changes in fund balances
76: for the General Fund, the Special Revenue Fund, the Debt Service Fund, and the Capital Project Fund, all of which
76: are considered to be major funds.
76: Proprietary funds are used to account for operations that are financed similarly to those found in the private
76: sector. These funds provide both long and short-term financial information. The District maintains two types of
76: proprietary funds. Enterprise funds are used to report the same type of information as reported in the government-
76: wide financial statements. The District uses enterprise funds to account for the employee cafeteria (MarketPlace)
76: and Medicaid programs. The District uses internal service funds to report activities that provide services for the
76: District's other programs and activities, i.e., health insurance, workers' compensation, print shop, and other internal
76: services. Because these services predominately benefit governmental rather than business-type functions, they
76: have been included within governmental activities within the government-wide financial statements.
76: Fiduciary funds are used to account for assets held by the District in a trustee capacity or as a custodian for
76: individuals, private organizations and/or other funds. The District uses fiduciary funds to account for scholarship
76: funds and student activity funds. No fiduciary funds are used as clearing accounts to distribute financial resources
76:                                                          - 18 -
76: 
77:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
77:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
77: to other funds. The District is responsible for ensuring that the assets reported in these funds are used for their
77: intended purposes. All the District's fiduciary activities are reported in a separate statement offiduciary net position
77: and a statement of changes in fiduciary net position. We exclude these activities from the District's government-
77: wide financial statements because the District cannot use these assets to finance its operations.
77: Notes to the Basic Financial Statements
77: The notes to the basic financial statements provide additional information that is essential to a complete
77: understanding of the data provided in the government-wide and fund financial statements.
77: Other Information
77: In addition to the basic financial statements and accompanying notes, this report also presents certain required
77: supplementary information that further explains and supports the information in the financial statements. Immediately
77: following the required supplementary information, combining statements are included for the non major enterprise
77: funds and the internal service funds.

78: GOVERNMENT-WIDE FINANCIAL ANALYSIS
78: As noted earlier, net position may serve as a useful indicator of the District's financial position . The District's
78: combined net position decreased $144 million. The District's net investment in capital assets is $2.45 billion and
78: includes investments in capital assets (e.g. land, buildings and improvements, furniture, equipment, right-to-use
78: assets, and construction in progress) less any related debt used to acquire those assets that is still outstanding.
78: The District uses these capital assets to provide services to students; consequently, these assets are not available
78: for future spending. Although the District's investment in its capital assets is reported net of related debt, it should
78: be noted that the resources needed to repay this debt must be provided from other sources, since the capital
78: assets themselves cannot be used to liquidate these liabilities.
78: The District's restricted net position of $241 million represents resources that are subject to external restrictions on
78: how they may be used. The remaining $(484.5) million is unrestricted net position.

82:     HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
82:     SCHOOL DISTRICT
82: FINANCIAL ANALYSIS OF THE DISTRICT'S FUNDS
82: Governmental Funds For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, the District's governmental funds reported ending
82: fund balances of $1 .032 billion. Of this amount, $448 million is unassigned and available for use in activities at the
82: District's discretion. The remainder of the fund balance is designated as nonspendable, restricted, committed, or
82: assigned, which indicates that it is not available for new spending because it has already been obligated for grants,
82: debt service, bond projects and other purposes of the District.
82: The General Fund is the primary operating fund of the District. The fund balance of the General Fund decreased
82: $299.1 million during the fiscal year. At the end of the fiscal year, the unassigned fund balance of $464 million
82: represented 21 percent of the total General Fund expenditures.
82: The Debt Service Fund has a total fund balance of $156.4 million all of which is restricted for the payment of debt
82: service. The fund balance during the fiscal year increased by $32.6 million. The District makes semi-annual debt
82: service payments in December/June, January/July, February/August and March/September of each year. Debt
82: service payments for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025 included all scheduled payments including payments
82: due within 30 days of year end.
82: The Special Revenue Fund accounts for all grants received by the District from local, state, and federal sources.
82: The balance decreased by $12 million to $102 million due to a decrease in federal funds.
82: The Capital Project Fund has a total fund balance of $25.5 million. The restricted fund balance at the end of the
82: fiscal year totaled $40.69 million and represents bond funds for facility construction projects. The assigned fund
82: balance of $1 .22 million represents encumbrances. The unassigned fund balance totaled $(16.37) million. The
82: fund balance decreased by $46.06 million due to expenditures for bond construction projects and transfers to the
82: general fund for debt service payments and capital projects.
82: Proprietary Funds The District maintains both enterprise funds and internal service funds. Information is presented
82: separately in the proprietary funds statement of net position and in the proprietary funds statement of revenues,
82: expenses, and changes in net position . See pages 33 and 34 ..

82: of capital assets, including land, buildings and improvements, furniture and equipment, right-to-use assets, and
82: vehicles. This represents a net decrease of $80 million from last year.

83:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
83:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
83: Long Term Debt (See Note 8)
83: As of June 30, 2025, the District had bonded debt outstanding of $1 .559 billion. The ratio of net general bonded
83: debt to assessed valuation and the amount of bonded debt per student are useful indicators of the District's
83: debt position. This data reflects a decrease in the ratio of net bonded debt to assessed value to 0.55 percent,
83: as compared to 0.74 percent last year.
83: The District debt totals included $0 in Variable Rate Bonds outstanding at fiscal year-end.
83: Outstanding variable-rate debt decreased by $190.435 million from the prior-year ending balance due
83: to redemptions funded through refunding bonds. In addition, on May 1, 2025, the District redeemed $92.26 million
83: in fixed-rate bonds as part of the same refunding transaction.
83: The District executed a targeted debt tender offer during the year ended June 30, 2025, which resulted in the
83: issuance of $20.55 million in refunding maintenance tax notes. The remaining outstanding balance of previously
83: issued maintenance tax notes was $143.210 million as of June 30, 2024.
83: On May 28, 2025, the District defeased $115.42 million in fixed-rate bonds utilizing available debt service funds.
83: The District did not issue any contractual obligations during the year ended June 30, 2025.
83: Interest earnings on proceeds from debt issued since May 15, 1989, are subject to arbitrage regulations contained
83: in the Federal Tax Reform Act of 1986. The District did not identify arbitrage liability as of June 30, 2025.
83: General Fund Budgetary Highlights
83: Over the course of the year, the District revised its budget several times. Significant budget adjustments include:
83:     • Decrease in property tax revenues of $24.6 million due to the increase in exemptions and refunds
83:     • Increase in foundation state revenues of $38.5 million
83:     • Increase in expenditures dues to carryover encumbrances of $17.3 million
83:     • Increase in school leadership of $6.7 million
83:     • Increase in recapture of $44.5 million
83:     • Increase of $47.7 million for facilities maintenance and transportation costs
83:     • Increase in transfers from other funds in the amount of $7.7 million
83: Total actual expenditures were $74.7 million more than the final budget. Following were the key variances:
83:     • $59.9 million over budget in instructional salary and Texas Connections expenditures
83:     • $12.5 million in school leadership
83:     • $12.4 million in recapture
83: The 2024-2025 final expenditure budget decreased by $51 .0 million from the prior year budget.
83: The final budgeted amount for revenues was $1.906 billion. Actual revenues were greater than the budget by
83: $33.8 million primarily due to:
83:     • $5.3 million under budget in property tax collections
83:     • $1 .5 million over budget in interest earnings
83:     • $9.9 million over budget in the Foundation School Program
83:     • $27.9 million over budget in other local sources

84:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
84:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
84: Budget amendments are presented to the Board of Education for consideration and approval throughout the year.
84: ECONOMIC FACTORS AND NEXT YEAR'S BUDGETS AND RATES
84: The District's General Fund is funded primarily between local property taxes and state revenue. Through the state's
84: funding formula, a school district receives a basic allotment for each student with weights added to that allotment
84: if the student receives additional services such as special education, at-risk (state compensatory education)
84: bilingual, dyslexia, early education, college, career or military readiness outcomes, career and technology and
84: transportation, which determines the district's Tier I allotment.
84: The 2025-2026 General Fund budget, adopted in June 2025, included projected increase of $175.4 million in
84: revenues and $54.3 million in expenditures. The state revenue projections are based on an estimated average
84: daily attendance (ADA) of 151,666 or 223,312 based on a weighted average daily attendance (WADA).
84: In FY2025-2026, HISD's total expenditures are estimated at $2.121 billion.
84: Actions of the 88th Legislature in 2025:
84:     1. The basic allotment increased to $6,215 for 2025-2026 and 2026-2027. This base amount is generated by
84:        every student in HISD.
84:     2.lncreased school safety funding from $10 per ADA to $20 per ADA Added additional safety funding of
84:       $33,540 per campus
84:     3.lncreased the state homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000 which was subsequently approved by
84:       voters in November 2025.
84:     4. Reduced the Maximum Compression Rate (MCR) by an additional $0.0194 for tax year 2025, subject to the
84:        90% equity band.
84:     5.lncluded Maintenance and Operations and Interest Sinking Hold Harmless (covers debt approved by voters
84:       as of September 1, 2025.)
84: Tax Rate
84: At budget adoption in June, it was projected that the total district tax rate per $100 of property value would
84: be $0.8783. This assumed the Maintenance and Operations (M&O rate) of $0.7116 consisting of a maximum
84: compressed rate of $0.6322 plus five Tier II "Golden Pennies" as well as an interest and sinking (l&S) rate of
84: $0.1667. These rates were approved by the Board of Managers in October.
84: CONTACTING THE DISTRICT'S FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
84: This financial report is designed to provide our citizens, taxpayers, customers, investors, and creditors with a
84: general overview of the District's finances and to demonstrate the District's accountability for the money it receives.
84: If you have questions about this report or need additional financial information, contact the Chief Finance and
84: Operations Officer at 4400 West 18th Street, Houston , Texas 77092, or call (713) 556-5500.

97:                        NOTES TO THE BASIC FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
97:                         FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JUNE 30, 2025
97:    NOTE 1: SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
97:   REPORTING ENTITY
97:   The Houston Independent School District ("District") is an independent school district created and
97:   incorporated through legislation enacted by the Thirty-Eighth Texas State Legislature in 1923.
97:   The District is the largest school district in Texas and is governed by the Board of Managers, appointed
97:   by the Texas Commissioner of Education in June 2023.
97:   In accordance with Governmental Accounting Standards, a financial reporting entity consists of the
97:   primary government and its component units. Component units are legally separate organizations
97:   for which the elected officials of the District are financially accountable, or for which the relationship
97:   to the District is such that exclusion would cause the District's financial statements to be misleading
97:   or incomplete. The District's blended component unit, although a legally separate entity, is in
97:   substance a part of the District's operations, and so data from this entity is combined with data of
97:   the primary government.
97:   The criteria used to determine whether an organization is a component unit of the District includes:
97:   financial accountability of the District for the component unit, whether the District appoints a voting
97:   majority of the entity's board, the ability to impose the District's will on the component unit, fiscal
97:   dependency criterion, if it is a financial benefit to or burden to the District, and whether services are
97:   provided entirely or almost entirely to the District.
97:   For financial reporting purposes, the Houston Independent School District GEAR UP Trust ("GEAR
97:   UP Trust") is included in the fiduciary activities of the District because of the financial accountability
97:   of the District, the appointment of a voting majority, and the fiscal dependency criteria whereby the
97:   GEAR UP Trust serves the District's students exclusively. The GEAR UP Trust was incorporated
97:   to ensure that the scholarship funds are properly spent and to guarantee a college scholarship to
97:   the eligible students at participating schools of the GEAR UP program. The GEAR UP financial
97:   information is blended with that of the District in the Private-Purpose Trust Funds column in the
97:   Statement of Fiduciary Net Position. Separate financial statements for GEAR UP Trust are not issued.
97:    IMPLEMENTATION OF NEW ACCOUNTING PRONOUNCEMENTS
97:   GASS Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences (GASS 101 ), improves the information needs of
97:   financial statements users by updating the recognition and measurement guidance for compensated
97:   absences under a unified model and amending certain previously required disclosures. The
97:   requirements of this statement are effective for reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2023,
97:   with earlier application encouraged. GASS 101 was implemented in the District's fiscal year 2025
97:   financial statements with a restatement of ($12,281,689) to net position as of July 1, 2024 to reflect
97:   the changes adopted to conform to the new standard.
97:   GASS Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures (GASS 102), improves financial reporting by
97:   providing users of financial statements with essential information regarding certain concentrations of
97:   constraints and related events that have occurred or have begun to occur that make a government
97:   vulnerable to a substantial impact. The requirements of this statement are effective for reporting periods
97:   beginning after June 15, 2024, with earlier application encouraged. GASS 102 was implemented
97:   in the District's fiscal year 2025 financial statements with no impact to amounts previously reported .
97:   RECENT ACCOUNTING PRONOUNCEMENTS
97:   GASS Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements (GASS 103), improves key
97:   components of the financial reporting model to enhance its effectiveness in providing information
97:   that is essential for decision making and assessing a government's accountability. This statement
97:   also addresses certain application issues. The requirements of this statement are effective for
97:   reporting periods beginning after June 15, 2025, with earlier application encouraged. GASS 103
97:   will be implemented in the District's fiscal year 2026 financial statements and the impact has not yet
97:   been determined.

98:   GASB Statement No. 104, Disclosure of Certain Capita/Assets (GASB 104), establishes requirements
98:   for certain types of capital assets to be disclosed separately in the capital assets note disclosures.
98:   It also establishes requirements for capital assets held for sale, including additional disclosures
98:   for those capital assets. The requirements of this statement are effective for reporting periods
98:   beginning after June 15, 2025, with earlier application encouraged. GASB 104 will be implemented
98:   in the District's fiscal year 2026 financial statements and the impact has not yet been determined.
98:   GOVERNMENT-WIDE AND FUND FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
98:   The Statement of Net Position and the Statement of Activities of the government-wide financial
98:   statements report information on all the nonfiduciary activities of the District and its blended
98:   component unit. The District eliminates from the Statement of Net Position and the Statement of
98:   Activities most interfund receivables, payables, and transfers between funds. lnterfund services
98:   provided and used are eliminated in the process of consolidation. Governmental activities, which
98:   normally are supported by taxes and intergovernmental revenues, are reported separately from
98:   business-type activities, which rely to a significant extent on fees and charges for support.
98:   The Statement of Activities demonstrates the degree to which the direct expenses of a given function
98:   are offset by program revenues. Program revenues include (1) charges to customers or applicants
98:   for goods or services provided, and (2) grants and contributions that are restricted to meeting
98:   operational requirements of a particular function . Program revenues included in the Statement of
98:   Activities reduce the cost of the function to be financed from general revenues. Taxes and other
98:   items not restricted to specific programs are properly excluded from program revenues and reported
98:   instead as general revenues.
98:   The District reports all direct expenses by function in the Statement of Activities. Direct expenses
98:   are those clearly identifiable with a function . Depreciation and amortization expense is specifically
98:   identified by function and is included in the direct expense to each function .
98:   Separate financial statements are provided for governmental funds, proprietary funds, and fiduciary
98:   funds. In accordance with the provisions of GASB Statement No. 34, the fiduciary funds are excluded
98:   from the government-wide financial statements. Major individual governmental funds are reported
98:   as separate columns in the fund financial statements.
98:   MEASUREMENT FOCUS, BASIS OF ACCOUNTING
98:   AND FINANCIAL STATEMENT PRESENTATION
98:   Government-wide Financial Statements - The government-wide financial statements are reported
98:   using the economic resources measurement focus and the accrual basis of accounting. Revenues,
98:   expenses, gains, losses, assets, deferred outflows of resources, liabilities, and deferred inflows
98:   of resources resulting from exchange and exchange-like transactions are recognized when the
98:   exchange takes place, regardless of the timing of the related cash flows. Revenues, expenses,
98:   gains, losses, assets, deferred outflows of resources, liabilities, and deferred inflows of resources
98:   resulting from nonexchange transactions are recognized in accordance with GASB Statement No.
98:   33, as amended. Property taxes are recognized as revenues in the year for which they are levied.
98:   Grants, and similar items, are recognized as revenue as soon as all eligibility requirements have
98:   been met and funds are available to meet current expenditures.
98:   Fund Financial Statements - Governmental fund financial statements are reported using the current
98:   financial resources measurement focus and the modified accrual basis of accounting. Revenues
98:   are recognized as soon as they are both measurable and available. State aid and miscellaneous
98:   revenues, other than property taxes and state and federal grants, are considered to be available
98:   if collected within the current period or within 90 days of the fiscal year end to pay liabilities of
98:   the current period. Property taxes are considered to be available if collected within 60 days of the
98:   fiscal year end. State and federal grants are considered to be available if collected within 120 days

99:   of the fiscal year end. Expenditures are generally recognized under the modified accrual basis of
99:   accounting in the accounting period in which the fund liability is incurred, if measurable. However,
99:   debt service expenditures are recognized in the current fiscal period for debt service principal and
99:   interest payments due within 30 days in the subsequent fiscal period as these funds have been set
99:   aside for that purpose. Compensated absences and claims and judgments are recorded only when
99:   payment is due. Both Proprietary fund statements and Fiduciary fund statements are reported using
99:   the economic resources measurement focus and the accrual basis of accounting.
99:   FUNDS
99:   The District's accounting system is organized and operated with the use of funds, each of which
99:   is a separate accounting entity with a self-balancing set of accounts. The District's resources are
99:   allocated to and accounted for in individual funds based on the intended purposes for spending
99:   and the means by which spending activities are controlled. The following fund types are included
99:   in the financial statements:
99:   Governmental Funds
99:   Governmental Funds are those through which most governmental functions of the District are
99:   financed . The acquisition, use, and balances of the District's expendable financial resources, and
99:   the related liabilities are accounted for through governmental funds. The following are the District's
99:   major governmental funds:
99:       • General Fund - The General Fund is the general operating fund of the District and accounts
99:         for all revenues and expenditures of the District not encompassed within other funds.
99:       • Special Revenue Fund - The Special Revenue Fund is used to account for and report the
99:         proceeds of specific revenue sources that are restricted or committed to expenditures for
99:         specified purposes other than debt service or capital projects. The District's Special Revenue
99:         Fund includes the National School Breakfast and Lunch Program, United States Department
99:         of Education grants, Campus Activity Funds, and all other federal, state and locally funded
99:         grants and programs. These grants are awarded to the District for the purpose of accomplishing
99:         specific educational tasks as defined in the grant awards. The schedules of federal and state
99:         awards are included in the compliance section of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report.
99:       • Debt Service Fund - The Debt Service Fund is used to account for the accumulation
99:         of resources for, and the retirement of, general long-term debt and related costs.
99:       • Capital Project Fund - The Capital Project Fund is used to account for financial resources
99:         to be used for the acquisition, renovation, or construction of capital facilities.
99:   Proprietary Funds
99:   Proprietary Funds are used to account for operations that are financed in a manner similar to those
99:   found in the private sector, where the determination of net income is appropriate for sound financial
99:   administration.
99:       • Enterprise Funds - The Enterprise Funds are used to account for operations that are financed
99:         and operated similar to a private enterprise where the District's intent is to provide services
99:         financed primarily through user charges. The District's enterprise funds include Medicaid and
99:         the Marketplace activities.
99:       • Internal Service Funds - The Internal Service Funds are used to account for operations
99:         related to the Print Shop, Alternative Certification Program, Athletics, University
99:         Interscholastic League ("UIL"), Shared Services, and risk financing activities of the District.

100:         Proprietary funds distinguish operating revenues and expenses from nonoperating items.
100:         Operating revenues and expenses generally result from providing services and producing
100:         and delivering goods in connection with a proprietary fund's principal ongoing operations.
100:         The principal operating revenues of the District's proprietary funds are charges to customers
100:         and other funds for sales and services. Operating expenses for proprietary funds include the
100:         cost of sales and services, administrative expenses, and depreciation on capital assets. All
100:         revenues and expenses not meeting this definition are reported as nonoperating revenues
100:         and expenses.
100:   Fiduciary Funds
100:   Fiduciary Funds are used to account for assets held by the District in a trustee capacity or as a
100:   custodian for individuals, private organizations and/or other funds.
100:       • Private-Purpose Trust Funds - Private-purpose trust funds are used to account for resources
100:         legally held in trust under which principal and income benefit individuals, private organizations
100:         or other governments. The District's private-purpose trust funds represent scholarship funds
100:         being held in trust for students.
100:       • Custodial Funds - Custodial funds are used to account for resources that the District has
100:         custody of, but is not the district's own-source revenue, and does not control the use of
100:         revenues. The District's custodial funds represent school class and club activity funds.
100:   Management's use of Estimates
100:   The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles
100:   requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect certain reported amounts
100:   and disclosures. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
100:   Stewardship. Compliance. and Accountability
100:   The District is required by law to prepare and file a budget with the Texas Education Agency (TEA).
100:   Activities of the General Fund, Nutrition Services Fund , and Debt Service Fund are included in the
100:   District's formally adopted budget. Budgets for the Special Revenue Fund (other than Nutrition
100:   Services) and Capital Project Fund are approved on a project basis. The District is required to
100:   present the adopted and final amended budgeted revenues and expenditures and actual revenues
100:   and expenditures for the General Fund, Nutrition Services Fund , and Debt Service Fund . These
100:   budgets are in the financial section of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report.
100:   Pensions
100:   The fiduciary net position of the Teacher Retirement System of Texas (TRS) has been determined
100:   using the flow of economic resources measurement focus and full accrual basis of accounting.
100:   This includes for purposes of measuring the net pension liability, deferred outflows of resources
100:   and deferred inflows of resources related to pensions, pension expense, and information about
100:   assets, liabilities, and additions to/deductions from TRS's fiduciary net position. Benefit payments
100:   (including refunds of employee contributions) are recogn ized when due and payable in accordance
100:   with the benefit terms. Investments are reported at fair value.
100:   Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB)
100:   The fiduciary net position of the Teacher Retirement System of Texas (TRS) Care Plan has been
100:   determined using the flow of economic resources measurement focus and full accrual basis of
100:   accounting. This includes for purposes of measuring the net OPEB liability, deferred outflows of
100:   resources and deferred inflows of resources related to other post-employment benefits, OPEB
100:   expense, and information about assets, liabilities, and additions to/deductions from TRS Care's
100:   fiduciary net position. Benefit payments are recognized when due and payable in accordance with
100:   the benefit terms. There are no investments as this is a pay-as-you-go plan and all cash is held in
100:   a cash account.

101:   ASSETS, LIABILITIES, AND DEFERRED OUTLFOWS AND INFLOWS OF RESOURCES
101:   Cash and Cash Equivalents
101:   The District requires all deposits to be fully collateralized with depository insurance; obligations
101:   of the United States of America or its agencies and instrumentalities (excluding those mortgage
101:   backed securities prohibited by the Public Funds Investment Act). At all times, such securities are
101:   to have a fair value sufficient to fully collateralize deposit balances as adjusted by the amount of
101:   applicable depository insurance pursuant to the Collateral for Public Funds Act, Texas Government
101:   Code Section 2257.022.
101:   The District considers cash and cash equivalents to be cash on hand and demand deposits. All
101:   other monetary assets are treated as investments including certificates of deposit, investment pools,
101:   money market instruments, and other securities defined under the Public Funds Investment Act.
101:   Investments
101:   Investments are stated at fair value where applicable under the GASB statements, which is the
101:   amount at which the investment can be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties.
101:   Management of the District believes that in the areas of investment practice, management reports,
101:   and establishment of appropriate policies, the District adhered to the requirements of the State
101:   of Texas Public Funds Investment Act. Additionally, management of the District believes that
101:   investment practices of the District were in accordance with local policies.
101:   Receivables
101:   All trade and property tax receivables are shown net of allowance for uncollectible balances. The
101:   property tax receivable allowance is 52.6 percent of outstanding property taxes at June 30, 2025.
101:   Inventories
101:   Under the moving average inventory method, the average cost of each inventory item in stock is
101:   recalculated after every inventory purchase. This method tends to yield inventory valuations and
101:   cost of goods sold that are in-between those derived under the first in, first out (FIFO) method
101:   and the last in, last out (LIFO) method. These materials and supplies are subsequently charged
101:   to expenditures when consumed. Inventories include instructional materials, plant maintenance
101:   operating supplies, as well as nutrition services food and supplies. Revenue for donated commodities
101:   is recognized when the commodities are received . Non-food inventories are offset at fiscal year-
101:   end by non-spendable fund balance in the governmental fund financial statements.
101:   Other Assets
101:   Other assets include accrued interest, prepaid insurance, and prepaid travel. Prepaids are charged
101:   to expenditures when consumed and are offset at year end by non-spendable fund balance in the
101:   governmental fund financial statements.

102:   capital Assets
102:   Capital assets, which include land, land improvements, buildings and improvements, construction
102:   in progress, furniture and equipment, library books and media, vehicles, and right-to-use assets are
102:   reported in the applicable governmental and business-type activities columns in the government-
102:   wide financial statements and proprietary fund financial statements. Capital acquisition and
102:   construction are reflected as expenditures in governmental funds. Land, land improvements,
102:   buildings and improvements, furniture and equipment, and vehicles are recorded at historical
102:   cost if purchased or constructed. The capitalization threshold is a unit cost of $5,000. Donated
102:   capital assets are recorded at estimated acquisition value at the date of donation. Depreciation or
102:   amortization on all depreciable capital assets begins on the date the asset is placed into service
102:   using the straight-line method of depreciation.
102:   The costs of normal maintenance and repairs that do not add to the value of the asset or materially
102:   extend the life of the asset are not capitalized. Major outlays for capital assets and improvements
102:   are capitalized as projects are constructed.

103:    Leases
103:   The District is a lessee for noncancellable leases of property and equipment. The District recognizes
103:   a lease liability, reported with long-term debt, and a right-to-use lease asset (lease asset), reported
103:   with other capital assets, in the government-wide and proprietary fund financial statements.
103:   The District recognizes lease liabilities with an initial, individual value of $5,000 or more.
103:   At the commencement of a lease, the District initially measures the lease liability at the present
103:   value of payments expected to be made during the lease term. Subsequently, the lease liability is
103:   reduced by the principal portion of lease payments made. The lease asset is initially measured as
103:   the initial amount of the lease liability, adjusted for lease payments made at or before the lease
103:   commencement date, plus certain initial direct costs. Subsequently, the lease asset is amortized on
103:   a straight-line basis over the shorter of the lease term or its useful life.
103:    Key estimates and judgments related to leases include how the District determines (1) the discount
103:    rate it uses to discount the expected lease payments to present value, (2) lease term, and (3) lease
103:    payments.
103:   The District uses the interest rate charged by the lessor as the discount rate. When the interest
103:   rate charged by the lessor is not provided, the District generally uses its estimated incremental
103:   borrowing rate as the discount rate for leases.
103:   The lease term includes the noncancellable period of the lease.
103:   Lease payments included in the measurement of the lease liability are composed of fixed payments,
103:   variable payments fixed in substance or that depend on an index or a rate, purchase option price
103:   that the District is reasonably certain to exercise, lease incentives receivable from the lessor, and
103:   any other payments that are reasonably certain of being required based on an assessment of all
103:   relevant factors.
103:   The District monitors changes in circumstances that would require a remeasurement of its leases
103:   and will remeasure the lease asset and liability if certain changes occur that are expected to
103:   significantly affect the amount of the lease liability.
103:   Subscription-Based Information Technology Agreements {SBITAs}
103:   The District has noncancellable contracts with SBITA vendors for the right to use information
103:   technology (IT) software, alone or in combination with tangible capital assets (the underlying IT
103:   assets). The District recognizes a subscription liability, reported with long-term debt, and a right-to-
103:   use subscription asset (an intangible asset), reported with other capital assets, in the government-
103:   wide and proprietary fund financial statements. The District recognizes subscription liabilities with
103:   an initial, individual value of $5,000 or more.

104:   At the commencement of an SBITA, the District initially measures the subscription liability at the
104:   present value of payments expected to be made during the subscription term. Subsequently, the
104:   subscription liability is reduced by the principal portion of SBITA payments made. The subscription
104:   asset is initially measured as the initial amount of the subscription liability, adjusted for SBITA
104:   payments made at or before the SBITA commencement date, plus certain initial implementation
104:   costs. Subsequently, the subscription asset is amortized on a straight-line basis over the shorter of
104:   the subscription term or the useful life of the underlying IT assets.
104:   Key estimates and judgments related to SBITAs include how the District determines (1) the discount
104:   rate it uses to discount the expected subscription payments to present value, (2) subscription term,
104:   and (3) subscription payments.
104:   The District uses the interest rate charged by the SBITA vendor as the discount rate. When the
104:   interest rate charged by the SBITA vendor is not provided, the District generally uses its estimated
104:   incremental borrowing rate as the discount rate for SBITAs.
104:   The subscription term includes the noncancellable period of the SBITA.
104:   Subscription payments included in the measurement of the subscription liability are composed
104:   of fixed payments, variable payments fixed in substance or that depend on an index or a rate,
104:   termination penalties if the District is reasonably certain to exercise such options, subscription
104:   contract incentives receivable from the SBITA vendor, and any other payments that are reasonably
104:   certain of being required based on an assessment of all relevant factors.
104:   The District monitors changes in circumstances that would require a remeasurement of its SBITAs
104:   and will remeasure the subscription asset and liability if certain changes occur that are expected to
104:   significantly affect the amount of the subscription liability.
104:   lnterfund Transactions
104:   Activities between funds that are representative of lending/borrowing arrangements outstanding at
104:   the end of the fiscal year are referred to as "due to/from other funds." All other balances between funds
104:   are reported as transfers. Any residual balances outstanding between the governmental activities and
104:   business-type activities are reported in the government-wide statements as "internal balances."
104:   A description of the basic types of interfund transactions and the related accounting policies are
104:   as follows:
104:       • Charges for services are reported as revenues for the performing fund and expenditures/
104:         expenses of the requesting fund.
104:       • Transactions to reimburse a fund for expenditures made by it for the benefit of another fund
104:         are recorded as expenditures or expenses in the reimbursing fund and as a reduction of
104:         expenditures or expenses in the fund that is reimbursed .
104:       • All other interfund transfers, such as legally authorized transfers from a fund receiving revenue
104:         to the fund through which the resources are to be expended, are transfers. Transfers are
104:         classified as other financing sources or uses in the Statement of Revenues, Expenditures,
104:         and Changes in Fund Balances.
104:       • For reporting at the government-wide financial statement level, the District eliminates direct
104:         interfund charges for services and the balances created within the same activity categories
104:         (i.e. governmental vs. business-type). This process ensures neither governmental nor
104:         business-type activities report direct internal revenue/expenditures. lnterfund activity and
104:         balances resulting from transactions with the fiduciary funds are not eliminated . Instead, the
104:         fiduciary interfund activity and balances are treated as transactions with an external party.
104:         The Internal Service Funds are essentially repositories for income, expenses, assets and
104:         liabilities of the District's health insurance, worker's compensation, print shop, alternative
104:         certification, athletics, shared services, and UIL activities.

105:   Compensated Absences
105:   The District's contract employees earn one day of personal leave per month for all months under
105:   contract, which may either be taken or accumulated with no limitation. Accumulated sick leave
105:   balances are paid upon termination from the District to employees meeting certain criteria and hired
105:   before October 10, 1972. In addition, the District may "buy-back" accrued but unused state leave in
105:   accordance with the "Attendance Incentive Plan."
105:   Twelve-month employees earn vacation ranging from two to four weeks per year based on length
105:   of service. Beginning with FY 2021, vacation days may be carried over from one contract year to
105:   another with a maximum limit of 50 days compared to previous years when only 30 days could
105:   be carried over. For twelve-month employees, the contract year runs from September 1st through
105:   August 31st.
105:   The District accrues vacation, state personal leave, and eligible sick leave in the government-wide
105:   and proprietary fund financial statements. A liability and related expenditure for these amounts is
105:   reported in the governmental funds only if they have matured as a result of employee retirements
105:   or resignations and are due.
105:   In June 2022, the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement No. 101,
105:   Compensated Absences, effective for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025, established updated
105:   recognition and measurement criteria for liabilities associated with compensated absences including
105:   vacation, sick leave, and other paid time off. A liability for compensated absences is recognized
105:   when all the following conditions are met:
105:       • The leave is attributable to services already rendered .
105:       • The leave accumulates and carries forward to future periods.
105:       • The leave is more likely than not to be used for time off or otherwise paid or settled.
105:   The implementation of GASB 101 resulted in a change in accounting principle. As a result, previous
105:   unrecognized liabilities for certain types of leave that meet the new recognition criteria have been
105:   recorded . The cumulative effect of this change has been reflected as a restatement of beginning
105:   net position in the government-wide financial statements.
105:   The liabilities are measured using the pay rates in effect at the financial statement date or the
105:   expected pay rates at the time of settlement. The District used 5 years of historical data and
105:   current employment policies to estimate the likelihood of leave usage. The accrued types of leave
105:   considered in the calculation was vacation, state personal leave, local personal leave, supplemental
105:   sick leave, and compensatory time earned.
105:    Lona-term Uabmtjes
105:   In the government-wide financial statements, long-term debt and other long-term obligations are
105:   reported as liabilities in the Statement of Net Position. Bond premiums and discounts are amortized
105:   over the life of the bonds. Gains and losses on bond refundings are amortized using the shorter of
105:   the life of the refunded or refunding using the debt effective interest method. Bond issuance costs
105:   are expensed as incurred .
105:   In the fund financial statements, governmental funds recognize bond premiums and discounts,
105:   as well as bond issuance costs, during the current period. The face amount of the debt issued
105:   is reported as other financing sources. Premiums received on debt issuances are reported as
105:   other financing sources while discounts on debt issuances are reported as other financing uses.
105:   Issuance costs, whether or not withheld from the actual debt proceeds received, are reported as
105:   debt service expenditures.

106:   Deferred Outflows and Inflows of Resources
106:   In addition to assets, the Statement of Net Position includes a separate section for deferred outflows
106:   of resources which represents a consumption of net assets that applies to a future period(s) and
106:   therefore, will not be recognized as an outflow of resources (expenses/expenditures) until then.
106:   Included in this category are deferred losses on refunding, TRS pension costs, and TRS OPEB costs.
106:   In addition to liabilities, the Statement of Net Position includes a separate section for deferred inflows
106:   of resources which represents an acquisition of net assets that applies to a future period(s) and
106:   therefore, will not be recognized as an inflow of resources (revenue) until then. Included in this
106:   category are deferred gain on refunding, TRS pension and OPEB. The Governmental Funds Balance
106:   Sheet also includes a section for deferred inflows of resources. Unavailable revenue is reported as
106:   deferred inflows of resources only in the Governmental Funds Balance Sheet.
106:   NET POSITION AND FUND BALANCES
106:   Government-wide Financial Statements
106:   The District's net position is composed of the following :
106:   Net Investment in Capital Assets - the component of net position that reports capital assets less
106:   both the accumulated depreciation and amortization and the outstanding balance of debt that is
106:   directly attributable to the acquisition, construction, or improvement of these capital assets.
106:   Restricted for Debt Service - the component of net position that reports the difference between
106:   assets and liabilities of the Debt Service Fund adjusted on a government-wide basis that consists
106:   of assets with constraints placed on their use by the bond covenants.
106:   Restricted for Grants - the component of net position that reports the difference between assets
106:   and liabilities of the Special Revenue Fund that consists of assets with constraints placed on their
106:   use by the Department of Education, Department of Agriculture, TEA, and other grantor agencies
106:   and organizations.
106:    Unrestricted - - the difference between the assets and liabilities that are not reported in net position
106:    invested in capital assets, net position restricted for debt service, and net position restricted for grants.
106:   The District applies restricted resources before unrestricted resources when an expense is incurred
106:   for which restricted net position is available.
106:   Governmental Fund Financial Statements
106:   In the fund financial statements, governmental funds report fund balances as either a non-spendable
106:   fund balance or a spendable fund balance.
106:    Non-spendable Fund Balance
106:   Non-spendable fund balance is that portion of fund balance that is not expendable (such as
106:   inventories) or is legally earmarked for a specific use. Non-spendable fund balance reserves
106:   include inventories and prepaid items.
106:   Spendable Fund Balance
106:   Spendable fund balance is the portion of fund balance that is comprised of restricted, committed,
106:   assigned, and unassigned fund balances.
106:   Restricted Fund Balance - the component of the spendable fund balance constrained to a specific
106:   purpose by the provider, such as a grantor. Restricted fund balance includes funds for the Nutrition
106:   Services program, funds restricted for construction programs, funds used to retire debt, and resources
106:   from other granting agencies.

107:                               HOUSTON INDEPENDENT SCHOOL DISTRICT
107:                              NOTES TO THE BASIC FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
107:                               FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JUNE 30, 2025
107:   Committed Fund Balance - the component of the spendable fund balance constrained to a specific
107:   purpose by a resolution approved by the Board. Those committed amounts cannot be used for any
107:   other purpose unless the Board removes or changes the specified use by taking the same action used
107:   to establish it. Committed fund balance includes funds for potential litigation, claims, and judgments.
107:   Assigned Fund Balance - the component of the spendable fund balance that is earmarked for a
107:   specific purpose by the Superintendent or Chief Financial Officer. The assigned amounts can only be
107:   removed by the Superintendent or Chief Financial Officer. Assigned fund balance includes funds for
107:   encumbrances which are purchase orders, contracts, and other commitments for the expenditure of
107:   funds that are carried forward, insurance deductibles, specific program costs, and other legal issues.
107:   Unassigned Fund Balance - the component of the spendable fund balance within the General Fund
107:   which may be spent for any legal purpose. This portion of the total fund balance in the general fund is
107:   available to finance operating expenditures. Per Board Policy, the District's unassigned fund balance
107:   at year end shall equal at least three months of operating expenditures.
107:   In general, it is the District's policy to consider restricted resources to have been spent first when
107:   an expenditure is incurred for purposes for which restricted and unrestricted (i.e. committed,
107:   assigned, or unassigned) fund balances are available, followed by committed and then assigned
107:   fund balances. Unassigned amounts are used only after the other resources have been used .

110:                        NOTES TO THE BASIC FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
110:                         FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JUNE 30, 2025
110:   GASB Statement No. 40, Deposit and Investment Risk Disclosures, an amendment to GASB
110:   Statement No. 3, establishes and modifies disclosure requirements related to deposits and
110:   investment risks: credit risk (including custodial credit risk and concentrations of credit risk) , interest
110:   rate risk, and foreign currency risk.
110:   To ensure compliance with the various risk factors addressed in GASB Statement No. 40, the
110:   Cash Management and Investment Policy is reviewed at least annually and presented to the
110:   School Board for approval. The Investment Officers submit Quarterly Investment Reports to the
110:   School Board certifying that all investments were purchased in compliance with the Public Fund
110:   Investment Act.
110:   The District's Cash Management and Investment Policy contains the following objectives:
110:    (1) assure the safety of District's funds;
110:    (2) maintain sufficient liquidity to provide adequate and timely working funds;
110:    (3) maintenance of the public trust as custodians and managers responsible for the investing of
110:        funds subject to state and federal laws;
110:    (4) optimization of yield as expressed in terms of rate of return and interest earnings;
110:    (5) diversification of investments as relating to maturity, instruments, and issuers shall be
110:        considered a priority within the context of the overall investment policy; and
110:    (6) avoid investments for speculation.
110:   All objectives are approached with the judgment and care, under the circumstances then prevailing ,
110:   which persons of prudence, discretion, and intelligence exercise in the management of their own
110:   affairs, not for speculation, but for investment, considering the safety of the capital, as well as
110:   the probable income to be derived. Preservation of District capital is of highest importance. All
110:   participants in the investment process seek to act responsibly as custodians of the public trust.
110:   Investment officials avoid any transaction that might impair public confidence in the District's ability
110:   to govern effectively.
110:   Interest Rate Bisk
110:   As a means of limiting its exposure to fair value losses that could occur from rising interest rates,
110:   the District's investment policy prohibits any investment for speculative gains. The available
110:   funds in the General Fund may be invested for greater than one year provided that all cash flow
110:   requ irements have been met. Bond proceeds can be invested for a period up to five years provided
110:   that the drawdown schedules permit such maturities.
110:   The District recognizes that investment risks can result from market price changes to mitigate the
110:   risk, all securities are purchased with the intention of holding to maturity. Portfolio diversification
110:   is employed as a way to control risk. Investment officers are expected to display prudence in the
110:   selection of securities, as a way to minimize risk. No individual investment transaction shall be
110:   undertaken which jeopardizes the total capital position of the overall portfolio.
110:                                                      - 52 -

111:   Credit Risk
111:   The District's Cash Management and Investment Policy allows for investments in commercial paper
111:   provided it meets the following criteria:
111:       1. the maximum maturity does not exceed 365 days from the date of issuance;
111:       2. it is rated at least A 1 or P1 by two nationally recognized credit rating agencies;
111:       3. be issued for a specific face amount;
111:       4. be issued either through a direct placement or through broker dealers; and
111:       5. the District will diversify its investment in commercial paper by issuer and by length of maturity.
111:   As of June 30, 2025, the District did not have any direct investments in commercial paper. The

112:   GASB Statement Number 72 established a hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs used to measure fair
112:   value. Certain investment types utilized by the District are not required to be measured at fair value.
112:   The District has investments in TexPool Prime which maintains stable net asset values of $1 per
112:   share and utilize the amortized cost method as allowed by GASB 79. The District has investments
112:   in Texas FIT which maintains a stable net asset value of $1 and measures fair value as provided
112:   in paragraph 11 of GASB Statement 31 . The District invests in the Lone Star Corporate Overnight
112:   Fund which maintains a stable net asset value of $1 and the underlying pool investments are
112:   reported at amortized cost per GASB 79. The District invests in the Lone Star Corporate Overnight
112:   Plus Fund which maintains a stable net asset value of $1 and the pool utilizes fair value reporting
112:   per GASB 72. The District invests in the Texas-CLASS fund which maintains a stable net asset
112:   value of $1 and measures fair value as provided in paragraph 11 of GASB Statement 31. The
112:   District invests in the Texas Range TexasDAILY Select fund which maintains a stable net asset
112:   value of $1 and the underlying pool investments are reported at amortized cost per GASB 79. The
112:   District has no unfunded commitments to these pools and may redeem investments at any time.
112:   Custodial Credit Risk - Investments purchased for the District are made in the name of the Houston
112:   Independent School District. All investments are purchased with the delivery versus payment
112:   method and are recorded in the District's name on the Federal Reserve's book entry system and
112:   confirmed to the District via safekeeping receipt maintained on the books of the depository bank's
112:   safekeeping department.
112:   Concentration of Credit Risk - The investment portfolio is diversified to eliminate the risk of loss
112:   resulting from over concentration of assets in a specific maturity, a specific issue, or a specific class
112:   of securities. Within the cash flow requirement constraints, investment maturities are staggered in
112:   a way that avoids undue concentration of assets in a specific maturity sector.
112:   The District does not invest its portfolio in any single investment pool. Funds are subdivided
112:   between various pools for diversification and security reasons.
112:   The District is prohibited from investing in the following types of investments:
112:        a. obligations whose payment represents the coupon payments on the outstanding principal
112:           balance of the underlying mortgage-backed security collateral and pays no principal;
112:        b. obligations whose payment represents the principal stream of cash flow from the underlying
112:           mortgage-backed security collateral and bears no interest;
112:        c. collateralized mortgage obligations that have a stated final maturity date of greater than
112:           10 years; and
112:        d. collateralized mortgage obligations whose interest rate is determined by an index that
112:           adjusts opposite to the changes in a market index.
112:   The District neither enters into reverse repurchase agreements nor trades in options or future
112:   contracts. Additionally, the District does not participate in any securities lending program.
112:   Foreign Currency Risk
112:   The District does not engage in any deposit or investment transactions involving foreign currency.
112:    NOTE 4: PROPERTY TAXES AND STATE AID REVENUE
112:   PROPERTY TAXES
112:   The appraisal of property within the District is the responsibility of the Harris County Appraisal
112:   District ("Appraisal District"). The District's ad valorem property tax is levied annually in October
112:   on the assessed value as of the prior January 1 for all real and business personal property located
112:   in the District. Taxes are due on receipt of the tax bill and are delinquent if not paid by January
112:   31 of the next calendar year. Such taxes are applicable to the fiscal year in which they are levied
112:   and become delinquent with an enforceable lien on property after January 31 of the subsequent
112:   calendar year. Delinquent taxes receivable on the government-wide statement of net position and
112:   the governmental fund balance sheet is net of estimated uncollectible taxes.

113:   revenues in the year of the levy in the governmental financial statements. Such unavailable
113:   revenues are recognized in the fund financial statements as revenue in the fiscal year in which they
113:   become available. In the government-wide financial statements, property taxes are recognized
113:   as revenues in the year for which the taxes are levied. Uncollectible property taxes in the current

119:    INFLOWS AND OUTFLOWS
119:   The District's long-term liabilities consist of bond and note indebtedness, leases and subscriptions,
119:   health insurance, workers' compensation, compensated absences, net pension liability and
119:   net OPES liability. The current requirements for general obligation bonds principal and interest
119:   expenditures are accounted for in the debt service fund. Current funding requirements for leases,
119:   subscriptions, health insurance, and workers' compensation are accounted for in the governmental
119:   and proprietary funds. Pension and OPES long-term liabilities are generally liquidated with
119:   resources of the general fund .

124:   Other long-term debt
124:   Federal Arbitrage - The Tax Reform Act of 1986 instituted certain arbitrage restrictions consisting
124:   of complex regulations with respect to issuance of tax-exempt bond proceeds at an interest yield
124:   greater than the interest yield paid to bondholders. Generally, all interest paid to bondholders can
124:   be retroactively rendered taxable if applicable rebates are not reported and paid to the Internal
124:   Revenue Service at least every five years for applicable bond issues. Accordingly, there is the risk
124:   that if such calculations are not performed or are not performed correctly, a liability to the District
124:   could result. The District periodically engages an arbitrage consultant to perform the calculations in
124:   accordance with the Internal Revenue Service's rules and regulations. The District did not identify
124:   arbitrage liability as of June 30, 2025.
124:   Compensated Absences - On retirement or death of certain employees hired before October 10,
124:   1972, the District pays any accumulated unused sick leave. Additionally, the District may "buy back"
124:   any accrued but unused state leave from employees in accordance with the Attendance Incentive
124:   Plan. Also, certain employees are entitled to receive accrued vacation pay in a lump-sum cash
124:   payment upon termination of employment with the District. The General Fund has typically been
124:   used in prior years to liquidate compensated absences.

125:    NOTE 11: RISK MANAGEMENT
125:   The District is exposed to various risks of loss related to torts, theft of, damage to and destruction
125:   of assets, errors and omissions, injuries to employees, and natural disasters. The District's risk
125:   management program encompasses various means of protecting the District against losses
125:   through policies with commercial insurance carriers or through self-insurance.
125:   Workers' Compensation
125:   The District maintains a self-insurance program for workers' compensation. Contributions are
125:   paid from all governmental and proprietary funds to the Workers' Compensation Internal Service
125:   Fund from which all claims and administrative expenses are paid. Claims administration, loss
125:   control, and consultant services are provided by a third-party administrator. The District maintains
125:   a catastrophic loss insurance policy for catastrophic losses exceeding $1,000,000 per occurrence
125:   up to statutory limit of liability.

127:    NOTE 12: EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT PLAN
127:   Pensions
127:   Plan Description
127:   The District participates in a cost-sharing multiple-employer defined benefit pension that has a
127:   special funding situation. The plan is administered by the Teacher Retirement System of Texas
127:   (TRS). It is a defined benefit pension plan established and administered in accordance with the
127:   Texas Constitution , Article XVI, Section 67 and Texas Government Code, Title 8, Subtitle C. The
127:   pension trust fund is a qualified pension trust under Section 401 (a) of the Internal Revenue Code.
127:   The Texas Legislature establishes benefits and contribution rates within the guidelines of the
127:   Texas Constitution . The pension's Board of Trustees does not have the authority to establish or
127:   amend benefit terms. All employees of public, state-supported educational institutions in Texas
127:   who are employed for one-half or more of the standard workload and who are not exempted from
127:   membership under Texas Government Code, Title 8, Section 822.002 are covered by the system.
