128:    Benefit Provisions and Service Requirements
128:   TRS administers retirement, disability, and death and survivor benefits to employees and
128:   beneficiaries of employees of the public school system of Texas. The pension formula is calculated
128:   using 2.3 percent times the average of the five highest annual creditable salaries times years of
128:   credited service to arrive at the annual standard annuity except for members who are grandfathered,
128:   the three highest annual salaries are used. Service requirements are as follows:
128:   Normal --Age 65 with 5 years of credited service, or when the sum of member's age and years of
128:   credit equals or exceeds 80.
128:   Reduced --Age 55 with at least 5 years of credited service, or earlier than 55 with 30 or more years
128:   of credited service.
128:   Members are fully vested after five years of creditable service and are entitled to any benefit for
128:   which eligibility requirements have been met. There are additional provisions for reduced retirement
128:   if the sum of the member's age and years of service credit total at least 80, but the member is less
128:   than age 60 or 62 depending on date of employment, or if the member was grandfathered under
128:   a previous rule. For more details about benefits see the Summary of Benefits section of TRS
128:   2024 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. There are no automatic post-employment benefit
128:   changes, including automatic COLAs. Ad hoc post-employment benefit changes, including ad hoc
128:   COLAs can be granted by the Texas Legislature as noted in the Plan description. The 2023 Texas
128:   Legislature passed Senate Bill (SB) 10 and House Joint Resolution (HJR) 2 to provide eligible
128:   retirees with a one-time stipend and an ad hoc cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA).
128:   One-Time Stipends
128:   Stipends were paid in September 2023 to annuitants who met the qualifying age requirement on or
128:   before August 31, 2023:
128:        • A one-time $7,500 stipend to 75 years of age and older eligible annuitants
128:        • A one-time $2,400 stipend to 70 to 74 years of age eligible annuitants

129:   Cost-of-Living Adjustment
129:   A cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) was dependent on Texas voters approving a constitutional
129:   amendment (Proposition 9) to authorize the COLA Voters approved the amendment in the
129:   November 2023 election and the following COLA was applied to eligible annuitants' payments
129:   beginning with their January 2024 payment:
129:       • 2% COLA for eligible retirees who retired between September 1, 2013 through August 31 , 2020.
129:       • 4% COLA for eligible retirees who retired between September 1, 2001 through August 31 , 2013.
129:       • 6% COLA for eligible retirees who retired on or before August 31, 2001.
129:   Texas Government Code section 821 .006 prohibits benefit improvements, if, as a result of the
129:   particular action , the time requ ired to amortize TRS unfunded actuarial liabilities would be increased
129:   to a period that exceeds 31 years, or, if the amortization period already exceeds 31 years, the
129:   period would be increased by such action. Actuarial implications of the funding provided in the
129:   manner are determined by the System's actuary.
129:   Contributions
129:   Contribution requirements are established or amended pursuant to Article 16, section 67 of the
129:   Texas Constitution which requires the Texas legislature to establish a member contribution rate
129:   of not less than 6 percent of the member's annual compensation and a state contribution of not
129:   less than 6 percent and not more than 10 percent of the aggregate annual compensation paid to
129:   members of the system during the fiscal year.
129:   Employee contribution rates are set in state statute, Texas Government Code 825.402. The TRS
129:   Pension Reform Bill (Senate Bill 12) of the 86th Texas Legislature amended Texas Government
129:   Code 825.402 for member contributions and increased employee and employer contribution rates
129:   for fiscal years 2019 through 2025.
129:   Contributors to the plan include members, employers, and the State of Texas as the only non-

134:   Other Post-Employment Benefit Plans
134:   Health Care Plan Description CTRS-Care)
134:   The District participates in the Texas Public School Retired Employees Group Insurance Program
134:   (TRS-Care). It is a multiple-employer, cost-sharing defined Other Post-Employment Benefit
134:   (OPEB) plan that has a special funding situation. The plan is administered through a trust by the
134:   Teacher Retirement System of Texas (TRS) Board of Trustees. It is established and administered
134:   in accordance with the Texas Insurance Code, Chapter 1575. The Board of Trustees is granted
134:   the authority to establish basic and optional group insurance coverage for participants as well as
134:   to amend benefit terms as needed under Chapter 1575.052. The Board may adopt rules, plans,
134:   procedures, and orders reasonably necessary to administer the program, including minimum
134:   benefits and financing standards.
134:   OPEB Plan Fiduciary Net Position
134:   Detail information about the TRS-Care's fiduciary net position is available in a separately issued
134:   TRS Annual Comprehensive Financial Report that includes financial statements and required
134:   supplementary information. That report may be obtained by visiting https://www.trs.texas.gov/
134:   learning-resources/publications; by writing to the Teacher Retirement System of Texas at PO Box
134:   149676, Austin, Texas 78714; or by calling 1-800-223-8778.
134:   The following information regards to OPEB plan fiduciary net position for the year ending August
134:   31, 2024.
134:    Net OPEB Liability                                      Total
134:    Total OPEB Liability                       $     35,168,178,563
134:    Less: Plan Fiduciary Net Position                  4,816,646,311
134:    Net OPEB Liability                         $     30,351,532,252
134:    Net Position as % ofTotal OPEB Liability                    13.70%
134:   Benefit Provided
134:   TRS-Care provides health insurance coverage to retirees from public schools who are members of
134:   the TRS pension plan. Optional dependent coverage is available for an additional fee.
134:   Eligible non-Medicare retirees and their dependents may enroll in TRS-Care Standard, a high-
134:   deductible health plan . Eligible Medicare retirees and their dependents may enroll in the TRS-Care
134:   Medicare Advantage medical plan and the TRS-Care Medicare Rx prescription drug plan . To qualify
134:   for TRS-Care coverage, a retiree must have at least 10 years of service credit in the TRS pension
134:   system. There are no automatic post-employment benefit changes, including automatic COLAs.

139:   Medicare Part D
139:   The Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 (MMA) created an outpatient prescription drug benefit
139:   program known as Medicare Part D. The Texas Public School Retired Employee Group Insurance
139:   Program (TRS-Care) is offering a Medicare Part D Plan and is participating in the Retiree Drug
139:   Subsidy plan for eligible TRS-Care participants. For the years ended August 31, 2025 and August
139:   31, 2024, the subsidy payments received by TRS-Care on behalf of the District were $14,251,299
139:   and $7,684,534, respectively. TRS issues a publicly available financial report. That report may be
139:   found by visiting the TRS Web site at www.trs.texas.gov/employers/gasb-statements/gasb-24.
139:    NOTE 13: COMMITMENTS AND CONTINGENCIES
139:   The District received significant financial assistance from numerous federal and state governmental
139:   agencies in the form of grants. The disbursements of funds received under these programs generally
139:   requires compliance with terms and conditions specified in the grant agreements and are subject
139:   to audit by the granter agencies and the Texas Education Agency. Any disallowed claims resulting
139:   from such audits could become a liability of the General Fund.
139:   The District is party to various other legal actions, none of which is believed by the administration or
139:   legal counsel to have a material effect on the financial condition of the District.Accordingly, no provision
139:   for losses has been recorded in the accompanying financial statements for such contingencies.
139:    NOTE 14: NONMONETARY TRANSACTIONS
139:   During fiscal year 2025, the District received goods purchased by the State of Texas for the
139:   benefit of the District through the Instructional Materials and Technology Allotment program. The
139:   instructional materials have been recorded in the amount $1 .28 million in the special revenue fund
139:   as both state revenues and expenditures, which represent the amount of consideration given by
139:   the State of Texas.
139:   The District received an award from TEA for the Learning Acceleration Support Opportunities
139:   (LASO) Grant which focused on high quality supplemental materials for accelerated instruction
139:   activities like high impact tutoring in math for students PK-12 curriculum. In-kind donations in
139:   the amount of $667,697 for high quality instructional licenses have been recorded in the special
139:   revenue fund as both federal revenues and expenditures in fiscal year 2025.
139:    NOTE15:SUBSEQUENTEVENT
139:   Series 2025 Variance Rate Maintenance Tax Notes issued on 7/31/2025 with Par value of
139:   $20,555,000. Proceeds of the tax-exempttender refunding were used to buy back select outstanding
139:   bonds tendered by existing Houston ISD investors at the tender price (which is composed of the
139:   current market value of those outstanding bonds plus a tender premium) and to pay the costs of
139:   issuance. The Maintenance Tax Refunding bonds were structured as serial bonds maturing from
139:   2032 to 2037. The bonds carried a 10-year optional par call, beginning on July 15, 2035, used 5%
139:   coupons for all maturities and were structured with uniform savings.

148:                       NOTES TO REQUIRED SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
148:                          FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JUNE 30, 2025
148: Note 1: Stewardship, Compliance, and Accountability
148:        The District uses the following procedures in establishing the budgets reflected in the financial
148:        statements:
148:            • Prior to June 30th of the preceding fiscal year, the District prepares a budget for the next
148:              succeeding fiscal year beginning July 1. The operating budget includes proposed expenditures
148:              and the means of financing them.
148:            • Public hearings are conducted to obtain citizens' comments. However, the final priorities
148:              and funding of projects are determined by the Board of Managers that establishes a tax rate
148:              to support the approved budget.
148:            • A meeting of the Board of Managers is then called for the purpose of adopting the proposed
148:              budget.
148:            • Budgets are approved on a fund-by-fund basis. The District can make amendments to the
148:              budget at any time during the year; however, amendments changing functional expenditure
148:              categories (as defined in the Texas Education Agency's Financial Accountability System
148:              Resource Guide) must be ratified by the Board of Managers. Budget amendments are
148:              presented to the Board of Managers monthly or as needed .
148:            • Budgets are considered a management control and planning tool and, as such, are
148:              incorporated into the accounting system of the District.
148:            • Annual budgets are legally adopted for the General Fund, the Debt Service Fund, and the
148:              Nutrition Services Fund. The budgets are prepared on a basis of accounting that is used for
148:              reporting in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles and are monitored
148:              by the Budget and Financial Planning Office. By state law, expenditures may not legally
148:              exceed budgeted appropriations, as amended, at the function level by fund. Unexpended
148:              appropriations lapse at the end of the fiscal year.
148:            • Per TEA requirements, the expenditure in any functional category should not exceed the
148:              approved budget. For the year ended June 30, 2025:
148:              General Fund, Function 11, Instruction exceeded budget due to payroll costs and Texas
148:              Connections Payment
148:              General Fund, Function 21, Instructional Leadership exceeded budget due to payroll costs
148:              General Fund, Function 23, School Leadership exceeded budget due to payroll costs
148:              General Fund, Function 31, Guidance & Counseling exceeded budget due to payroll costs
148:              General Fund, Function 32, Social Work Services exceeded budget due to software purchases
148:              General Fund, Function 33, Health Services exceeded budget due to payroll costs
148:              General Fund, Function 52, Security exceeded budget due to overtime costs
148:              General Fund, Function 71, Date Processing exceeded budget due to SBITAs
148:              General Fund, Function 91, Contracted instructional services between public schools
148:              exceeded budget due to an increased local fund assignment which increases the cost
148:              of recapture

153: The Medicaid Fund is used to account for the financial operations of the district’s school-based federal Medicaid
153: program that provides health and medical services to Medicaid eligible special education students. In addition,
153: the district currently provides consulting services and Medicaid claims management services to approximately 90
153: Texas school districts.

153: located on the first level of the Hattie Mae White (HMW) Educational Support Center. The district established this
153: Marketplace as a benefit to employees working in the HMW building. The Starbucks® coffee and snack bar
153: provides a variety Starbucks® drinks and grab-and-go items made available to guests and employees at HMW.

157:  HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
157:  SCHOOL DISTRICT
157:                                          INTERNAL SERVICE FUNDS
157: The Print Shop Fund is used to account for all the printing and distribution activities of the District’s print shop.
157: Schools and departments are charged for the costs of printing and distribution requests. During non-peak
157: times, the Print Shop contracts with other governmental agencies requiring assistance during their peak
157: periods.   In addition, the Print Shop handles the districtwide copier contract/services for all schools and
157: departments.
157: The Health Insurance Fund is used to account for the health insurance plan administered by the District. The
157: plan is a self-insured plan requiring the District and its employees to contribute the cost.            The District
157: contributes approximately 81.45 percent of the annual cost of the plan with employees paying for the remaining
157: 18.55 percent.    These contributions are paid from all governmental and proprietary funds to the Health
157: Insurance Fund from which all claims and administrative expenses are paid.
157: The Workers’ Compensation Fund is used to account for risk financing activities related to the self-insured
157: workers’ compensation program. All employees of the District are covered by this plan for injuries occurring on
157: the job. The District contributes 100 percent of the funding for this program.
157: The Internal Services Fund is used to account for the fee-for-services offered by the District to serve the
157: specific needs of schools and departments. The Alternative Certification, Athletics, UIL, and Shared Services
157: programs are accounted for within this fund.

189:   In fiscal year 2017, Houston ISO began sending "local excess revenue" to the state. The district is
189:   considered property rich and is required to send back local tax revenue in excess of entitlement.
189:   Chapter 49 of the Texas Education Code (TEC) makes provisions for certain school districts to
189:   share their local tax revenue with other school districts. These provisions are sometimes referred
189:   to as "share the wealth", "Robin Hood" or "recapture" because recaptured funds are redistributed
189:   by the school finance system.

189:   ** No payment required due to tax compression and $100k homestead exemption

231:                            Independent Auditor’s Report on Internal Control over Financial
231:                             Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an
231:                                Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance
231:                                         with Government Auditing Standards
231:    To the School Board and Management of
231:    Houston Independent School District
231:    Houston, Texas
231:    We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America and the
231:    standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller
231:    General of the United States ( Government Auditing Standards), the financial statements of the governmental
231:    activities, the business-type activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of Houston
231:    Independent School District (the District) as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025, and the related notes to the
231:    financial statements, which collectively comprise the District’s basic financial statements, and have issued our report
231:    thereon dated January 12, 2026.
231:    Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
231:    In planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the District’s internal control over
231:    financial reporting (internal control) as a basis for designing audit procedures that are appropriate in the
231:    circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinions on the financial statements, but not for the purpose of
231:    expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the District’s internal control. Accordingly, we do not express an
231:    opinion on the effectiveness of the District’s internal control.
231:    A deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
231:    employees in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct
231:    misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal
231:    control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s financial statements
231:    will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is a deficiency, or a
231:    combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material weakness, yet important enough
231:    to merit attention by those charged with governance.
231:    Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this section and
231:    was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses or significant
231:    deficiencies and therefore, material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist that have not been identified.
231:    Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in internal control that we consider to
231:    be material weaknesses. We identified a certain deficiency in internal control, described in the accompanying
231:    schedule of findings and questioned costs as item 2025-001, that we consider to be a significant deficiency.
231:    Report on Compliance and Other Matters
231:    As part of obtaining reasonable assurance about whether the District’s financial statements are free from material
231:    misstatement, we performed tests of its compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant
231:    agreements, noncompliance with which could have a direct and material effect on the financial statements. However,
231:    providing an opinion on compliance with those provisions was not an objective of our audit and, accordingly, we
231:    do not express such an opinion. The results of our tests disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters
231:    that are required to be reported under Government Auditing Standards.

234: Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of Compliance
234: Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether material noncompliance with the compliance
234: requirements referred to above occurred, whether due to fraud or error, and express an opinion on the District’s
234: compliance based on our audit. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not absolute assurance and
234: therefore is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with GAAS, Government Auditing Standards,
234: the Uniform Guidance and TxGMS will always detect material noncompliance when it exists. The risk of not detecting
234: material noncompliance resulting from fraud is higher than for that resulting from error, as fraud may involve
234: collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control. Noncompliance with
234: the compliance requirements referred to above is considered material, if there is a substantial likelihood that,
234: individually or in the aggregate, it would influence the judgment made by a reasonable user of the report on
234: compliance about the District’s compliance with the requirements of each major federal and state program as a
234: whole.
234: In performing an audit in accordance with GAAS, Government Auditing Standards, the Uniform Guidance and
234: TxGMS, we:
234:     •    Exercise professional judgment and maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit.
234:     •    Identify and assess the risks of material noncompliance, whether due to fraud or error, and design and
234:          perform audit procedures responsive to those risks. Such procedures include examining, on a test basis,
234:          evidence regarding the District’s compliance with the compliance requirements referred to above and
234:          performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
234:     •    Obtain an understanding of the District’s internal control over compliance relevant to the audit in order to
234:          design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances and to test and report on internal control
234:          over compliance in accordance with the Uniform Guidance and TxGMS, but not for the purpose of
234:          expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the District’s internal control over compliance. Accordingly,
234:          no such opinion is expressed.
234: We are required to communicate with those charged with governance regarding, among other matters, the planned
234: scope and timing of the audit and any significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in internal control over
234: compliance that we identified during the audit.
234: Other Matters
234: The results of our auditing procedures disclosed instances of noncompliance which are required to be reported in
234: accordance with the Uniform Guidance and which are described in the accompanying schedule of findings and
234: questioned costs as item 2025-002. Our opinion on each major federal program is not modified with respect to
234: these matters. Government Auditing Standards require the auditor to perform limited procedures on the District’s
234: response to the noncompliance findings identified in our compliance audit described in the accompanying schedule
234: of findings and questioned costs. The District’s response was not subjected to the other auditing procedures applied
234: in the audit of compliance and, accordingly, we express no opinion on the response.
234: Report on Internal Control over Compliance
234: Our consideration of internal control over compliance was for the limited purpose described in the Auditor’s
234: Responsibilities for the Audit of Compliance section above and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in
234: internal control over compliance that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in internal control
234: over compliance and therefore, material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist that were not identified.
234: We did not identify any deficiencies in internal control over compliance that we consider to be material weaknesses.
234: However, as discussed below, we did identify certain deficiencies in internal control over compliance that we
234: consider to be significant deficiencies.

235: The School Board and Management of
235: Houston Independent School District
235: A deficiency in internal control over compliance exists when the design or operation of a control over compliance
235: does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent,
235: or detect and correct, noncompliance with a type of compliance requirement of a federal or state program on a
235: timely basis. A material weakness in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies,
235: in internal control over compliance, such that there is a reasonable possibility that material noncompliance with a
235: type of compliance requirement of a federal or state program will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on
235: a timely basis. A significant deficiency in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or a combination of
235: deficiencies, in internal control over compliance with a type of compliance requirement of a federal or state program
235: that is less severe than a material weakness in internal control over compliance, yet important enough to merit
235: attention by those charged with governance. We consider the deficiencies in internal control over compliance
235: described in the accompanying schedule of findings and questioned costs as items 2025-002 and 2025-003, to be
235: significant deficiencies.
235: Our audit was not designed for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control over
235: compliance. Accordingly, no such opinion is expressed. Government Auditing Standards requires the auditor to
235: perform limited procedures on the District’s response to the internal control over compliance findings identified in
235: our compliance audit described in the accompanying schedule of findings and questioned costs. The District’s
235: response was not subjected to the other auditing procedures applied in the audit of compliance and, accordingly,
235: we express no opinion on the response.
235: The purpose of this report on internal control over compliance is solely to describe the scope of our testing of
235: internal control over compliance and the results of that testing based on the requirements of the Uniform Guidance
235: and TxGMS. Accordingly, this report is not suitable for any other purpose.

238:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
238:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
238: Houston Independent School District
238: Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs
238: For the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2025
238: Section II – Findings Related to Financial Statements
238: 2025-001
238: Significant deficiency in Internal Control over Financial Reporting: School Health And Related Services
238: (SHARS) Revenue
238: Criteria
238: Management is responsible for the accuracy and completeness of all financial records and related information and
238: for establishing and maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting. Reimbursement requests for
238: SHARS revenue must meet the requirements applicable under federal and state laws. The Texas Health and Human
238: Services Commission (HHSC) reviews the reimbursement requests and provides estimated Cost Settlement reports
238: identifying any unallowable amounts. Any amounts determined to be unallowable should not be recognized as
238: revenue in the reporting entity’s financial statements.
238: Condition
238: The estimated SHARS claims revenue and accrual recognized in the District's financial statements for the year ended
238: June 30, 2025 were misstated due to failure to consider the HHSC 2023 Cost Settlement report findings and results
238: in evaluation of the estimates.
238: Cause
238: The HHSC 2023 Cost Settlement Report was received by the District during the year ended June 30, 2025 and was
238: not properly evaluated to determine if an adjustment should be recorded in the financial statements. The 2023 Cost
238: Settlement Report was not provided timely to the Controller’s Office for review.
238: Effect
238: Misstatement of the District’s financial statements was not prevented, or detected and corrected, by the District’s
238: system of internal control. Failure to establish effective monitoring and closing procedures will allow possible
238: irregularities to exist and continue without notice.
238: Recommendation
238: We recommend that the District implement additional procedures to ensure all Cost Settlement reports are provided
238: to the Controller’s Office to ensure proper evaluation of the estimated revenue adjustments in accordance with
238: generally accepted accounting principles.
238: Views of Responsible Officials and Planned Corrective Actions
238: See corrective action plan

239:    HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
239:    SCHOOL DISTRICT
239: Houston Independent School District
239: Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs
239: For the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2025
239: Section III – Federal and State Award Findings and Questioned Costs
239: 2025-002
239: Information on Federal Program:
239: Federal Program: COVID-19 – Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund (ARP ESSER III)
239: Federal Agency: U.S. Department of Education
239: Federal Award Identification Number and Year: 21528001101912 & 21533002101912 - 2021
239: Passthrough Agency: Texas Education Agency
239: Assistance Listing: 84.425U & 84.425W
239: Compliance Requirement: Equipment
239: Significant deficiency in Internal Control over Compliance and Noncompliance
239: Criteria
239: In accordance with federal regulations, under 2 CFR § 200.313, a non-Federal entity must conduct a physical
239: inventory of all equipment purchased with federal funds at least once every two years. Furthermore, under 2 CFR §
239: 200.303, the entity must maintain effective internal controls designed to ensure compliance with federal
239: requirements for safeguarding assets.
239: Condition
239: A physical inventory count was not performed for all school campuses within the District during the last two years,
239: with equipment purchased with federal grant awards.
239: Cause
239: A recent inventory of capital assets acquired with federal awards, performed by the District as of June 30, 2024, had
239: incomplete participation from approximately 45% of the District's campuses. The District’s internal controls over
239: compliance failed to trigger action to verify sufficient participation and completeness, to prevent or detect and
239: correct noncompliance.
239: Effect
239: The District was not in compliance with the physical inventory requirements of the Uniform Guidance. Possible
239: effects include unaccounted for equipment purchased with federal funds.
239: Questioned Cost
239: None
239: Context
239: During our audit, 20 out of the 25 assets we selected to verify if a physical inventory count took place were either
239: shown as “unaccounted for” or excluded from the counts performed. The heating, ventilation and cooling
239: equipment purchased and added to school campuses was excluded from the counts performed and totaled 6 units.
239: The remaining items were primarily buses and band instruments which were inventoried at schools that did not
239: count or were noted as “unaccounted for” during the inventory count process.
239: Recommendation
239: We recommend the District provide training for campus fixed asset administrators on inventory procedures
239: including inventory audit and reconciliation practices to ensure timely completion of inventory count procedures at
239: all campuses.
239: Views of Responsible Officials and Planned Corrective Actions
239: See corrective action plan

240: 2025-003
240: Information on Federal Program:
240: Federal Program: COVID-19 – Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund (ARP ESSER III)
240: Federal Agency: U.S. Department of Education
240: Federal Award Identification Number and Year: 215280587110070 - 2021
240: Passthrough Agency: Texas Education Agency
240: Assistance Listing: 84.425U & 84.425W
240: Compliance Requirement: Allowable Cost/Cost Principals
240: Significant deficiency in Internal Control over Compliance and Questioned Costs
240: Criteria
240: Grant award terms provide a start and end date of the federal award and all expenditures must be incurred during
240: the grant period, including any liquidation period.
240: Condition
240: For the TCLAS ARP ESSER III grant, expenditures were incurred after the liquidation period ended on November 30,
240: 2024.The approval of subscription costs was not obtained for liquidation extension as required by the Department
240: of Education.
240: Cause
240: The District was required to liquidate approximately $450 thousand of remaining TCLAS High-Quality After-School
240: funds within five months of its fiscal year. During this period, the existing expenditure review process did not provide
240: sufficient oversight to prevent costs related to the period beyond the liquidation deadline from being processed.
240: Effect
240: The District’s internal controls failed to ensure expenses were compliant with grant-specific restrictions before
240: payment and therefore the District incurred and charged unallowable costs to the federal program.
240: Questioned Cost
240: $54,626 of subscription services expenditures
240: Context
240: During our audit, 3 of 60 expenditures we selected for testing were associated with software subscription contracts
240: that had service periods which commenced prior to the liquidation period deadline but extended beyond the
240: standard grant liquidation period deadline of November 30, 2024.
240: Recommendation
240: We recommend the District to provide training for staff responsible for reviewing grant expenditures on federal cost
240: principles and the specific restrictions of grant awards.
240: Views of Responsible Officials and Planned Corrective Actions
240: See corrective action plan

247: HOUSTON INDEPENDENT
247: SCHOOL DISTRICT
247: HOUSTON INDEPENDENT SCHOOL DISTRICT
247: NOTES TO SCHEDULE OF EXPENDITURES OF FEDERAL AND STATE AWARDS
247: JUNE 30, 2025
247: 1. The Houston Independent School District (the "District") utilizes the funds specified in the Texas Education
247:    Agency Financial Accountability System Resource Guide. The information in the Schedule of Expenditures of
247:    Federal Awards (SEFA) is presented in accordance with the requirements of the Uniform Guidance and the
247:    Schedule of Expenditures of State Awards (SESA) is presented in accordance with the requirements of Texas
247:    Uniform Grant Management Standards.
247:   The Special Revenue Fund is used to account for resources restricted to, or designated for, specific purposes
247:   by a grantor. Federal and state financial assistance generally is accounted for in a Special Revenue Fund.
247:   Generally, unused balances are returned to the grantor at the close of specified project periods.
247: 2. The accounting and financial reporting treatment applied to a fund is determined by its measurement focus.
247:    The governmental funds are accounted for using a current-financial-resources measurement focus. All federal
247:    and state grant funds are accounted for in the Special Revenue Fund, a component of the governmental
247:    funds. With this measurement focus, only current assets and current liabilities, generally, are included on the
247:    balance sheet. Operating statements of these funds present increases (i.e., revenues and other financing
247:    sources) and decreases (i.e., expenditures and other financing uses) in net current assets.
247:   The modified-accrual basis of accounting is used for the governmental funds. This basis of accounting
247:   recognizes revenues in the accounting period in which they become both measurable and available and
247:   expenditures in the accounting period in which the fund liability is incurred, except that principal and interest
247:   on general long-term debt are recognized when due.
247:   National School Lunch Program and Summer Food Service Program non-cash commodities are recorded at
247:   their estimated market value at the time of donation.
247:   Federal and state grant funds are considered to be earned when all eligibility requirements have been met. Any
247:   excess of revenues or expenditures is recorded as unearned revenues or accounts receivable, respectively.
247: 3. The period of availability for federal funds for the purpose of liquidating all financial obligations incurred on or
247:    before the ending date of the federal project period extended 120 calendar days beyond the federal project
247:    period ending date as specified in the terms and conditions (2 CFR section 200.344(b)).
247: 4. The disbursement of funds received under federal grant programs generally requires compliance with
247:    terms and conditions specified in the grant agreements and is subject to audit by the grantor agencies. Any
247:    disallowed claims resulting from such audits could become a liability of the General Fund . In the opinion of
247:    management, such disallowed claims, if any, will not have a material effect on any of the financial statements
247:    of the individual fund types or on the overall financial position of the District at June 30, 2025.
247:  Total Expenditures of Federal Financial Assistance:                    $                    389,630,012

253:      APPENDIX C
253: BOOK-ENTRY-ONLY SYSTEM
253: 
254: [THIS PAGE INTENTIONALLY LEFT BLANK]
254: 
255:                                                  BOOK-ENTRY-ONLY SYSTEM
255: This appendix describes how ownership of the Bonds is to be transferred and how the principal of, premium, if any, and interest
255: on the Bonds are to be paid to and accredited by DTC while the Bonds are registered in its nominee name. The information in this
255: appendix concerning DTC and the book-entry-only system has been provided by DTC for use in disclosure documents such as this
255: Official Statement. The District, the Underwriters and the Municipal Advisor believe the source of such information to be reliable,
255: but take no responsibility for the accuracy or completeness thereof.
255: The District cannot and does not give any assurance that (1) DTC will distribute payments of debt service on the Bonds or other
255: notices, to DTC Participants, (2) DTC Participants or others will distribute debt service payments paid to DTC or its nominee (as
255: the registered owner of the Bonds), or other notices, to the Beneficial Owners, or that they will do so on a timely basis, or (3) DTC
255: will serve and act in the manner described in this Official Statement. The current rules applicable to DTC are on file with the
255: United States Securities and Exchange Commission, and the current procedures of DTC to be followed in dealing with DTC
255: Participants are on file with DTC.
255: DTC will act as securities depository for the Bonds. The Bonds will be issued as fully-registered securities registered in the name
255: of Cede & Co. (DTC’s partnership nominee) or such other name as may be requested by an authorized representative of DTC. One
255: fully-registered certificate will be issued for each stated maturity of the Bonds, in the aggregate principal amount of such issue, and
255: will be deposited with DTC.
255: DTC, the world’s largest securities depository, is a limited-purpose trust company organized under the New York Banking Law, a
255: “banking organization” within the meaning of the New York Banking Law, a member of the Federal Reserve System, a “clearing
255: corporation” within the meaning of the New York Uniform Commercial Code, and a “clearing agency” registered pursuant to the
255: provisions of Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. DTC holds and provides asset servicing for over 3.5 million
255: issues of U.S. and non-U.S. equity issues, corporate and municipal debt issues, and money market instruments (from over 100
255: countries) that DTC’s participants (“Direct Participants”) deposit with DTC. DTC also facilitates the post-trade settlement among
255: Direct Participants of sales and other securities transactions in deposited securities, through electronic computerized book-entry
255: transfers and pledges between Direct Participants’ accounts. This eliminates the need for physical movement of securities
255: certificates. Direct Participants include both U.S. and non-U.S. securities brokers and dealers, banks, trust companies, clearing
255: corporations, and certain other organizations. DTC is a wholly-owned subsidiary of The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation
255: (“DTCC”). DTCC is the holding company for DTC, National Securities Clearing Corporation and Fixed Income Clearing
255: Corporation, all of which are registered clearing agencies. DTCC is owned by the users of its regulated subsidiaries. Access to the
255: DTC system is also available to others such as both U.S. and non-U.S. securities brokers and dealers, banks, trust companies, and
255: clearing corporations that clear through or maintain a custodial relationship with a Direct Participant, either directly or indirectly
255: (“Indirect Participants”). DTC has a S&P Global Ratings rating of “AA+.” The DTC Rules applicable to its Participants are on file
255: with the Securities and Exchange Commission. More information about DTC can be found at www.dtcc.com.
255: Purchases of Bonds under the DTC system must be made by or through Direct Participants, which will receive a credit for the
255: Bonds on DTC’s records. The ownership interest of each actual purchaser of each Bond (“Beneficial Owner”) is in turn to be
255: recorded on the Direct and Indirect Participants’ records. Beneficial Owners will not receive written confirmation from DTC of
255: their purchase. Beneficial Owners are, however, expected to receive written confirmations providing details of the transaction, as
255: well as periodic statements of their holdings, from the Direct or Indirect Participant through which the Beneficial Owner entered
255: into the transaction. Transfers of ownership interests in the Bonds are to be accomplished by entries made on the books of Direct
255: and Indirect Participants acting on behalf of Beneficial Owners. Beneficial Owners will not receive certificates representing their
255: ownership interests in Bonds except in the event that use of the book-entry system for the Bonds is discontinued.
255: To facilitate subsequent transfers, all Bonds deposited by Direct Participants with DTC are registered in the name of DTC’s
255: partnership nominee, Cede & Co., or such other name as may be requested by an authorized representative of DTC. The deposit of
255: Bonds with DTC and their registration in the name of Cede & Co. or such other DTC nominee do not effect any change in beneficial
255: ownership. DTC has no knowledge of the actual Beneficial Owners of the Bonds; DTC’s records reflect only the identity of the
255: Direct Participants to whose accounts such Bonds are credited, which may or may not be the Beneficial Owners. The Direct and
255: Indirect Participants will remain responsible for keeping account of their holdings on behalf of their customers.
255: Conveyance of notices and other communications by DTC to Direct Participants, by Direct Participants to Indirect Participants,
255: and by Direct Participants and Indirect Participants to Beneficial Owners will be governed by arrangements among them, subject
255: to any statutory or regulatory requirements as may be in effect from time to time. Beneficial Owners of Bonds may wish to take
255: certain steps to augment the transmission to them of notices of significant events with respect to the Bonds, such as tenders, defaults,
255: and proposed amendments to the Bonds documents. For example, Beneficial Owners of Bonds may wish to ascertain that the
255: nominee holding the Bonds for their benefit has agreed to obtain and transmit notices to Beneficial Owners. In the alternative,
255: Beneficial Owners may wish to provide their names and addresses to the registrar and request that copies of notices be provided
255: directly to them.
255:                                                                  C-1
255: 
256: Neither DTC nor Cede & Co. (nor any other DTC nominee) will consent or vote with respect to Bonds unless authorized by a
256: Direct Participant in accordance with DTC’s MMI Procedures. Under its usual procedures, DTC mails an Omnibus Proxy to the
256: District as soon as possible after the record date. The Omnibus Proxy assigns Cede & Co.’s consenting or voting rights to those
256: Direct Participants to whose accounts Bonds are credited on the record date (identified in a listing attached to the Omnibus Proxy).
256: Principal and interest payments on the Bonds will be made to Cede & Co., or such other nominee as may be requested by an
256: authorized representative of DTC. DTC’s practice is to credit Direct Participants’ accounts upon DTC’s receipt of funds and
256: corresponding detail information from the District or Paying Agent/Registrar, on payable date in accordance with their respective
256: holdings shown on DTC’s records. Payments by Participants to Beneficial Owners will be governed by standing instructions and
256: customary practices, as is the case with securities held for the accounts of customers in bearer form or registered in “street name,”
256: and will be the responsibility of such Participant and not of DTC, Paying Agent/Registrar, or the District, subject to any statutory
256: or regulatory requirements as may be in effect from time to time. Payment of principal and interest payments to Cede & Co. (or
256: such other nominee as may be requested by an authorized representative of DTC) is the responsibility of District or Paying
256: Agent/Registrar, disbursement of such payments to Direct Participants will be the responsibility of DTC, and disbursement of such
256: payments to the Beneficial Owners will be the responsibility of Direct and Indirect Participants.
256: A Beneficial Owner shall give notice to elect to have its Bonds purchased or tendered, through its Participant, to the Tender Agent,
256: and shall effect delivery of such Bonds by causing the Direct Participant to transfer the Participant’s interest in the Bonds, on
256: DTC’s records, to the Tender Agent. The requirement for physical delivery of Bonds in connection with an optional tender or a
256: mandatory purchase will be deemed satisfied when the ownership rights in the Bonds are transferred by Direct Participants on
256: DTC’s records and followed by a book-entry credit of tendered Bonds to the Tender Agent’s DTC account.
256: DTC may discontinue providing its services as depository with respect to the Bonds at any time by giving reasonable notice to the
256: District or Tender Agent. Under such circumstances, in the event that a successor depository is not obtained, Bond certificates are
256: required to be printed and delivered.
256: The District may decide to discontinue use of the system of book-entry-only transfers through DTC (or a successor securities
256: depository). In that event, Bond certificates will be printed and delivered to DTC.
256: The information in this appendix concerning DTC and DTC’s book-entry system has been obtained from sources that the District,
256: the Underwriters and the Municipal Advisor believe to be reliable, but the District, the Underwriters, and the Municipal Advisor
256: take no responsibility for the accuracy thereof.
256: Use of Certain Terms in Other Sections of this Official Statement. In reading this Official Statement it should be understood that
256: while the Bonds are in the book-entry-only system, references in other sections of this Official Statement to registered owners
256: should be read to include the person for which the Participant acquires an interest in the Bonds, but (i) all rights of ownership must
256: be exercised through DTC and the book-entry-only system, and (ii) except as described above, notices that are to be given to
256: registered owners under the Order will be given only to DTC. Information concerning DTC and the book-entry-only system has
256: been obtained from DTC and is not guaranteed as to accuracy or completeness by, and is not to be construed as a representation by
256: the District, the Municipal Advisor or the Underwriters.
256: Effect of Termination of Book-Entry-Only System. In the event that the book-entry-only system is discontinued by DTC or the
256: use of the book-entry-only system is discontinued by the District, printed Bonds will be issued to the holders and the Bonds will
256: be subject to transfer, exchange and registration provisions as set forth in the Order and summarized under “THE BONDS -
256: TRANSFER, EXCHANGE AND REGISTRATION” in the Official Statement.

257:                                                            APPENDIX D
257:                               THE PERMANENT SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM
257: This disclosure statement provides information relating to the program (the “Guarantee Program”) administered by the Texas
257: Education Agency (the “TEA”) with respect to the Texas Permanent School Fund guarantee of tax-supported bonds issued by
257: Texas school districts and the guarantee of revenue bonds issued by or for the benefit of Texas charter districts. The Guarantee
257: Program was authorized by an amendment to the Texas Constitution in 1983 and is governed by Subchapter C of Chapter 45 of the
257: Texas Education Code, as amended (the “Act”). While the Guarantee Program applies to bonds issued by or for both school districts
257: and charter districts, as described below, the Act and the program rules for the two types of districts have some distinctions. For
257: convenience of description and reference, those aspects of the Guarantee Program that are applicable to school district bonds and
257: to charter district bonds are referred to herein as the “School District Bond Guarantee Program” and the “Charter District Bond
257: Guarantee Program,” respectively.
257: Some of the information contained in this Section may include projections or other forward-looking statements regarding future
257: events or the future financial performance of the Texas Permanent School Fund (the “PSF” or the “Fund”). Actual results may
257: differ materially from those contained in any such projections or forward-looking statements.
257: The regular session of the 89th Texas Legislature (the “Legislature”) convened on January 14, 2025, and concluded on June 2,
257: 2025. The Legislature meets in regular session in odd numbered years for 140 days. When the Legislature is not in session, the
257: Governor may call one or more special sessions, at the Governor’s discretion, each lasting no more than 30 days, and for which the
257: Governor sets the agenda. The Governor called a first special session, which began on July 21, 2025, and ended on August 15,
257: 2025. The Governor called a second special session, which began on August 15, 2025, and ended on September 4, 2025 (the
257: regular session together with the special sessions may hereinafter be referred to as the “89th Legislative Session”). The TEA, the
257: State Board of Education (the “SBOE”), and the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation (the “PSF Corporation”) are in the
257: process of monitoring the implementation of legislation signed by the Governor and make no representation regarding any actions
257: taken by the Legislature in the 89th Legislative Session that may materially impact themselves, the Guarantee Program, the Act,
257: and Texas school finance in general.
257: History and Purpose
257: The PSF supports the State’s public school system in two major ways: distributions to the constitutionally established Available
257: School Fund (the “ASF”), as described below, and the guarantee of school district and charter district issued bonds through the
257: Guarantee Program. The PSF was created in 1845 and received its first significant funding with a $2,000,000 appropriation by the
257: Legislature in 1854 expressly for the benefit of the public schools of Texas, with the sole purpose of assisting in the funding of
257: public education for present and future generations. The Constitution of 1876 described that the PSF would be “permanent,” and
257: stipulated that certain lands and all proceeds from the sale of these lands should also constitute the PSF. Additional acts later gave
257: more public domain land and rights to the PSF. In 1953, the U.S. Congress passed the Submerged Lands Act that relinquished to
257: coastal states all rights of the U.S. navigable waters within state boundaries. If the State, by law, had set a larger boundary prior to
257: or at the time of admission to the Union, or if the boundary had been approved by Congress, then the larger boundary applied. After
257: three years of litigation (1957-1960), the U.S. Supreme Court on May 31, 1960, affirmed Texas’ historic three marine leagues
257: (10.35 miles) seaward boundary. Texas proved its submerged lands property rights to three leagues into the Gulf of Mexico by
257: citing historic laws and treaties dating back to 1836. All lands lying within that limit belong to the PSF. The proceeds from the sale
257: and the mineral-related rental of these lands, including bonuses, delay rentals and royalty payments, become the corpus of the Fund.
257: Prior to the approval by the voters of the State of an amendment to the constitutional provision under which the Fund was
257: established and administered, which occurred on September 13, 2003 (the “Total Return Constitutional Amendment”), and which
257: is further described below, only the income produced by the PSF could be used to complement taxes in financing public education,
257: which primarily consisted of income from securities, capital gains from securities transactions, and royalties from the sale of oil
257: and natural gas. The Total Return Constitutional Amendment provides that interest and dividends produced by Fund investments
257: will be additional revenue to the PSF.
257: On November 8, 1983, the voters of the State approved a constitutional amendment that provides for the guarantee by the PSF of
257: bonds issued by school districts. On approval by the State Commissioner of Education (the “Education Commissioner”), bonds
257: properly issued by a school district are fully guaranteed by the PSF. See “The School District Bond Guarantee Program.”
257: In 2011, legislation was enacted that established the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program as a new component of the Guarantee
257: Program. That legislation authorized the use of the PSF to guarantee revenue bonds issued by or for the benefit of certain open-
257: enrollment charter schools that are designated as “charter districts” by the Education Commissioner. On approval by the Education
257: Commissioner, bonds properly issued by a charter district participating in the Guarantee Program are fully guaranteed by the PSF.
257: The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program became effective on March 3, 2014. See “The Charter District Bond Guarantee
257: Program.”
257:                                                                  D-1
257: 
258: State law also permits charter schools to be chartered and operated by school districts and other political subdivisions, but bond
258: financing of facilities for school district-operated charter schools is subject to the School District Bond Guarantee Program, not the
258: Charter District Bond Guarantee Program.
258: While the School District Bond Guarantee Program and the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program relate to different types of
258: bonds issued for different types of Texas public schools, and have different program regulations and requirements, a bond
258: guaranteed under either part of the Guarantee Program has the same effect with respect to the guarantee obligation of the Fund
258: thereto, and all guaranteed bonds are aggregated for purposes of determining the capacity of the Guarantee Program (see “Capacity
258: Limits for the Guarantee Program”). The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program as enacted by State law has not been reviewed
258: by any court, nor has the Texas Attorney General (the “Attorney General”) been requested to issue an opinion, with respect to its
258: constitutional validity.

258: Investment Policy Statement (the “IPS”), and (iv) monthly updates with respect to the capacity of the Guarantee Program

258: Management and Administration of the Fund
258: The Texas Constitution and applicable statutes delegate to the SBOE and the PSF Corporation the authority and responsibility for
258: investment of the PSF’s financial assets. The SBOE consists of 15 members who are elected by territorial districts in the State,
258: generally, to four-year terms of office. The PSF Corporation is a special-purpose governmental corporation and instrumentality of
258: the State entitled to sovereign immunity, and is governed by a nine-member board of directors (the “PSFC Board”), which consists
258: of five members of the SBOE, the Land Commissioner, and three appointed members who have substantial background and
258: expertise in investments and asset management, with one member being appointed by the Land Commissioner and the other two
258: appointed by the Governor with confirmation by the Senate.
258: The PSF’s non-financial real assets, including land, mineral and royalty interests, and individual real estate holdings, are held by
258: the GLO and managed by the SLB. The SLB is required to send PSF mineral and royalty revenues to the PSF Corporation for
258: investment, less amounts specified by appropriation to be retained by the SLB.
258: The Texas Constitution provides that the Fund shall be managed through the exercise of the judgment and care under the
258: circumstances then prevailing which persons of ordinary prudence, discretion, and intelligence exercise in the management of their
258: own affairs, not in regard to speculation, but in regard to the permanent disposition of their funds, considering the probable income
258: therefrom as well as the probable safety of their capital (the “Prudent Person Standard”). In accordance with the Texas Constitution,
258: the SBOE views the PSF as a perpetual endowment, and the Fund is managed as an endowment fund with a long-term investment
258: horizon. For a detailed description of the PSFC Board’s investment objectives, as well as a description of the PSFC Boards’s roles
258: and responsibilities in managing and administering the Fund, see the IPS and Board meeting materials (available on the PSF
258: Corporation’s website).
258:                                                                 D-2
258: 
259: As described below, the Total Return Constitutional Amendment restricts the annual pay-out from the Fund to both (i) 6% of the
259: average of the market value of the Fund, excluding real property, on the last day of each of the sixteen State fiscal quarters preceding
259: the Regular Session of the Legislature that begins before that State fiscal biennium, and (ii) the total-return on all investment assets
259: of the Fund over a rolling ten-year period.
259: By law, the Education Commissioner is appointed by the Governor, with Senate confirmation, and assists the SBOE, but the
259: Education Commissioner can neither be hired nor dismissed by the SBOE. The PSF Corporation has internal and external legal
259: counsel to advise it as to its duties with respect to the Fund, including specific actions regarding the investment of the PSF to ensure
259: compliance with fiduciary standards, and to provide transactional advice in connection with the investment of Fund assets in non-
259: traditional investments. TEA’s General Counsel provides legal advice to the SBOE but will not provide legal advice directly to the
259: PSF Corporation.
259: The Total Return Constitutional Amendment shifted administrative costs of the Fund from the ASF to the PSF, providing that
259: expenses of managing the PSF are to be paid “by appropriation” from the PSF. In January 2005, the Attorney General issued a
259: legal opinion, Op. Tex. Att’y Gen. No. GA-0293 (2005), stating that the Total Return Constitutional Amendment does not require
259: the SBOE to pay from such appropriated PSF funds the indirect management costs deducted from the assets of a mutual fund or
259: other investment company in which PSF funds have been invested.
259: The Act requires that the Education Commissioner prepare, and the SBOE approve, an annual status report on the Guarantee
259: Program (which is included in the Annual Report). The State Auditor or a certified public accountant audits the financial statements
259: of the PSF, which are separate from other financial statements of the State. Additionally, not less than once each year, the PSFC
259: Board must submit an audit report to the Legislative Budget Board (“LBB”) regarding the operations of the PSF Corporation. The
259: PSF Corporation may contract with a certified public accountant or the State Auditor to conduct an independent audit of the
259: operations of the PSF Corporation, but such authorization does not affect the State Auditor’s authority to conduct an audit of the
259: PSF Corporation in accordance with State laws.
259: For each biennium, beginning with the 2024-2025 State biennium, the PSF Corporation is required to submit a legislative
259: appropriations request (“LAR”) to the LBB and the Office of the Governor that details a request for appropriation of funds to enable
259: the PSF Corporation to carry out its responsibilities for the investment management of the Fund. The appropriated funding, budget
259: structure, and riders are sufficient to fully support all operations of the PSF Corporation in state fiscal years 2026 and 2027. As
259: described therein, the LAR is designed to provide the PSF Corporation with the ability to operate as a stand-alone state entity in
259: the State budget while retaining the flexibility to fulfill its fiduciary duty and provide oversight and transparency to the Legislature
259: and Governor.
259: The Total Return Constitutional Amendment
259: The Total Return Constitutional Amendment requires that PSF distributions to the ASF be determined using a “total-return-based”
259: approach that provides that the total amount distributed from the Fund to the ASF: (1) in each year of a State fiscal biennium must
259: be an amount that is not more than 6% of the average of the market value of the Fund, excluding real property (the “Distribution
259: Rate”), on the last day of each of the sixteen State fiscal quarters preceding the Regular Session of the Legislature that begins before
259: that State fiscal biennium, in accordance with the rate adopted by: (a) a vote of two-thirds of the total membership of the SBOE,
259: taken before the Regular Session of the Legislature convenes or (b) the Legislature by general law or appropriation, if the SBOE
259: does not adopt a rate as provided by clause (a); and (2) over the ten-year period consisting of the current State fiscal year and the
259: nine preceding State fiscal years may not exceed the total return on all investment assets of the Fund over the same ten-year period
259: (the “Ten Year Total Return”). In April 2009, the Attorney General issued a legal opinion, Op. Tex. Att’y Gen. No. GA-0707
259: (2009) (“GA-0707”), with regard to certain matters pertaining to the Distribution Rate and the determination of the Ten Year Total
259: Return. In GA-0707 the Attorney General opined, among other advice, that (i) the Ten Year Total Return should be calculated on
259: an annual basis, (ii) a contingency plan adopted by the SBOE, to permit monthly transfers equal in aggregate to the annual
259: Distribution Rate to be halted and subsequently made up if such transfers temporarily exceed the Ten Year Total Return, is not
259: prohibited by State law, provided that such contingency plan applies only within a fiscal year time basis, not on a biennium basis,
259: and (iii) the amount distributed from the Fund in a fiscal year may not exceed 6% of the average of the market value of the Fund
259: or the Ten Year Total Return. In accordance with GA-0707, in the event that the Ten Year Total Return is exceeded during a fiscal
259: year, transfers to the ASF will be halted. However, if the Ten Year Total Return subsequently increases during that biennium,
259: transfers may be resumed, if the SBOE has provided for that contingency, and made in full during the remaining period of the
259: biennium, subject to the limit of 6% in any one fiscal year. Any shortfall in the transfer that results from such events from one
259: biennium may not be paid over to the ASF in a subsequent biennium as the SBOE would make a separate payout determination for
259: that subsequent biennium.
259: In determining the Distribution Rate, the SBOE has adopted the goal of maximizing the amount distributed from the Fund in a
259: manner designed to preserve “intergenerational equity.” The definition of intergenerational equity that the SBOE has generally
259: followed is the maintenance of purchasing power to ensure that endowment spending keeps pace with inflation, with the ultimate
259: goal being to ensure that current and future generations are given equal levels of purchasing power in real terms. In making this
259: determination, the SBOE takes into account various considerations, and relies upon PSF Corporation and TEA staff and external
259: investment consultants, which undertake analysis for long-term projection periods that includes certain assumptions. Among the
259:                                                                  D-3
259: 
260: assumptions used in the analysis are a projected rate of growth of student enrollment State-wide, the projected contributions and
260: expenses of the Fund, projected returns in the capital markets and a projected inflation rate.
260: The Texas Constitution also provides authority to the GLO or another entity (described in statute as the SLB or the PSF Corporation)
260: that has responsibility for the management of revenues derived from land or other properties of the PSF to determine whether to
260: transfer an amount each year to the ASF from the revenue derived during the current year from such land or properties. The Texas
260: Constitution limits the maximum transfer to the ASF to $600 million in each year from the revenue derived during that year from
260: the PSF from the GLO, the SBOE or another entity to the extent such entity has the responsibility for the management of revenues
260: derived from such land or other properties. Any amount transferred to the ASF pursuant to this constitutional provision is excluded
260: from the 6% Distribution Rate limitation applicable to SBOE transfers.

260: PSF Corporation Strategic Asset Allocation
260: The PSFC Board sets the asset allocation policy for the Fund, including determining the available asset classes for investment and
260: approving target percentages and ranges for allocation to each asset class, with the goal of delivering a long-term risk adjusted
260: return through all economic and market environments. The IPS includes a combined asset allocation for all Fund assets and allows
260: for the use of derivatives and other leverage. The IPS provides that the Fund’s investment objectives are as follows:
260:            Generate continuous distributions for the benefit of public schools in Texas;
260:            Maintain purchasing power, after spending, inflation, and student population growth, in order to maintain
260:             intergenerational equity with respect to distributions;
260:            Provide a maximum level of return consistent with prudent risk levels, while maintaining sufficient liquidity needed to
260:             support distributions and BGP obligations; and
260:            Strive to maintain a AAA credit rating, as assigned by a Nationally Recognized Securities Rating Organization.
