263: The School District Bond Guarantee Program
263: The School District Bond Guarantee Program requires an application be made by a school district to the Education Commissioner
263: for a guarantee of its bonds. If the conditions for the School District Bond Guarantee Program are satisfied, the guarantee becomes
263: effective upon approval of the bonds by the Attorney General and remains in effect until the guaranteed bonds are paid or defeased,
263: by a refunding or otherwise.
263: In the event of default, holders of guaranteed school district bonds will receive all payments as and when may become due from
263: the corpus of the PSF. Following a determination that a school district will be or is unable to pay maturing or matured principal or
263: interest on any guaranteed bond, the Act requires the school district to notify the Education Commissioner not later than the fifth
263: day before the stated maturity date of such bond or interest payment. Immediately following receipt of such notice, the Education
263: Commissioner must cause to be transferred from the appropriate account in the PSF to the Paying Agent/Registrar an amount
263: necessary to pay the maturing or matured principal and interest, as applicable. Upon receipt of funds for payment of such principal
263: or interest, the Paying Agent/Registrar must pay the amount due and forward the canceled bond or evidence of payment of the
263: interest to the State Comptroller of Public Accounts (the “Comptroller”). The Education Commissioner will instruct the
263: Comptroller to withhold the amount paid, plus interest, from the first State money payable to the school district. The amount
263: withheld pursuant to this funding “intercept” feature will be deposited to the credit of the PSF. The Comptroller must hold such
263: canceled bond or evidence of payment of the interest on behalf of the PSF. Following full reimbursement of such payment by the
263: school district to the PSF with interest, the Comptroller will cancel the bond or evidence of payment of the interest and forward it
263: to the school district. The Act permits the Education Commissioner to order a school district to set a tax rate sufficient to reimburse
263: the PSF for any payments made with respect to guaranteed bonds, and also sufficient to pay future payments on guaranteed bonds,
263: and provides certain enforcement mechanisms to the Education Commissioner, including the appointment of a board of managers
263: or annexation of a defaulting school district to another school district.
263:                                                                  D-7
263: 
264: If a school district fails to pay principal or interest on a bond as it is stated to mature, other amounts not due and payable are not
264: accelerated and do not become due and payable by virtue of the district’s default. The School District Bond Guarantee Program
264: does not apply to the payment of principal and interest upon redemption of bonds, except upon mandatory sinking fund redemption,
264: and does not apply to the obligation, if any, of a school district to pay a redemption premium on its guaranteed bonds. The guarantee
264: applies to all matured interest on guaranteed school district bonds, whether the bonds were issued with a fixed or variable interest
264: rate and whether the interest rate changes as a result of an interest reset provision or other bond order provision requiring an interest
264: rate change. The guarantee does not extend to any obligation of a school district under any agreement with a third party relating to
264: guaranteed bonds that is defined or described in State law as a “bond enhancement agreement” or a “credit agreement,” unless the
264: right to payment of such third party is directly as a result of such third party being a bondholder.
264: In the event that two or more payments are made from the PSF on behalf of a district, the Education Commissioner shall request
264: the Attorney General to institute legal action to compel the district and its officers, agents and employees to comply with the duties
264: required of them by law in respect to the payment of guaranteed bonds.
264: Generally, the regulations that govern the School District Bond Guarantee Program (the “SDBGP Rules”) limit guarantees to
264: certain types of notes and bonds, including, with respect to refunding bonds issued by school districts, a requirement that the bonds
264: produce debt service savings. The SDBGP Rules include certain accreditation criteria for districts applying for a guarantee of their
264: bonds, and limit guarantees to districts that have less than the amount of annual debt service per average daily attendance that
264: represents the 90th percentile of annual debt service per average daily attendance for all school districts, but such limitation will
264: not apply to school districts that have enrollment growth of at least 25% over the previous five school years. The SDBGP Rules
264: are codified in the Texas Administrative Code at 19 TAC section 33.6 and are available at https://tea.texas.gov/finance-and-
264: grants/state-funding/facilities-funding-and-standards/bond-guarantee-program.
264: The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program
264: The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program became effective March 3, 2014. The SBOE published final regulations in the Texas
264: Register that provide for the administration of the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program (the “CDBGP Rules”). The CDBGP
264: Rules are codified at 19 TAC section 33.7 and are available at https://tea.texas.gov/finance-and-grants/state-funding/facilities-
264: funding-and-standards/bond-guarantee-program.
264: The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program has been authorized through the enactment of amendments to the Act, which provide
264: that a charter holder may make application to the Education Commissioner for designation as a “charter district” and for a guarantee
264: by the PSF under the Act of bonds issued on behalf of a charter district by a non-profit corporation. If the conditions for the Charter
264: District Bond Guarantee Program are satisfied, the guarantee becomes effective upon approval of the bonds by the Attorney General
264: and remains in effect until the guaranteed bonds are paid or defeased, by a refunding or otherwise.
264: Pursuant to the CDBGP Rules, the Education Commissioner annually determines the ratio of charter district students to total public
264: school students, for the 2026 fiscal year, the ratio is 8.17%. At February 23, 2026, there were 182 active open-enrollment charter
264: schools in the State and there were 1,027 charter school campuses authorized under such charters, though as of such date, 41 of
264: such campuses are not currently serving students for various reasons; therefore, there are 986 charter school campuses actively
264: serving students in Texas. Section 12.101, Texas Education Code, limits the number of charters that the Education Commissioner
264: may grant to a total number of 305 charters. While legislation limits the number of charters that may be granted, it does not limit
264: the number of campuses that may operate under a particular charter. For information regarding the capacity of the Guarantee
264: Program, see “Capacity Limits for the Guarantee Program.” The Act provides that the Education Commissioner may not approve
264: the guarantee of refunding or refinanced bonds under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program in a total amount that exceeds
264: one-half of the total amount available for the guarantee of charter district bonds under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program.
264: In accordance with the Act, the Education Commissioner may not approve charter district bonds for guarantee if such guarantees
264: will result in lower bond ratings for public school district bonds that are guaranteed under the School District Bond Guarantee
264: Program. To be eligible for a guarantee, the Act provides that a charter district’s bonds must be approved by the Attorney General,
264: have an unenhanced investment grade rating from a nationally recognized investment rating firm, and satisfy a limited investigation
264: conducted by the TEA.
264: The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program does not apply to the payment of principal and interest upon redemption of bonds,
264: except upon mandatory sinking fund redemption, and does not apply to the obligation, if any, of a charter district to pay a
264: redemption premium on its guaranteed bonds. The guarantee applies to all matured interest on guaranteed charter district bonds,
264: whether the bonds were issued with a fixed or variable interest rate and whether the interest rate changes as a result of an interest
264: reset provision or other bond resolution provision requiring an interest rate change. The guarantee does not extend to any obligation
264: of a charter district under any agreement with a third party relating to guaranteed bonds that is defined or described in State law as
264: a “bond enhancement agreement” or a “credit agreement,” unless the right to payment of such third party is directly as a result of
264: such third party being a bondholder.
264:                                                                   D-8
264: 
265: In the event of default, holders of guaranteed charter district bonds will receive all payments as and when they become due from
265: the corpus of the PSF. Following a determination that a charter district will be or is unable to pay maturing or matured principal or
265: interest on any guaranteed bond, the Act requires a charter district to notify the Education Commissioner not later than the fifth
265: day before the stated maturity date of such bond or interest payment and provides that immediately following receipt of notice that
265: a charter district will be or is unable to pay maturing or matured principal or interest on a guaranteed bond, the Education
265: Commissioner is required to instruct the Comptroller to transfer from the Charter District Reserve Fund to the district's paying
265: agent an amount necessary to pay the maturing or matured principal or interest, as applicable. If money in the Charter District
265: Reserve Fund is insufficient to pay the amount due on a bond for which a notice of default has been received, the Education
265: Commissioner is required to instruct the Comptroller to transfer from the PSF to the district’s paying agent the amount necessary
265: to pay the balance of the unpaid maturing or matured principal or interest, as applicable. If a total of two or more payments are
265: made under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program on charter district bonds and the Education Commissioner determines
265: that the charter district is acting in bad faith under the program, the Education Commissioner may request the Attorney General to
265: institute appropriate legal action to compel the charter district and its officers, agents, and employees to comply with the duties
265: required of them by law in regard to the guaranteed bonds. As is the case with the School District Bond Guarantee Program, the
265: Act provides a funding “intercept” feature that obligates the Education Commissioner to instruct the Comptroller to withhold the
265: amount paid with respect to the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program, plus interest, from the first State money payable to a
265: charter district that fails to make a guaranteed payment on its bonds. The amount withheld will be deposited, first, to the credit of
265: the PSF, and then to restore any amount drawn from the Charter District Reserve Fund as a result of the non-payment.
265: The CDBGP Rules provide that the PSF may be used to guarantee bonds issued for the acquisition, construction, repair, or
265: renovation of an educational facility for an open-enrollment charter holder and equipping real property of an open-enrollment
265: charter school and/or to refinance promissory notes executed by an open-enrollment charter school, each in an amount in excess of
265: $500,000 the proceeds of which loans were used for a purpose described above (so-called new money bonds) or for refinancing
265: bonds previously issued for the charter school that were approved by the Attorney General (so-called refunding bonds). Refunding
265: bonds may not be guaranteed under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program if they do not result in a present value savings to
265: the charter holder.
265: The CDBGP Rules provide that an open-enrollment charter holder applying for charter district designation and a guarantee of its
265: bonds under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program satisfy various provisions of the regulations, including the following: It
265: must (i) have operated at least one open-enrollment charter school with enrolled students in the State for at least three years; (ii)
265: agree that the bonded indebtedness for which the guarantee is sought will be undertaken as an obligation of all entities under
265: common control of the open-enrollment charter holder, and that all such entities will be liable for the obligation if the open-
265: enrollment charter holder defaults on the bonded indebtedness, provided, however, that an entity that does not operate a charter
265: school in Texas is subject to this provision only to the extent it has received state funds from the open-enrollment charter holder;
265: (iii) have had completed for the past three years an audit for each such year that included unqualified or unmodified audit opinions;
265: and (iv) have received an investment grade credit rating within the last year. Upon receipt of an application for guarantee under the
265: Charter District Bond Guarantee Program, the Education Commissioner is required to conduct an investigation into the financial
265: status of the applicant charter district and of the accreditation status of all open-enrollment charter schools operated under the
265: charter, within the scope set forth in the CDBGP Rules. Such financial investigation must establish that an applying charter district
265: has a historical debt service coverage ratio, based on annual debt service, of at least 1.1 for the most recently completed fiscal year,
265: and a projected debt service coverage ratio, based on projected revenues and expenses and maximum annual debt service, of at
265: least 1.2. The failure of an open-enrollment charter holder to comply with the Act or the applicable regulations, including by making
265: any material misrepresentations in the charter holder’s application for charter district designation or guarantee under the Charter
265: District Bond Guarantee Program, constitutes a material violation of the open-enrollment charter holder’s charter.
265: From time to time, TEA has limited new guarantees under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program to conform to capacity
265: limits specified by the Act. The Charter District Bond Guarantee Program Capacity (the “CDBGP Capacity”) is made available
265: from the capacity of the Guarantee Program but is not reserved exclusively for the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program. See
265: “Capacity Limits for the Guarantee Program.” Other factors that could increase the CDBGP Capacity include Fund investment
265: performance, future increases in the Guarantee Program multiplier, changes in State law that govern the calculation of the CDBGP
265: Capacity, as described below, changes in State or federal law or regulations related to the Guarantee Program limit, growth in the
265: relative percentage of students enrolled in open-enrollment charter schools to the total State scholastic census, legislative and
265: administrative changes in funding for charter districts, changes in level of school district or charter district participation in the
265: Guarantee Program, or a combination of such circumstances.
265: Capacity Limits for the Guarantee Program
265: The capacity of the Fund to guarantee bonds under the Guarantee Program is limited to the lesser of that imposed by State law (the
265: “State Capacity Limit”) and that imposed by regulations and a notice issued by the IRS (the “IRS Limit”, with the limit in effect at
265: any given time being the “Capacity Limit”). From 2005 through 2009, the Guarantee Program twice reached capacity under the
265: IRS Limit, and in each instance the Guarantee Program was closed to new bond guarantee applications until relief was obtained
265: from the IRS. The most recent closure of the Guarantee Program commenced in March 2009 and the Guarantee Program reopened
265: in February 2010 after the IRS updated regulations relating to the PSF and similar funds.
265:                                                                  D-9
265: 
266: Prior to 2007, various legislation was enacted modifying the calculation of the State Capacity limit; however, in 2007, Senate Bill
266: 389 (“SB 389”) was enacted, providing for increases in the capacity of the Guarantee Program, and specifically providing that the
266: SBOE may by rule increase the capacity of the Guarantee Program from two and one-half times the cost value of the PSF to an
266: amount not to exceed five times the cost value of the PSF, provided that the increased limit does not violate federal law and
266: regulations and does not prevent bonds guaranteed by the Guarantee Program from receiving the highest available credit rating, as
266: determined by the SBOE. SB 389 further provided that the SBOE shall at least annually consider whether to change the capacity
266: of the Guarantee Program. Additionally, on May 21, 2010, the SBOE modified the SDBGP Rules, and increased the State Capacity
266: Limit to an amount equal to three times the cost value of the PSF. Such modified regulations, including the revised capacity rule,
266: became effective on July 1, 2010. The SDBGP Rules provide that the Education Commissioner will estimate the available capacity
266: of the PSF each month and may increase or reduce the State Capacity Limit multiplier to prudently manage fund capacity and
266: maintain the AAA credit rating of the Guarantee Program but also provide that any changes to the multiplier made by the Education
266: Commissioner are to be ratified or rejected by the SBOE at the next meeting following the change. See “Valuation of the PSF and
266: Guaranteed Bonds” below.
266: Since September 2015, the SBOE has periodically voted to change the capacity multiplier as shown in the following table.
266:                       Changes in SBOE-determined multiplier for State Capacity Limit
266:                       Date                                              Multiplier
266:                       Prior to May 2010                                 2.50
266:                       May 2010                                          3.00
266:                       September 2015                                    3.25
266:                       February 2017                                     3.50
266:                       September 2017                                    3.75
266:                       February 2018 (current)                           3.50
266: Since December 16, 2009, the IRS Limit was a static limit set at 500% of the total cost value of the assets held by the PSF as of
266: December 16, 2009; however, on May 10, 2023, the IRS released Notice 2023-39 (the “IRS Notice”), stating that the IRS would
266: issue regulations amending the existing regulations to amend the calculation of the IRS limit to 500% of the total cost value of
266: assets held by the PSF as of the date of sale of new bonds, effective as of May 10, 2023.
266: The IRS Notice changed the IRS Limit from a static limit to a dynamic limit for the Guarantee Program based upon the cost value
266: of Fund assets, multiplied by five. As of December 31, 2025 the cost value of the Guarantee Program was $51,913,224,643
266: (unaudited), thereby producing an IRS Limit of $259,566,123,215 in principal amount of guaranteed bonds outstanding.
266: As of December 31, 2025, the estimated State Capacity Limit is $181,696,286,251, which is lower than the IRS Limit, making the
266: State Capacity Limit the current Capacity Limit for the Fund.
266: Since July 1991, when the SBOE amended the Guarantee Program Rules to broaden the range of bonds that are eligible for
266: guarantee under the Guarantee Program to encompass most Texas school district bonds, the principal amount of bonds guaranteed
266: under the Guarantee Program has increased sharply. In addition, in recent years a number of factors have caused an increase in the
266: amount of bonds issued by school districts in the State. See the table “Permanent School Fund Guaranteed Bonds” below. Effective
266: March 1, 2023, the Act provides that the SBOE may establish a percentage of the Capacity Limit to be reserved from use in
266: guaranteeing bonds (the “Capacity Reserve”). The SDBGP Rules provide for a maximum Capacity Reserve for the overall
266: Guarantee Program of 5% and provide that the amount of the Capacity Reserve may be increased or decreased by a majority vote
266: of the SBOE based on changes in the cost value, asset allocation, and risk in the portfolio, or may be increased or decreased by the
266: Education Commissioner as necessary to prudently manage fund capacity and preserve the AAA credit rating of the Guarantee
266: Program (subject to ratification or rejection by the SBOE at the next meeting for which an item can be posted). The CDBGP Rules
266: provide for an additional reserve of CDBGP Capacity determined by calculating an equal percentage as established by the SBOE
266: for the Capacity Reserve, applied to the CDBGP Capacity. Effective March 1, 2023, the Capacity Reserve is 0.25%. The Capacity
266: Reserve is noted in the monthly updates with respect to the capacity of the Guarantee Program on the PSF Corporation’s web site
266: at https://texaspsf.org/monthly-disclosures/, which are also filed with the MSRB.
266: Based upon historical performance of the Fund, the legal restrictions relating to the amount of bonds that may be guaranteed has
266: generally resulted in a lower ratio of guaranteed bonds to available assets as compared to many other types of credit enhancements
266: that may be available for Texas school district bonds and charter district bonds. However, the ratio of Fund assets to guaranteed
266: bonds and the growth of the Fund in general could be adversely affected by a number of factors, including Fund investment
266: performance, investment objectives of the Fund, an increase in bond issues by school districts in the State or legal restrictions on
266: the Fund, changes in State laws that implement funding decisions for school districts and charter districts, which could adversely
266: affect the credit quality of those districts, the implementation of the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program, or significant
266: changes in distributions to the ASF. The issuance of the IRS Notice and the Final IRS Regulations resulted in a substantial increase
266: in the amount of bonds guaranteed under the Guarantee Program.
266: No representation is made as to how the capacity will remain available, and the capacity of the Guarantee Program is subject to
266: change due to a number of factors, including changes in bond issuance volume throughout the State and some bonds receiving

267: guarantee approvals may not close. If the amount of guaranteed bonds approaches the State Capacity Limit, the SBOE or Education
267: Commissioner may increase the State Capacity Limit multiplier as discussed above.
267: 2017 Legislative Changes to the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program
267: The CDBGP Capacity is established by the Act. During the 85th Texas Legislature, which concluded on May 29, 2017, Senate Bill
267: 1480 (“SB 1480”) was enacted. SB 1480 amended the Act to modify how the CDBGP Capacity is established effective as of
267: September 1, 2017, and made other substantive changes to the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program. Prior to the enactment of
267: SB 1480, the CDBGP Capacity was calculated as the Capacity Limit less the amount of outstanding bond guarantees under the
267: Guarantee Program multiplied by the percentage of charter district scholastic population relative to the total public school scholastic
267: population. SB 1480 amended the CDBGP Capacity calculation so that the Capacity Limit is multiplied by the percentage of charter
267: district scholastic population relative to the total public school scholastic population prior to the subtraction of the outstanding bond
267: guarantees, thereby increasing the CDBGP Capacity.
267: The percentage of the charter district scholastic population to the overall public school scholastic population has grown from 3.53%
267: in September 2012 to 7.86% in December 2025. TEA is unable to predict how the ratio of charter district students to the total State
267: scholastic population will change over time.
267: In addition to modifying the manner of determining the CDBGP Capacity, SB 1480 provided that the Education Commissioner’s
267: investigation of a charter district application for guarantee may include an evaluation of whether the charter district bond security
267: documents provide a security interest in real property pledged as collateral for the bond and the repayment obligation under the
267: proposed guarantee. The Education Commissioner may decline to approve the application if the Education Commissioner
267: determines that sufficient security is not provided. The Act and the CDBGP Rules also require the Education Commissioner to
267: make an investigation of the accreditation status and financial status for a charter district applying for a bond guarantee.
267: Since the initial authorization of the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program, the Act has established a bond guarantee reserve
267: fund in the State treasury (the “Charter District Reserve Fund”). Formerly, the Act provided that each charter district that has a
267: bond guaranteed must annually remit to the Education Commissioner, for deposit in the Charter District Reserve Fund, an amount
267: equal to 10% of the savings to the charter district that is a result of the lower interest rate on its bonds due to the guarantee by the
267: PSF. SB 1480 modified the Act insofar as it pertains to the Charter District Reserve Fund. Effective September 1, 2017, the Act
267: provides that a charter district that has a bond guaranteed must remit to the Education Commissioner, for deposit in the Charter
267: District Reserve Fund, an amount equal to 20% of the savings to the charter district that is a result of the lower interest rate on the
267: bond due to the guarantee by the PSF. The amount due shall be paid on receipt by the charter district of the bond proceeds. However,
267: the deposit requirement will not apply if the balance of the Charter District Reserve Fund is at least equal to 3.00% of the total
267: amount of outstanding guaranteed bonds issued by charter districts. At December 31, 2025, the Charter District Reserve Fund
267: contained $153,914,605, which represented approximately 2.61% of the guaranteed charter district bonds. The Reserve Fund is
267: held and invested as a non-commingled fund under the administration of the PSF Corporation staff.
267: Charter District Risk Factors
267: Open-enrollment charter schools in the State may not charge tuition and, unlike school districts, charter districts have no taxing
267: power. Funding for charter district operations is largely from amounts appropriated by the Legislature. Additionally, the amount of
267: State payments a charter district receives is based on a variety of factors, including the enrollment at the schools operated by a
267: charter district, and may be affected by the State’s economic performance and other budgetary considerations and various political
267: considerations.
267: Other than credit support for charter district bonds that is provided to qualifying charter districts by the Charter District Bond
267: Guarantee Program, State funding for charter district facilities construction is limited to a program established by the Legislature
267: in 2017, which provides $60 million per year for eligible charter districts with an acceptable performance rating for a variety of
267: funding purposes, including for lease or purchase payments for instructional facilities. Since State funding for charter facilities is
267: limited, charter schools generally issue revenue bonds to fund facility construction and acquisition, or fund facilities from cash
267: flows of the school. Some charter districts have issued non-guaranteed debt in addition to debt guaranteed under the Charter District
267: Bond Guarantee Program, and such non-guaranteed debt is likely to be secured by a deed of trust covering all or part of the charter
267: district’s facilities. In March 2017, the TEA began requiring charter districts to provide the TEA with a lien against charter district
267: property as a condition to receiving a guarantee under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program. However, charter district
267: bonds issued and guaranteed under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program prior to the implementation of the new
267: requirement did not have the benefit of a security interest in real property, although other existing debts of such charter districts
267: that are not guaranteed under the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program may be secured by real property that could be foreclosed
267: on in the event of a bond default.
267: As a general rule, the operation of a charter school involves fewer State requirements and regulations for charter holders as
267: compared to other public schools, but the maintenance of a State-granted charter is dependent upon on-going compliance with State
267: law and regulations, which are monitored by TEA. TEA has a broad range of enforcement and remedial actions that it can take as
267: corrective measures, and such actions may include the loss of the State charter, the appointment of a new board of directors to
267:                                                                  D-11
267: 
268: govern a charter district, the assignment of operations to another charter operator, or, as a last resort, the dissolution of an open-
268: enrollment charter school. Charter holders are governed by a private board of directors, as compared to the elected boards of trustees
268: that govern school districts.
268: As described above, the Act includes a funding “intercept” function that applies to both the School District Bond Guarantee
268: Program and the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program. However, school districts are viewed as the “educator of last resort”
268: for students residing in the geographical territory of the district, which makes it unlikely that State funding for those school districts
268: would be discontinued, although the TEA can require the dissolution and merger into another school district if necessary to ensure
268: sound education and financial management of a school district. That is not the case with a charter district, however, and open-
268: enrollment charter schools in the State have been dissolved by TEA from time to time. If a charter district that has bonds outstanding
268: that are guaranteed by the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program should be dissolved, debt service on guaranteed bonds of the
268: district would continue to be paid to bondholders in accordance with the Charter District Bond Guarantee Program, but there would
268: be no funding available for reimbursement of the PSF by the Comptroller for such payments. As described under “The Charter
268: District Bond Guarantee Program,” the Act established the Charter District Reserve Fund, to serve as a reimbursement resource for
268: the PSF.
268: Ratings of Bonds Guaranteed Under the Guarantee Program
268: Moody’s Ratings, S&P Global Ratings, and Fitch Ratings, Inc. rate bonds guaranteed by the PSF “Aaa,” “AAA” and “AAA,”
268: respectively. Not all districts apply for multiple ratings on their bonds, however. See the applicable rating section within the offering
268: document to which this is attached for information regarding a district’s underlying rating and the enhanced rating applied to a
268: given series of bonds.

269: Discussion and Analysis Pertaining to Fiscal Year Ended August 31, 2025
269: The following discussion is derived from the Annual Report for the year ended August 31, 2025, including the Message from the
269: Chief Executive Officer of the Fund, the Management’s Discussion and Analysis, and other schedules contained therein. Reference
269: is made to the Annual Report, as filed with the MSRB, for the complete Message and MD&A. Investment assets managed by the
269: PSF Corporation are referred to throughout this MD&A as the PSF(CORP). The Fund’s non-financial real assets are managed by
269: the SLB and these assets are referred to throughout as the PSF(SLB) assets.
269: At the end of fiscal year 2025, the PSF(CORP) net position was $60.6 billion. During the year, the PSF(CORP) continued updating
269: and implementing the long-term strategic asset allocation, diversifying the investment mix to strengthen the Fund. The asset
269: allocation aims to pursue the objectives of the Fund at an acceptable risk level. The PSF(CORP) is invested in global markets and
269: liquid and illiquid assets experience volatility commensurate with the related indices. The PSF(CORP) is broadly diversified and
269: benefits from the cost structure of its investment program. Changes continue to be researched, crafted, and implemented to make
269: the cost structure more effective and efficient. The PSF(CORP) annual rates of return for the one-year, five-year, and ten-year
269: periods ending August 31, 2025, net of fees, were 8.20%, 7.95%, and 7.40%, respectively (total return takes into consideration the
269: change in the market value of the Fund during the year as well as the interest and dividend income generated by the Fund’s
269: investments). See “Comparative Investment Schedule - PSF(CORP)” for the PSF(CORP) holdings as of August 31, 2025.
269: Effective February 1, 2024, Texas PSF transitioned into a new strategic asset allocation. The new allocation of the PSF Corporation
269: updated the strategic asset allocation among public equities, fixed income, and alternative assets, as discussed herein. Alternative
269: assets now include private credit 1, absolute return, private equity, real estate, natural resources, and infrastructure. For a description

271: Other Events and Disclosures
271: State ethics laws govern the ethics and disclosure requirements for financial advisors and other service providers who advise certain
271: State governmental entities, including the PSF. The SBOE code of ethics provides ethical standards for SBOE members, the
271: Education Commissioner, TEA staff, and persons who provide services to the SBOE relating to the Fund. The PSF Corporation
271: developed its own ethics policy that provides basic ethical principles, guidelines, and standards of conduct relating to the
271: management and investment of the Fund in accordance with the requirements of §43.058 of the Texas Education Code, as amended.
271: The SBOE code of ethics is codified in the Texas Administrative Code at 19 TAC sections 33.4 et seq. and is available on the TEA
271: web site at https://tea.texas.gov/sites/default/files/ch033a.pdf. The PSF Corporation’s ethics policy is posted to the PSF
271: Corporation’s website at texaspsf.org.
271: In addition, the SLB and GLO have established processes and controls over the administration of real estate transactions and are
271: subject to provisions of the Texas Natural Resources Code and internal procedures in administering real estate transactions for
271: Fund assets it manages.
271: As of August 31, 2025, certain lawsuits were pending against the State and/or the GLO, which challenge the Fund’s title to certain
271: real property and/or past or future mineral income from that property, and other litigation arising in the normal course of the
271: investment activities of the PSF. Reference is made to the Annual Report, when filed, for a description of such lawsuits that are
271: pending, which may represent contingent liabilities of the Fund.
271: PSF Continuing Disclosure Undertaking
271: As of March 1, 2023, the TEA’s undertaking pursuant to Rule 15c2-12 (the “TEA Undertaking”) pertaining to the PSF and the
271: Guarantee Program, is codified at 19 TAC 33.8, which relates to the Guarantee Program and is available at available at
271: https://tea.texas.gov/sites/default/files/ch033a.pdf.
271: Through the codification of the TEA Undertaking and its commitment to guarantee bonds, the TEA has made the following
271: agreement for the benefit of the issuers, holders, and beneficial owners of guaranteed bonds. The TEA (or its successor with respect
271: to the management of the Guarantee Program) is required to observe the agreement for so long as it remains an “obligated person,”
271: within the meaning of Rule 15c2-12, with respect to guaranteed bonds. Nothing in the TEA Undertaking obligates the TEA to make
271:                                                                D-15
271: 
272: any filings or disclosures with respect to guaranteed bonds, as the obligations of the TEA under the TEA Undertaking pertain solely
272: to the Guarantee Program. The issuer or an “obligated person” of the guaranteed bonds has assumed the applicable obligation under
272: Rule 15c2-12 to make all disclosures and filings relating directly to guaranteed bonds, and the TEA takes no responsibility with
272: respect to such undertakings. Under the TEA Undertaking, the TEA is obligated to provide annually certain updated financial
272: information and operating data, and timely notice of specified material events, to the MSRB.
272: The MSRB has established the Electronic Municipal Market Access (“EMMA”) system, and the TEA is required to file its
272: continuing disclosure information using the EMMA system. Investors may access continuing disclosure information filed with the
272: MSRB at www.emma.msrb.org, and the continuing disclosure filings of the TEA with respect to the PSF can be found at
272: https://emma.msrb.org/IssueView/Details/ER355077 or by searching for “Texas Permanent School Fund Bond Guarantee
272: Program” on EMMA.
272: Annual Reports
272: The PSF Corporation, on behalf of the TEA, and the TEA will annually provide certain updated financial information and operating
272: data to the MSRB. The information to be updated includes all quantitative financial information and operating data with respect to
272: the Guarantee Program and the PSF of the general type included in this offering document under the heading “THE PERMANENT
272: SCHOOL FUND GUARANTEE PROGRAM.” The information also includes the Annual Report. The PSF Corporation will update
272: and provide this information within six months after the end of each fiscal year.
272: The TEA and the PSF Corporation may provide updated information in full text or may incorporate by reference certain other
272: publicly-available documents, as permitted by Rule 15c2-12. The updated information includes audited financial statements of, or
272: relating to, the State or the PSF, when and if such audits are commissioned and available. In the event audits are not available by
272: the filing deadline, unaudited financial statements will be provided by such deadline, and audited financial statements will be
272: provided when available. Financial statements of the State will be prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting
272: principles as applied to state governments, as such principles may be changed from time to time, or such other accounting principles
272: as the State Auditor is required to employ from time to time pursuant to State law or regulation. The financial statements of the
272: Fund are required to be prepared to conform to U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles as established by the Governmental
272: Accounting Standards Board.
272: The Fund is composed of two primary segments: the financial assets (PSF(CORP)) managed by PSF Corporation, and the non-
272: financial assets (PSF(SLB)) managed by the SLB. Each of these segments is reported separately und different bases of accounting.
272: The PSF Corporation reports as a special-purpose government engaged in business-type activities and reports to the State of Texas
272: as a discretely presented component unit accounted for on an economic resources measurement focus and the accrual basis of
272: accounting. Measurement focus refers to the definition of the resource flows measured. Under the accrual basis of accounting, all
272: revenues reported are recognized in the period they are earned or when the PSF Corporation has a right to receive them. Expenses
272: are recognized in the period they are incurred, and the subsequent amortization of any deferred outflows. Additionally, costs related
272: to capital assets are capitalized and subsequently depreciated over the useful life of the assets. Both current and long-term assets
272: and liabilities are presented in the statement of net position.
272: The SLB manages the Fund’s non-financial assets (PSF(SLB)), is classified as a governmental permanent fund and accounted for
272: using the current financial resources measurement focus and the modified accrual basis of accounting. Under the modified accrual
272: basis of accounting, amounts are recognized as revenues in the period in which they are available to finance expenditures of the
272: current period and are measurable. Amounts are considered measurable if they can be estimated or otherwise determined.
272: Expenditures are recognized in the period in which the related liability is incurred, if measurable.
272: The State’s current fiscal year end is August 31. Accordingly, the TEA and the PSF Corporation must provide updated information
272: by the last day of February in each year, unless the State changes its fiscal year. If the State changes its fiscal year, the TEA and
272: PSF Corporation will notify the MSRB of the change.

273: The continuing disclosure agreement is made only with respect to the PSF and the Guarantee Program. The issuer of guaranteed

273: Rule 15c2-12 with respect to its obligations arising under Rule 15c2-12 pertaining to financial information and operating data

273: operations of the TEA or the PSF Corporation, but only if (1) the provisions, as so amended, would have permitted an underwriter
273: to purchase or sell guaranteed bonds in the primary offering of such bonds in compliance with Rule 15c2-12, taking into account

274: Compliance with Prior Undertakings
274: Except as stated below, during the last five years, the TEA and the PSF Corporation have not failed to substantially comply with
274: their previous continuing disclosure agreements in accordance with Rule 15c2-12. On April 28, 2022, TEA became aware that it
274: had not timely filed its 2021 Annual Report with EMMA due to an administrative oversight. TEA took corrective action and filed
274: the 2021 Annual Report with EMMA on April 28, 2022, followed by a notice of late filing made with EMMA on April 29, 2022.
274: TEA notes that the 2021 Annual Report was timely filed on the TEA website by the required filing date and that website posting
274: has been incorporated by reference into TEA’s Bond Guarantee Program disclosures that are included in school district and charter
274: district offering documents. On March 31, 2025, the TEA and the PSF Corporation became aware that the 2022 operating data was
274: not timely filed with EMMA due to an administrative oversight. TEA and PSF Corporation took corrective action and filed a notice
274: of late filing with EMMA on April 4, 2025. The annual operating data was previously posted to EMMA on March 31, 2023.
274: SEC Exemptive Relief
274: On February 9, 1996, the TEA received a letter from the Chief Counsel of the SEC that pertains to the availability of the “small
274: issuer exemption” set forth in paragraph (d)(2) of Rule 15c2-12. The letter provides that Texas school districts which offer
274: municipal securities that are guaranteed under the Guarantee Program may undertake to comply with the provisions of paragraph
274: (d)(2) of Rule 15c2-12 if their offerings otherwise qualify for such exemption, notwithstanding the guarantee of the school district
274: securities under the Guarantee Program. Among other requirements established by Rule 15c2-12, a school district offering may
274: qualify for the small issuer exemption if, upon issuance of the proposed series of securities, the school district will have no more
274: than $10 million of outstanding municipal securities.
